item.title: 动捕资产的下游还有绑骨、重定向、渲染：FlashMotion 把「超快长时 3D 动作生成」当成管线问题来做 ｜ FlashMotion: Ultra-Fast Long-Term 3D Motion Generation
item.description:
一句话：论文自己把落点写清了：游戏、XR、数字人、具身仿真，且下游还要过绑骨、重定向与渲染。

要点：

  • 定位很游戏：3D 人体动作生成对游戏开发、XR、数字人与具身仿真都关键，而实用管线在生成之后还有**绑骨、重定向与渲染**
  • 因此「超快 + 长时间跨度 + 不掉质量」不是锦上添花，而是能否进实时交互应用的前置条件
  • 作者指出在严苛推理预算下做高质量长时程动作生成仍很难，并把这一点当作主要矛盾来解决

为什么值得看：动作生成的研究大多只看单段短动作的指标，而工程上真正卡的是「长时程 + 低延迟 + 能过下游管线」。这篇罕见地在摘要里就写明了落地约束，值得按管线需求去读。

中文摘要：3D 人体动作生成在游戏开发、扩展现实（XR）、数字人与具身仿真中都很关键，而实际管线在「生成」之后还要经过绑骨、重定向与渲染等步骤。因此，能否做到超快、支持长时间跨度且不牺牲质量，直接决定它能不能进实时交互应用。这篇指出现有方法在严格推理预算下仍难兼顾长时程与质量，并把「超快长时程生成」作为核心问题来处理。对引擎侧动作系统来说，这类明确承认下游管线的论文，比只比 FID 的动作生成工作更接近可用。

主题：AI Native Engine

来源：arXiv·cs.CV（English）

原文发布：2026-11-11

本期推送：2026-11-13

:
Ultra-Fast Long-Term 3D Motion Generation

Abstract

3D human motion generation plays a crucial role in game development, extended reality (XR), digital humans, and embodied simulation. Beyond motion generation, practical pipelines include rigging, retargeting, and rendering, making ultra-fast long-term 3D motion generation without compromising quality valuable for real-time interactive applications. Despite promising progress, high-quality long-horizon motion generation under tight inference budgets remains challenging, owing to 2 coupled bottlenecks: (1) generative strategies that require many sampling steps for high-quality 3D motion generation and (2) model architectures with substantial per-step computational and memory costs for long sequences. We present FlashMotion, a co-designed framework for high-quality long-horizon 3D motion generation under a strict inference budget, covering text-to-motion, music-to-dance, and speech-to-gesture tasks. To enhance trajectory-level efficiency, we introduce a 3D motion-space MeanFlow formulation with kinematic and dynamic consistency constraints for few-step generation, together with an Adaptive Soft masking mechanism for temporally coherent motion editing. To improve per-step efficiency, we design a lightweight non-autoregressive BiMamba architecture with condition-guided state selection and AdaIN-based condition fusion mechanism, enhancing cross-modal alignment and generalization to longer motion sequences. Extensive experiments demonstrate that FlashMotion achieves overall state-of-the-art performance in both quality and efficiency across text-to-motion, speech-to-gesture, and music-to-dance generation. Code is available at FlashMotion.

Index Terms:

Digital Humans, 3D Motion Generation, Efficient Motion Generation, Long-Horizon Generation. ††aftertitle:

I Introduction

With advances in AI-generated content and cross-modal motion modeling [1, 2], 3D human motion generation has attracted increasing interest for translating text, speech, and music into expressive human motion. This capability supports applications in robot motion generation, extended reality (XR) character animation, and mobile motion interaction (Fig. 7). These applications require responsive and sustained interaction. As a key enabler of such interaction, a broadly applicable 3D motion generation method should satisfy 3 key requirements: (1) Motion Quality: generating physically plausible and semantically expressive motion that aligns with the input conditions; (2) Generation Efficiency: achieving low inference latency and memory consumption to leave sufficient computational resources for other pipeline stages, including rigging, retargeting, and rendering; and (3) Long-Horizon Generation: sustaining high motion fidelity and smooth temporal transitions over extended sequences.

Across text-to-motion, speech-to-gesture, and music-to-dance tasks, 3D human motion generation has advanced along 2 complementary dimensions. (1) Generative Strategy. Representative strategies include direct motion regression [3, 4], adversarial learning [5, 6], autoregressive generation [7, 8], diffusion [9, 10], and flow matching [11, 12], with different trade-offs between generation quality and sampling efficiency. (2) Model Architecture. Temporal backbones range from recurrent networks, including LSTMs [13, 14], to Transformers [7, 4] and Mamba-based models [15, 16], with different capabilities for temporal modeling and conditional integration. However, high-quality long-horizon generation under a strict inference budget remains challenging due to 2 coupled bottlenecks: (1) generative strategies that require many sampling steps for high-quality 3D motion generation and (2) model architectures with substantial per-step computational and memory costs for long sequences. These costs leave limited computational resources for other production stages, such as rigging, retargeting, and rendering, potentially degrading the user experience in interactive applications.

To this end, we present FlashMotion, a co-designed framework for high-quality long-horizon 3D motion generation under a strict inference budget. The framework supports diverse conditional motion generation tasks, including text-to-motion, music-to-dance, and speech-to-gesture. Our key observation is that end-to-end generation efficiency is jointly determined by (1) the number of sampling steps and (2) the computational cost of each step. Optimizing either factor alone limits practical speedups: few-step sampling remains costly with an expensive backbone, while a lightweight architecture still incurs substantial latency when many sampling steps are required. FlashMotion therefore jointly optimizes trajectory-level and per-step efficiency. To improve trajectory-level efficiency, we introduce a 3D motion-space MeanFlow formulation with kinematic and dynamic consistency constraints for few-step generation, along with an Adaptive Soft masking mechanism for temporally coherent motion editing. To improve per-step efficiency, we design a lightweight non-autoregressive architecture that combines a BiMamba-based backbone with condition-guided state selection and AdaIN-based condition fusion. Together, FlashMotion achieves state-of-the-art motion quality across all 3 tasks, generating physically plausible, semantically expressive motion at leading throughput with a compact ∼60M-parameter model. Fig. 1 presents quality–throughput comparisons with representative baselines (top) and conditioned motion examples (bottom). Panels (a)-(c) report results on BABEL, BEAT2, and FineDance, respectively. FPS is measured for 10,000-frame outputs on an RTX 3090 at batch size 1.

Trajectory-level efficiency via generative strategy. To reduce sampling steps without sacrificing motion quality, FlashMotion combines a 3D motion-space MeanFlow formulation with kinematic and dynamic consistency constraints. From a kinematic perspective, coherent 3D human motion requires coordinated joint trajectories and smooth temporal evolution, motivating a generative process that continuously transforms noise into structured motion. Flow Matching provides a natural framework for modeling this transformation through a learned velocity field [17, 18]. However, standard Flow Matching learns instantaneous velocities, whereas few-step sampling requires accurate finite-interval updates, making generation sensitive to numerical integration errors. MeanFlow [19] addresses this limitation by modeling interval-averaged velocity. Nevertheless, directly predicting velocity makes it less straightforward to impose structural constraints on the resulting 3D motion. Since 3D human motion representation is subject to tightly coupled kinematic and dynamic constraints, errors in large-step updates can manifest as temporal jitter, root drift, foot sliding, and implausible articulations. This motivates predicting clean motion explicitly, where motion-specific supervision can be applied directly, while deriving the velocity required for sampling from the prediction. We therefore introduce a 3D motion-space MeanFlow formulation that takes the noisy motion zₜ and the time pair (t,r) as inputs and predicts clean motion ẑ₀. During training, we construct the corresponding intermediate state ẑᵣ by interpolating between zₜ and ẑ₀, and use its displacement from zₜ to parameterize the interval-averaged velocity for MeanFlow training. This formulation also enables direct supervision in 3D motion space: reconstruction and forward-kinematics losses encourage faithful motion recovery and kinematic consistency, while velocity and dynamics losses regularize temporal evolution. At inference, the predicted clean motion is converted into the corresponding interval-averaged velocity for few-step ODE sampling. In addition, FlashMotion provides flexible motion editing to support human-in-the-loop authoring and responsive streaming applications. Specifically, we apply an Adaptive Soft mask during sampling, which gradually relaxes the constraints over time and alleviates the boundary discontinuities caused by hard masks in the few-step setting.

Per-step efficiency via model architecture. We design a lightweight non-autoregressive BiMamba architecture with condition-guided state selection and AdaIN-based condition fusion. BiMamba is well suited to temporally coherent 3D human motion generation because its sequential inductive bias better captures local temporal dependencies than attention-only backbones, while retaining linear-time complexity O(n) compared with the O(n²) cost of Transformers [20]. Its bidirectional design further improves temporal coherence and condition-motion alignment, and the non-autoregressive formulation avoids the latency of sequential decoding while mitigating exposure bias in autoregressive-based methods [21, 8] and boundary artifacts in iterative inpainting-based methods [22, 23]. Condition-guided state selection regulates temporal information flow, while AdaIN modulates motion features through frame-wise scaling and shifting. Shared projections support variable sequence lengths without constructing pairwise cross-attention matrices. Together, these architectural choices reduce per-step computational and memory costs while supporting high-quality long-horizon motion generation.

This work extends our previous work, FlowerDance [12], in 4 aspects: (1) Task Coverage: generalizing the method to conditional 3D human motion generation, including text-to-motion, speech-to-gesture, and music-to-dance; (2) Generative Strategy: reformulating MeanFlow in 3D motion space through explicit clean-motion prediction; (3) Model Architecture: introducing condition-guided state selection and AdaIN-based condition fusion to enhance cross-modal alignment and long-sequence generalization; and (4) Experiments: expanding evaluations across tasks and targeted ablation studies, alongside application demonstrations.

In summary, our main contributions are as follows:

  • •

    We present FlashMotion, a co-designed framework for high-quality long-horizon 3D motion generation under a strict inference budget. By jointly optimizing trajectory-level sampling efficiency and per-step inference efficiency, FlashMotion achieves state-of-the-art (SOTA) performance in both quality and efficiency across text-to-motion, speech-to-gesture, and music-to-dance generation.

  • •

    We propose a few-step 3D motion generation strategy comprising: (1) a 3D motion-space MeanFlow formulation with kinematic and dynamic consistency constraints, and (2) Adaptive Soft masking for coherent motion editing.

  • •

    We design a lightweight non-autoregressive architecture for efficient long-horizon motion generation, comprising: (1) a BiMamba-based backbone, (2) a condition-guided state selection mechanism, and (3) AdaIN-based cross-modal alignment.

    • II Related Work

    II-AFlow Matching Generative Models

    Flow Matching (FM) [17] learns continuous transport from noise to data, with substantial methodological advances [18, 19] and broad generative applications [24, 25], while its adoption in 3D human motion generation remains nascent [26, 27, 12].

    Methodological Advances. FM enables simulation-free training through velocity regression [17]. Rectified Flow [18] promotes straighter transport trajectories through reflow, while optimal-transport conditional flow matching (OT-CFM) [28] uses minibatch transport couplings to simplify learned flows. To reduce sampling cost, Consistency Flow Matching [29] encourages velocity consistency, Flow Map Matching [30] learns mappings between pairs of generation times, and Shortcut Models [31] condition predictions on the desired step size. Complementing these approaches, GMFlow [32] models multimodal velocity distributions with Gaussian mixtures. MeanFlow [19] instead learns interval-averaged velocities, directly targeting finite-interval updates for 1- or few-step generation.

    Applications Across Domains. FM has demonstrated its scalability across diverse generative tasks. In image generation, Stable Diffusion 3 [24] combines rectified flow with large-scale multimodal Transformer training. Video applications include sparsely conditioned video prediction [33], audio-driven portrait animation with FLOAT [34], and multiscale video synthesis with Pyramid Flow Matching [35]. In audio, Voicebox [25] and Audiobox [36] employ FM for speech and audio generation, while Matcha-TTS [37] and VoiceFlow [38] explore efficient text-to-speech synthesis.

    Few studies have explored FM for 3D human motion synthesis, yet ultra-few-step long-horizon generation remains challenging: (1) approximately 50 steps for FlowMotion [11], Match-TTSG [27], and UMF’s prior generation stage [39], and (2) 10 steps for Motion Flow Matching [26], FloodDiffusion [40], and FlowerDance [12].

    II-B3D Motion Generation

    3D human motion generation has made substantial progress across text-to-motion, speech-to-gesture, and music-to-dance tasks. We review existing methods from 2 complementary perspectives: generative strategy, which determines how motion is synthesized, and model architecture, which determines how temporal dependencies and conditioning signals are modeled.

    Generative Strategy. Representative strategies include: (1) Direct Regression, which directly predicts motion from conditioning signals, including Language2Pose [3] for text-to-motion, Gesticulator [41] for speech-to-gesture, and FACT [4] for music-to-dance; (2) Adversarial Learning, which encourages realistic motion through discriminator-based training, including the trimodal gesture model [6] for speech-to-gesture, and Choreography cGAN [42], Dancing to Music [43], and CoheDancers [5] for music-driven dance generation; (3) Autoregressive Generation, which synthesizes motion sequentially, including T2M-GPT [7] for text-to-motion, and Dance Revolution [44], Bailando [21], and MEGA [8] for music-to-dance, as well as CoDancers [45] for group choreography; (4) Diffusion, which models conditional motion distributions through iterative denoising [46], including MDM [9] and MLD [47] for text-to-motion, DiffGesture [10] and PersonaGesture [48] for speech-to-gesture, EDGE [22] and CustomDance [49] for dance generation and editing, and BiTDiff [50] for conducting motion; and (5) Flow Matching, which learns continuous transformations from noise to motion, including Motion Flow Matching [26] and FlowMotion [11] for text-driven motion, the unified speech-gesture synthesis framework [27], and FlowerDance [12] for few-step music-to-dance generation.

    Model Architecture. Representative temporal backbones include: (1) Recurrent Networks, which capture temporal dependencies through sequential hidden-state updates, as exemplified by ERD [13] and the residual RNN [14] for human motion prediction, and the recurrent decoder in Dance Revolution [44] for music-to-dance; (2) Transformers, which use attention for temporal and conditional modeling, including T2M-GPT [7] for text-to-motion, DiffGesture [10] and StreamTalk [51] for speech-to-gesture, and FACT [4] and EDGE [22] for music-to-dance; and (3) Mamba-Based Models, which exploit selective state-space modeling for efficient sequence processing, including Motion Mamba [52] for text-to-motion, MambaTalk [15] and MambaGesture [53] for speech-to-gesture, and FlowerDance [12], TokenDance [16], and the hybrid Mamba-Transformer model MATHDance [54] for music-to-dance.

    However, high-quality long-horizon generation under a strict inference budget remains challenging due to 2 coupled bottlenecks: (1) generative strategies that require many sampling steps for high-quality 3D motion generation and (2) model architectures with substantial per-step computational and memory costs for long sequences. These costs leave limited computational resources for other production stages, such as rigging, retargeting, and rendering, potentially degrading the user experience in interactive applications.

    III Methodology

    III-AOverview

    Since condition encoding, motion retargeting, and rendering also consume the end-to-end latency budget, motion generation must remain highly efficient. For example, interactively creating and revising an extended dance or action sequence requires rapid generation of long, coherent motions so that users can promptly preview and refine the results. Ultra-fast long-term 3D motion generation that preserves physical plausibility, conditional alignment, and motion expressiveness is therefore essential for responsive avatar animation.

    Given a conditioning sequence C=(cᵢ)ᵢ₌₁^N, our objective is to generate a corresponding 3D motion sequence M=(mᵢ)ᵢ₌₁^N, where cᵢ∈ℝ^d_c and mᵢ∈ℝ^dₘ denote the condition and motion features at frame i, respectively. We consider text, speech, and music conditioning, with a separate model trained for each task. (1) Text-to-Motion. For text description qₖ and its frame interval Iₖ, cᵢ=Eₜₑₓₜ(qₖ)∈ℝ⁴⁰⁹⁶ uses UMT5-XXL [55]; mᵢ∈ℝ²⁶³ follows HumanML3D [56] at 20 FPS. (2) Speech-to-Gesture. The condition cᵢ combines frame-aligned 1024-dimensional HuBERT speech features and 300-dimensional text features; mᵢ∈ℝ³³³ comprises local 6D rotations [57] for 55 SMPL-X joints and 3 root-motion components at 30 FPS. (3) Music-to-Dance.cᵢ∈ℝ³⁵ contains frame-aligned Librosa music features [58]; mᵢ∈ℝ¹⁴⁷ comprises 3D root motion (horizontal displacements and height) and 24-joint 6D rotations [57] at 30 FPS.

    To meet this strict inference budget in practice, we co-design FlashMotion across both the generative strategy and model architecture, as summarized in Fig. 2. (1) At the generative-strategy level, we formulate MeanFlow in 3D motion space by directly predicting clean motion and deriving the interval-averaged velocity for few-step sampling, with auxiliary kinematic and dynamic constraints to preserve motion fidelity. (2) At the model-architecture level, we develop a lightweight non-autoregressive BiMamba backbone with condition-guided state selection and AdaIN-based condition fusion mechanism, enhancing cross-modal alignment and generalization to longer motion sequences. (3) To support real-time human-in-the-loop motion authoring and responsive streaming applications under few-step sampling, we further introduce an Adaptive Soft masking strategy that enables coherent motion editing without additional training.

    III-BGenerative Strategy

    MeanFlow. From a kinematic perspective, 3D human motion consists of continuous trajectories of root translation and joint rotations, coupled through skeletal structure and temporal dependencies [59, 60]. Generating coherent motion therefore requires jointly modeling spatial coordination and temporal evolution, motivating continuous refinement of the entire sequence from unstructured noise toward a condition-consistent trajectory. Flow Matching (FM) [17] learns a velocity field for an ordinary differential equation (ODE) transporting Gaussian noise ε∼ℕ(0,I) to motion x∼p_\rmdata. Training uses the linear conditional path zₜ=FP(x,t), with time t∼U(0,1):

    FP(x,t)=(1-t)x+tε(1)

    The conditional path velocity is v_\rmcond=ε-x. We regress v_θ against this sample-wise target; the optimal regressor estimates the marginal velocity field v(zₜ,t)=𝔼[v_\rmcond|zₜ,t]:

    L_FM=𝔼[∥v_θ(zₜ,t)-v_\rmcond∥²].(2)

    At inference, generation starts from an initial prior sample z₁ and iteratively integrates the learned velocity field v_θ(zₜ,t) until reaching z₀ in the data distribution:

    v_θ(zₜ,t)=dzₜ/dt,(3)
    z₀=z₁+∫₁⁰v_θ(z_τ,τ) dτ.

    Even when conditional flows are designed to be straight, latent trajectories in the high-dimensional space are often highly curved. When using large integration intervals, Flow Matching [17], which models the instantaneous velocity field, cannot accurately capture these curved trajectories, leading to degraded generation quality. Thus, MeanFlow[19] replaces instantaneous velocity v(zₜ,t) with the interval mean velocity u(zₜ,r,t), leading to a training objective aligned with the actual ODE inference procedure:

    u(zₜ,r,t)=1/t-r∫ᵣᵗv(z_τ,τ) dτ,

    		(4)

    where (r,t) are 2 timesteps randomly sampled from a uniform distribution U(0,1) with the constraint t>r. Differentiating Eq. 4 with respect to t yields the MeanFlow identity:

    u(zₜ,r,t)=v(zₜ,t)-(t-r)d/dtu(zₜ,r,t).

    		(5)

    A velocity estimator u_θ is trained to satisfy the MeanFlow identity:

    L_MF=𝔼[∥u_θ(zₜ,r,t)-sg(u_tgt)∥₂²],(6)
    where u_tgt=v_\rmcond-(t-r)Dₜu_θ,
    Dₜu_θ=∂_zu_θ v_\rmcond+∂ₜu_θ.

    where sg(·) denotes stop-gradient. Notably, this reduces to the FM loss when r=t. During inference, MeanFlow uses a constant interval-averaged velocity for each update. The general update and its equivalent integral form over the full interval are:

    zᵣ=zₜ-(t-r)u(zₜ,r,t),(7)

    Training. Although MeanFlow has shown promising results in image generation [19], video rendering [61], and audio synthesis [62], directly applying it to few-step 3D motion generation is non-trivial. A key reason is that these modalities often exhibit explicit local continuity in their native representations, such as spatially neighboring pixels, adjacent video frames, or temporally continuous waveforms, which provides a relatively direct structure for learning smooth generative fields. In contrast, SMPL-based 3D motion is represented as a sequence of pose parameters whose temporal continuity is explicit across frames, while the intra-frame dependencies among joints are only implicitly encoded by the human kinematic chain. Under large integration intervals, small errors in the predicted velocity field can therefore accumulate over time and disrupt these latent kinematic constraints, leading to temporal jitter, global drift, foot sliding, and implausible articulations. Moreover, the vanilla MeanFlow objective only constrains the averaged velocity field, without explicitly regularizing the recovered motion in kinematic or physical spaces.

    To enable direct motion-level supervision, FlashMotion predicts the clean-motion estimate ẑ₀ from the current state zₜ, frame-aligned conditioning sequence C, and time interval (r,t). The interval-averaged velocity is then derived as:

    u_θ(zₜ,r,t;C)=(zₜ-ẑ₀)/(t).

    		(8)

    We optimize the induced velocity using the MeanFlow objective in Eq. (6), with JVP-based differentiation, t² time weighting, and adaptive loss weighting.

    Empirically, training with L_MF alone still remains unstable and fails to converge in our SMPL-based experiments, as corroborated by the results in Sec. IV-E. We therefore add reconstruction supervision to anchor the clean-motion estimate to ground truth:

    L_rec=𝔼[∥ẑ₀-z₀∥₂²].

    		(9)

    To improve kinematic consistency, we match the recovered 3D joint positions to ground truth, encouraging spatially coordinated poses:

    Lₖᵢₙ=𝔼[∥P̂-P∥₂²].

    		(10)

    Here, P̂=K(ẑ₀) and P=K(z₀), where K recovers joint positions from 3D rotation representations.

    To improve temporal dynamics, we match joint velocities and accelerations to ground truth, encouraging temporally coherent motion evolution:

    L_dyn=𝔼[∥ΔP̂-ΔP∥₂²+β∥Δ²P̂-Δ²P∥₂²].

    		(11)

    Here, Δ denotes frame-wise finite differences, and β balances velocity and acceleration supervision.

    Overall, the shared training objective is:

    L=λ_mfL_MF+λ_recL_rec+λₖᵢₙLₖᵢₙ+λ_dynL_dyn.

    		(12)

    Inference. Starting from Gaussian noise ε, we progressively generate motion over uniformly spaced time intervals. At each step, we predict the clean motion ẑ₀ and obtain zᵣ by linearly interpolating between ẑ₀ and the current noisy state zₜ. This update is equivalent to Eq. 7, without explicit velocity computation or additional noise injection.

    Motion Editing. Extending the inpainting idea in diffusion-based motion generation [23, 22], FlashMotion supports training-free constraint-based editing with multiple sampling steps; 1-step editing is not supported. This capability serves 2 complementary uses. (1) Human-in-the-loop motion authoring. Users can fill temporal gaps or modify selected joint trajectories, such as interpolating between dance clips or adjusting hand paths (Fig. 6). (2) Responsive Streaming Applications. Temporal inpainting enables sequential window extension by constraining each new window with the previous window’s tail. This allows FlashMotion to adapt to incoming conditions for conversational avatars or interactive NPCs. With few sampling steps, fixed hard masks may cause dynamic mismatches at constraint boundaries. We therefore apply an Adaptive Soft mask, gradually relaxing the influence of known regions to improve coupling between constrained and unconstrained motions. Given a joint-wise or temporal constraint x^′∈ℝ^N×dₘ with positions indicated by a binary mask M∈{0,1}^N×dₘ at time t, where N is the sequence length and dₘ=263, 333, and 147 for text-to-motion, speech-to-gesture, and music-to-dance, respectively, FlashMotion performs constraint-aware denoising as follows:

    zₜ:=(t·M)⊙FP(x^′,t)+(1-(t·M))⊙zₜ,(13)

    where ⊙ denotes the Hadamard product, and known regions follow the constraint flow.
