I Introduction

With advances in AI-generated content and cross-modal motion modeling [1, 2], 3D human motion generation has attracted increasing interest for translating text, speech, and music into expressive human motion. This capability supports applications in robot motion generation, extended reality (XR) character animation, and mobile motion interaction (Fig. 7). These applications require responsive and sustained interaction. As a key enabler of such interaction, a broadly applicable 3D motion generation method should satisfy 3 key requirements: (1) Motion Quality: generating physically plausible and semantically expressive motion that aligns with the input conditions; (2) Generation Efficiency: achieving low inference latency and memory consumption to leave sufficient computational resources for other pipeline stages, including rigging, retargeting, and rendering; and (3) Long-Horizon Generation: sustaining high motion fidelity and smooth temporal transitions over extended sequences.

Across text-to-motion, speech-to-gesture, and music-to-dance tasks, 3D human motion generation has advanced along 2 complementary dimensions. (1) Generative Strategy. Representative strategies include direct motion regression [3, 4], adversarial learning [5, 6], autoregressive generation [7, 8], diffusion [9, 10], and flow matching [11, 12], with different trade-offs between generation quality and sampling efficiency. (2) Model Architecture. Temporal backbones range from recurrent networks, including LSTMs [13, 14], to Transformers [7, 4] and Mamba-based models [15, 16], with different capabilities for temporal modeling and conditional integration. However, high-quality long-horizon generation under a strict inference budget remains challenging due to 2 coupled bottlenecks: (1) generative strategies that require many sampling steps for high-quality 3D motion generation and (2) model architectures with substantial per-step computational and memory costs for long sequences. These costs leave limited computational resources for other production stages, such as rigging, retargeting, and rendering, potentially degrading the user experience in interactive applications.

To this end, we present FlashMotion, a co-designed framework for high-quality long-horizon 3D motion generation under a strict inference budget. The framework supports diverse conditional motion generation tasks, including text-to-motion, music-to-dance, and speech-to-gesture. Our key observation is that end-to-end generation efficiency is jointly determined by (1) the number of sampling steps and (2) the computational cost of each step. Optimizing either factor alone limits practical speedups: few-step sampling remains costly with an expensive backbone, while a lightweight architecture still incurs substantial latency when many sampling steps are required. FlashMotion therefore jointly optimizes trajectory-level and per-step efficiency. To improve trajectory-level efficiency, we introduce a 3D motion-space MeanFlow formulation with kinematic and dynamic consistency constraints for few-step generation, along with an Adaptive Soft masking mechanism for temporally coherent motion editing. To improve per-step efficiency, we design a lightweight non-autoregressive architecture that combines a BiMamba-based backbone with condition-guided state selection and AdaIN-based condition fusion. Together, FlashMotion achieves state-of-the-art motion quality across all 3 tasks, generating physically plausible, semantically expressive motion at leading throughput with a compact ∼60M-parameter model. Fig. 1 presents quality–throughput comparisons with representative baselines (top) and conditioned motion examples (bottom). Panels (a)-(c) report results on BABEL, BEAT2, and FineDance, respectively. FPS is measured for 10,000-frame outputs on an RTX 3090 at batch size 1.

Trajectory-level efficiency via generative strategy. To reduce sampling steps without sacrificing motion quality, FlashMotion combines a 3D motion-space MeanFlow formulation with kinematic and dynamic consistency constraints. From a kinematic perspective, coherent 3D human motion requires coordinated joint trajectories and smooth temporal evolution, motivating a generative process that continuously transforms noise into structured motion. Flow Matching provides a natural framework for modeling this transformation through a learned velocity field [17, 18]. However, standard Flow Matching learns instantaneous velocities, whereas few-step sampling requires accurate finite-interval updates, making generation sensitive to numerical integration errors. MeanFlow [19] addresses this limitation by modeling interval-averaged velocity. Nevertheless, directly predicting velocity makes it less straightforward to impose structural constraints on the resulting 3D motion. Since 3D human motion representation is subject to tightly coupled kinematic and dynamic constraints, errors in large-step updates can manifest as temporal jitter, root drift, foot sliding, and implausible articulations. This motivates predicting clean motion explicitly, where motion-specific supervision can be applied directly, while deriving the velocity required for sampling from the prediction. We therefore introduce a 3D motion-space MeanFlow formulation that takes the noisy motion zₜ and the time pair (t,r) as inputs and predicts clean motion ẑ₀. During training, we construct the corresponding intermediate state ẑᵣ by interpolating between zₜ and ẑ₀, and use its displacement from zₜ to parameterize the interval-averaged velocity for MeanFlow training. This formulation also enables direct supervision in 3D motion space: reconstruction and forward-kinematics losses encourage faithful motion recovery and kinematic consistency, while velocity and dynamics losses regularize temporal evolution. At inference, the predicted clean motion is converted into the corresponding interval-averaged velocity for few-step ODE sampling. In addition, FlashMotion provides flexible motion editing to support human-in-the-loop authoring and responsive streaming applications. Specifically, we apply an Adaptive Soft mask during sampling, which gradually relaxes the constraints over time and alleviates the boundary discontinuities caused by hard masks in the few-step setting.

Per-step efficiency via model architecture. We design a lightweight non-autoregressive BiMamba architecture with condition-guided state selection and AdaIN-based condition fusion. BiMamba is well suited to temporally coherent 3D human motion generation because its sequential inductive bias better captures local temporal dependencies than attention-only backbones, while retaining linear-time complexity O(n) compared with the O(n²) cost of Transformers [20]. Its bidirectional design further improves temporal coherence and condition-motion alignment, and the non-autoregressive formulation avoids the latency of sequential decoding while mitigating exposure bias in autoregressive-based methods [21, 8] and boundary artifacts in iterative inpainting-based methods [22, 23]. Condition-guided state selection regulates temporal information flow, while AdaIN modulates motion features through frame-wise scaling and shifting. Shared projections support variable sequence lengths without constructing pairwise cross-attention matrices. Together, these architectural choices reduce per-step computational and memory costs while supporting high-quality long-horizon motion generation.

This work extends our previous work, FlowerDance [12], in 4 aspects: (1) Task Coverage: generalizing the method to conditional 3D human motion generation, including text-to-motion, speech-to-gesture, and music-to-dance; (2) Generative Strategy: reformulating MeanFlow in 3D motion space through explicit clean-motion prediction; (3) Model Architecture: introducing condition-guided state selection and AdaIN-based condition fusion to enhance cross-modal alignment and long-sequence generalization; and (4) Experiments: expanding evaluations across tasks and targeted ablation studies, alongside application demonstrations.

In summary, our main contributions are as follows:

  • •

    We present FlashMotion, a co-designed framework for high-quality long-horizon 3D motion generation under a strict inference budget. By jointly optimizing trajectory-level sampling efficiency and per-step inference efficiency, FlashMotion achieves state-of-the-art (SOTA) performance in both quality and efficiency across text-to-motion, speech-to-gesture, and music-to-dance generation.

  • •

    We propose a few-step 3D motion generation strategy comprising: (1) a 3D motion-space MeanFlow formulation with kinematic and dynamic consistency constraints, and (2) Adaptive Soft masking for coherent motion editing.

  • •

    We design a lightweight non-autoregressive architecture for efficient long-horizon motion generation, comprising: (1) a BiMamba-based backbone, (2) a condition-guided state selection mechanism, and (3) AdaIN-based cross-modal alignment.

    • II Related Work

    II-AFlow Matching Generative Models

    Flow Matching (FM) [17] learns continuous transport from noise to data, with substantial methodological advances [18, 19] and broad generative applications [24, 25], while its adoption in 3D human motion generation remains nascent [26, 27, 12].

    Methodological Advances. FM enables simulation-free training through velocity regression [17]. Rectified Flow [18] promotes straighter transport trajectories through reflow, while optimal-transport conditional flow matching (OT-CFM) [28] uses minibatch transport couplings to simplify learned flows. To reduce sampling cost, Consistency Flow Matching [29] encourages velocity consistency, Flow Map Matching [30] learns mappings between pairs of generation times, and Shortcut Models [31] condition predictions on the desired step size. Complementing these approaches, GMFlow [32] models multimodal velocity distributions with Gaussian mixtures. MeanFlow [19] instead learns interval-averaged velocities, directly targeting finite-interval updates for 1- or few-step generation.

    Applications Across Domains. FM has demonstrated its scalability across diverse generative tasks. In image generation, Stable Diffusion 3 [24] combines rectified flow with large-scale multimodal Transformer training. Video applications include sparsely conditioned video prediction [33], audio-driven portrait animation with FLOAT [34], and multiscale video synthesis with Pyramid Flow Matching [35]. In audio, Voicebox [25] and Audiobox [36] employ FM for speech and audio generation, while Matcha-TTS [37] and VoiceFlow [38] explore efficient text-to-speech synthesis.

    Few studies have explored FM for 3D human motion synthesis, yet ultra-few-step long-horizon generation remains challenging: (1) approximately 50 steps for FlowMotion [11], Match-TTSG [27], and UMF’s prior generation stage [39], and (2) 10 steps for Motion Flow Matching [26], FloodDiffusion [40], and FlowerDance [12].

    II-B3D Motion Generation

    3D human motion generation has made substantial progress across text-to-motion, speech-to-gesture, and music-to-dance tasks. We review existing methods from 2 complementary perspectives: generative strategy, which determines how motion is synthesized, and model architecture, which determines how temporal dependencies and conditioning signals are modeled.

    Generative Strategy. Representative strategies include: (1) Direct Regression, which directly predicts motion from conditioning signals, including Language2Pose [3] for text-to-motion, Gesticulator [41] for speech-to-gesture, and FACT [4] for music-to-dance; (2) Adversarial Learning, which encourages realistic motion through discriminator-based training, including the trimodal gesture model [6] for speech-to-gesture, and Choreography cGAN [42], Dancing to Music [43], and CoheDancers [5] for music-driven dance generation; (3) Autoregressive Generation, which synthesizes motion sequentially, including T2M-GPT [7] for text-to-motion, and Dance Revolution [44], Bailando [21], and MEGA [8] for music-to-dance, as well as CoDancers [45] for group choreography; (4) Diffusion, which models conditional motion distributions through iterative denoising [46], including MDM [9] and MLD [47] for text-to-motion, DiffGesture [10] and PersonaGesture [48] for speech-to-gesture, EDGE [22] and CustomDance [49] for dance generation and editing, and BiTDiff [50] for conducting motion; and (5) Flow Matching, which learns continuous transformations from noise to motion, including Motion Flow Matching [26] and FlowMotion [11] for text-driven motion, the unified speech-gesture synthesis framework [27], and FlowerDance [12] for few-step music-to-dance generation.

    Model Architecture. Representative temporal backbones include: (1) Recurrent Networks, which capture temporal dependencies through sequential hidden-state updates, as exemplified by ERD [13] and the residual RNN [14] for human motion prediction, and the recurrent decoder in Dance Revolution [44] for music-to-dance; (2) Transformers, which use attention for temporal and conditional modeling, including T2M-GPT [7] for text-to-motion, DiffGesture [10] and StreamTalk [51] for speech-to-gesture, and FACT [4] and EDGE [22] for music-to-dance; and (3) Mamba-Based Models, which exploit selective state-space modeling for efficient sequence processing, including Motion Mamba [52] for text-to-motion, MambaTalk [15] and MambaGesture [53] for speech-to-gesture, and FlowerDance [12], TokenDance [16], and the hybrid Mamba-Transformer model MATHDance [54] for music-to-dance.

    However, high-quality long-horizon generation under a strict inference budget remains challenging due to 2 coupled bottlenecks: (1) generative strategies that require many sampling steps for high-quality 3D motion generation and (2) model architectures with substantial per-step computational and memory costs for long sequences. These costs leave limited computational resources for other production stages, such as rigging, retargeting, and rendering, potentially degrading the user experience in interactive applications.

    III Methodology

    III-AOverview

    Since condition encoding, motion retargeting, and rendering also consume the end-to-end latency budget, motion generation must remain highly efficient. For example, interactively creating and revising an extended dance or action sequence requires rapid generation of long, coherent motions so that users can promptly preview and refine the results. Ultra-fast long-term 3D motion generation that preserves physical plausibility, conditional alignment, and motion expressiveness is therefore essential for responsive avatar animation.

    Given a conditioning sequence C=(cᵢ)ᵢ₌₁^N, our objective is to generate a corresponding 3D motion sequence M=(mᵢ)ᵢ₌₁^N, where cᵢ∈ℝ^d_c and mᵢ∈ℝ^dₘ denote the condition and motion features at frame i, respectively. We consider text, speech, and music conditioning, with a separate model trained for each task. (1) Text-to-Motion. For text description qₖ and its frame interval Iₖ, cᵢ=Eₜₑₓₜ(qₖ)∈ℝ⁴⁰⁹⁶ uses UMT5-XXL [55]; mᵢ∈ℝ²⁶³ follows HumanML3D [56] at 20 FPS. (2) Speech-to-Gesture. The condition cᵢ combines frame-aligned 1024-dimensional HuBERT speech features and 300-dimensional text features; mᵢ∈ℝ³³³ comprises local 6D rotations [57] for 55 SMPL-X joints and 3 root-motion components at 30 FPS. (3) Music-to-Dance.cᵢ∈ℝ³⁵ contains frame-aligned Librosa music features [58]; mᵢ∈ℝ¹⁴⁷ comprises 3D root motion (horizontal displacements and height) and 24-joint 6D rotations [57] at 30 FPS.

    To meet this strict inference budget in practice, we co-design FlashMotion across both the generative strategy and model architecture, as summarized in Fig. 2. (1) At the generative-strategy level, we formulate MeanFlow in 3D motion space by directly predicting clean motion and deriving the interval-averaged velocity for few-step sampling, with auxiliary kinematic and dynamic constraints to preserve motion fidelity. (2) At the model-architecture level, we develop a lightweight non-autoregressive BiMamba backbone with condition-guided state selection and AdaIN-based condition fusion mechanism, enhancing cross-modal alignment and generalization to longer motion sequences. (3) To support real-time human-in-the-loop motion authoring and responsive streaming applications under few-step sampling, we further introduce an Adaptive Soft masking strategy that enables coherent motion editing without additional training.

    III-BGenerative Strategy

    MeanFlow. From a kinematic perspective, 3D human motion consists of continuous trajectories of root translation and joint rotations, coupled through skeletal structure and temporal dependencies [59, 60]. Generating coherent motion therefore requires jointly modeling spatial coordination and temporal evolution, motivating continuous refinement of the entire sequence from unstructured noise toward a condition-consistent trajectory. Flow Matching (FM) [17] learns a velocity field for an ordinary differential equation (ODE) transporting Gaussian noise ε∼ℕ(0,I) to motion x∼p_\rmdata. Training uses the linear conditional path zₜ=FP(x,t), with time t∼U(0,1):

    FP(x,t)=(1-t)x+tε(1)

    The conditional path velocity is v_\rmcond=ε-x. We regress v_θ against this sample-wise target; the optimal regressor estimates the marginal velocity field v(zₜ,t)=𝔼[v_\rmcond|zₜ,t]:

    L_FM=𝔼[∥v_θ(zₜ,t)-v_\rmcond∥²].(2)

    At inference, generation starts from an initial prior sample z₁ and iteratively integrates the learned velocity field v_θ(zₜ,t) until reaching z₀ in the data distribution:

    v_θ(zₜ,t)=dzₜ/dt,(3)
    z₀=z₁+∫₁⁰v_θ(z_τ,τ) dτ.

    Even when conditional flows are designed to be straight, latent trajectories in the high-dimensional space are often highly curved. When using large integration intervals, Flow Matching [17], which models the instantaneous velocity field, cannot accurately capture these curved trajectories, leading to degraded generation quality. Thus, MeanFlow[19] replaces instantaneous velocity v(zₜ,t) with the interval mean velocity u(zₜ,r,t), leading to a training objective aligned with the actual ODE inference procedure:

    u(zₜ,r,t)=1/t-r∫ᵣᵗv(z_τ,τ) dτ,

    		(4)

    where (r,t) are 2 timesteps randomly sampled from a uniform distribution U(0,1) with the constraint t>r. Differentiating Eq. 4 with respect to t yields the MeanFlow identity:

    u(zₜ,r,t)=v(zₜ,t)-(t-r)d/dtu(zₜ,r,t).

    		(5)

    A velocity estimator u_θ is trained to satisfy the MeanFlow identity:

    L_MF=𝔼[∥u_θ(zₜ,r,t)-sg(u_tgt)∥₂²],(6)
    where u_tgt=v_\rmcond-(t-r)Dₜu_θ,
    Dₜu_θ=∂_zu_θ v_\rmcond+∂ₜu_θ.

    where sg(·) denotes stop-gradient. Notably, this reduces to the FM loss when r=t. During inference, MeanFlow uses a constant interval-averaged velocity for each update. The general update and its equivalent integral form over the full interval are:

    zᵣ=zₜ-(t-r)u(zₜ,r,t),(7)

    Training. Although MeanFlow has shown promising results in image generation [19], video rendering [61], and audio synthesis [62], directly applying it to few-step 3D motion generation is non-trivial. A key reason is that these modalities often exhibit explicit local continuity in their native representations, such as spatially neighboring pixels, adjacent video frames, or temporally continuous waveforms, which provides a relatively direct structure for learning smooth generative fields. In contrast, SMPL-based 3D motion is represented as a sequence of pose parameters whose temporal continuity is explicit across frames, while the intra-frame dependencies among joints are only implicitly encoded by the human kinematic chain. Under large integration intervals, small errors in the predicted velocity field can therefore accumulate over time and disrupt these latent kinematic constraints, leading to temporal jitter, global drift, foot sliding, and implausible articulations. Moreover, the vanilla MeanFlow objective only constrains the averaged velocity field, without explicitly regularizing the recovered motion in kinematic or physical spaces.

    To enable direct motion-level supervision, FlashMotion predicts the clean-motion estimate ẑ₀ from the current state zₜ, frame-aligned conditioning sequence C, and time interval (r,t). The interval-averaged velocity is then derived as:

    u_θ(zₜ,r,t;C)=(zₜ-ẑ₀)/(t).

    		(8)

    We optimize the induced velocity using the MeanFlow objective in Eq. (6), with JVP-based differentiation, t² time weighting, and adaptive loss weighting.

    Empirically, training with L_MF alone still remains unstable and fails to converge in our SMPL-based experiments, as corroborated by the results in Sec. IV-E. We therefore add reconstruction supervision to anchor the clean-motion estimate to ground truth:

    L_rec=𝔼[∥ẑ₀-z₀∥₂²].

    		(9)

    To improve kinematic consistency, we match the recovered 3D joint positions to ground truth, encouraging spatially coordinated poses:

    Lₖᵢₙ=𝔼[∥P̂-P∥₂²].

    		(10)

    Here, P̂=K(ẑ₀) and P=K(z₀), where K recovers joint positions from 3D rotation representations.

    To improve temporal dynamics, we match joint velocities and accelerations to ground truth, encouraging temporally coherent motion evolution:

    L_dyn=𝔼[∥ΔP̂-ΔP∥₂²+β∥Δ²P̂-Δ²P∥₂²].

    		(11)

    Here, Δ denotes frame-wise finite differences, and β balances velocity and acceleration supervision.

    Overall, the shared training objective is:

    L=λ_mfL_MF+λ_recL_rec+λₖᵢₙLₖᵢₙ+λ_dynL_dyn.

    		(12)

    Inference. Starting from Gaussian noise ε, we progressively generate motion over uniformly spaced time intervals. At each step, we predict the clean motion ẑ₀ and obtain zᵣ by linearly interpolating between ẑ₀ and the current noisy state zₜ. This update is equivalent to Eq. 7, without explicit velocity computation or additional noise injection.

    Motion Editing. Extending the inpainting idea in diffusion-based motion generation [23, 22], FlashMotion supports training-free constraint-based editing with multiple sampling steps; 1-step editing is not supported. This capability serves 2 complementary uses. (1) Human-in-the-loop motion authoring. Users can fill temporal gaps or modify selected joint trajectories, such as interpolating between dance clips or adjusting hand paths (Fig. 6). (2) Responsive Streaming Applications. Temporal inpainting enables sequential window extension by constraining each new window with the previous window’s tail. This allows FlashMotion to adapt to incoming conditions for conversational avatars or interactive NPCs. With few sampling steps, fixed hard masks may cause dynamic mismatches at constraint boundaries. We therefore apply an Adaptive Soft mask, gradually relaxing the influence of known regions to improve coupling between constrained and unconstrained motions. Given a joint-wise or temporal constraint x^′∈ℝ^N×dₘ with positions indicated by a binary mask M∈{0,1}^N×dₘ at time t, where N is the sequence length and dₘ=263, 333, and 147 for text-to-motion, speech-to-gesture, and music-to-dance, respectively, FlashMotion performs constraint-aware denoising as follows:

    zₜ:=(t·M)⊙FP(x^′,t)+(1-(t·M))⊙zₜ,(13)

    where ⊙ denotes the Hadamard product, and known regions follow the constraint flow.

item.title: 给视频的「物理常识」打分不能只给一个总分：PhyRubric 按物理原理分条评，能指出破的是哪一条 ｜ PhyRubric: Rubric-Grounded Diagnostic Evaluation of Physical Commonsense in Text-to-Video Generation
item.description:
一句话：现有基准让标注者凭直觉打一个分，既主观，又说不清违反了哪条物理规律。

要点：

  • 前提变了：文生视频模型越来越被当作**世界模拟器**来用，于是「是否符合物理常识」必须被评估
  • 现有基准的缺陷很清楚：标注者凭直觉给每条视频打一个总分，结果既主观，也无法说明**违反了哪一条物理原理**
  • PhyRubric 改为基于评分细则（rubric）的诊断式评测，按物理原理分条给判断

为什么值得看：「世界模型物理不对」已经是共识，但缺的是可定位的诊断。分条评分让「哪里不对」变成可比较的数据——这对训练与验收世界模型都有直接价值，也是把「世界模拟」从口号变成指标的一步。

中文摘要：随着文生视频模型越来越多地被当作世界模拟器来使用，评估其输出是否符合物理常识就变得必要。但现有基准的做法是让标注者凭直觉给每条视频打一个总体分数，结果既主观，也无法说明违反的究竟哪一条物理原理。PhyRubric 因此提出基于评分细则（rubric）的诊断式评测框架：针对每段生成视频，按物理原理分条给出判断，使「哪里不对」成为可定位、可比较的信息。对要训练或验收世界模型的团队，这比一个总分的价值高得多。

主题：AI Native Engine

来源：arXiv·cs.CV（English）

原文发布：2026-11-11

本期推送：2026-11-13

PhyRubric: Rubric-Grounded Diagnostic Evaluation of Physical Commonsense in Text-to-Video Generation

Abstract

As text-to-video (T2V) models are increasingly positioned as world simulators, it is essential to evaluate whether their videos conform to physical commonsense. However, existing benchmarks rely on annotators who rate each video with a single score based on intuition, yielding ratings that are subjective and do not tell which physical principle is violated. We introduce PhyRubric, a rubric-grounded diagnostic framework for evaluating physical commonsense in T2V generation. For each caption, PhyRubric constructs a caption-specific rubric before any video is seen, decomposing the caption into semantic and physical items, and derives scores from item-level verdicts grounded in timestamped evidence. We instantiate this framework as PhyRubric-Bench, which spans 34 categories across five physical domains, and scale it up to PhyRubric-Train with 3,788 videos, on which we fine-tune the open-source PhyRubric-Judge. Empirical results across ten T2V models show that physical commonsense remains far from solved, and that PhyRubric-Judge correlates more closely with human judgments than existing open-source judges while matching the frontier proprietary Gemini 4 Argon. Further analysis provides actionable insights for T2V models.

1 Introduction

Text-to-video (T2V) generation has advanced rapidly, and recent T2V models [59, 62, 1, 14, 67, 57, 45] can now render complex scenes from text prompts. As these models are increasingly positioned as world simulators [68, 33, 1], a basic requirement is that their videos conform to physical commonsense, the shared expectations about the physical world that everyone acquires from everyday experience, without any textbook physics [37, 55]. A reliable and comprehensive evaluation of this ability is therefore essential for tracking progress and guiding model development.

Existing benchmarks for physical commonsense have made notable progress [7, 8, 47, 19], but they share two limitations (Fig. 1). First, the ratings are subjective. Annotators rate each video and its caption with a single score on a discrete scale, but no rule defines how physical violations map to scores. Each rater thus applies an intuitive mapping, weighing the severity of violations by personal standards, so the same video may receive different scores. This inconsistency introduces noise into both benchmark results and the automatic evaluators trained on these ratings. Second, the ratings are uninterpretable. A discrete scale is easier to rate than a continuous one, since fractional scores would be harder to assign and more scattered. However, a single score reflects only how implausible a video is overall, not which physical principle is violated. Evaluations can thus only rank models and categories, yielding coarse findings that offer little guidance for improvement.

To address these limitations, we introduce PhyRubric, a rubric-grounded diagnostic framework for evaluating physical commonsense in T2V generation (Fig. 2). For each caption, PhyRubric constructs a caption-specific rubric before any video is seen, and reuses it for every video generated from that caption. The rubric decomposes the caption into verifiable items of two types: semantic items list the visible facts the caption requires, while physical items specify which visible events count as violations and are each assigned a severity level inspired by the order in which infants acquire physical knowledge [55, 6, 41]. Given a video, each item receives a verdict grounded in timestamped evidence, and scores are derived deterministically from these verdicts rather than rated directly. Every score thus comes with a diagnosis of which expectation failed and why.

We instantiate this framework as PhyRubric-Bench. Unlike prior benchmarks dominated by mechanics (Suppl. Tab. 4), it spans 34 categories across five physical domains: mechanics, optics, heat, electricity, and acoustics111 Since generated videos are silent, the acoustics domain covers only the visible consequences of sound, such as water rippling beside a speaker.. Every caption describes a complete causal event and states its outcome explicitly, so that semantic adherence requires rendering the cause, the action, and its physical consequence, e.g., “the key switch is turned, and the lamp lights” rather than “the key switch is turned.”

Beyond PhyRubric-Bench, we scale up to PhyRubric-Train, 947 captions that share the taxonomy of the benchmark but no scenes, each paired with its own rubric. Here the rubric plays a different role: rather than defining the evaluation as in PhyRubric-Bench, it guides an agentic annotator, telling it which expectations to check and where to look, yielding 3,788 labeled videos from four T2V models with 45.9K rubric-item verdicts. On these labels, we train PhyRubric-Judge, an open-source VLM that needs no rubric at inference. Given only a caption and a video, it predicts semantic adherence and physical commonsense scores together with a diagnosis of which physical expectation is violated and why.

We evaluate ten T2V models on PhyRubric-Bench and find that basic physical commonsense remains far from solved: even the strongest model, Seedance 2.5, produces videos that are both faithful to the caption and physically plausible in fewer than half of cases. Moreover, PhyRubric-Judge correlates more closely with human judgments than the judges released with existing benchmarks, generalizes well to unseen generators and domains, and provides a diagnosis that locates each violation.

Our contributions are summarized as follows:

  • •

    We propose PhyRubric, a rubric-grounded framework that constructs a caption-specific rubric before any video is seen and derives every score from evidence-grounded item verdicts, so that each score comes with a diagnosis.

  • •

    We construct PhyRubric-Bench, spanning 34 categories across five physical domains with human-verified rubrics and labels, and PhyRubric-Train, labeled by a rubric-guided agentic annotator, on which we train the open-source PhyRubric-Judge that generalizes to unseen generators and domains.

  • •

    Rather than proposing a definitive standard, we show that our rubric-grounded evaluation serves as an analysis tool that yields deeper insights: semantic adherence is the main bottleneck, physical errors are all-or-nothing, and models often avoid physical errors by not depicting the event at all, a shortcut that prior protocols reward.

    • 2 Related Work

    2.1 Physical Commonsense Benchmarks for Text-to-Video Generation

    The rapid advancement of text-to-video (T2V) generation has motivated a range of benchmarks for its assessment [30, 66, 31, 43, 60, 56, 44, 39]. Moving beyond general visual quality, a growing line of work focuses on physical commonsense in T2V generation [7, 8, 47, 19, 20, 53, 36], while other works study physical understanding in settings where models are conditioned on observed frames and predict how the scene evolves [48, 33, 40]. However, most of these physical commonsense benchmarks are dominated by mechanics [7, 8, 20], and some include prompts that require specialized knowledge beyond everyday experience [47, 19, 20, 36]. In contrast, PhyRubric-Bench spans five physical domains with prompts grounded in physical commonsense, and pairs each prompt with a caption-specific rubric that enables diagnostic evaluation.

    2.2 VLM-as-a-Judge for Physical Commonsense

    Existing evaluation of video generation mainly follows two paradigms: standard metrics such as FVD [58], SSIM [61], and CLIP score [27], and VLM-based evaluation [12, 52, 23] such as VideoScore [26]. As standard metrics cannot capture physical plausibility, physical commonsense evaluation mainly adopts the latter, employing VLMs as dedicated judges. On the open-source side, judges such as VideoCon-Physics [7] and VideoPhy-2-AutoEval [8] are fine-tuned on the human annotations of their corresponding datasets. On the proprietary side, recent works prompt commercial models such as GPT-4o, Gemini-2.5-Pro, and GPT-5.5 as judges [47, 19, 53, 51]. Nevertheless, most of these judges output a holistic score rather than a detailed diagnosis, failing to reveal what goes wrong and why.

    2.3 Rubric-Based Evaluation

    A rubric is an explicit set of criteria that decomposes a holistic quality judgment into verifiable items, making the assessment transparent, consistent, and interpretable [32, 13]. Recently, rubrics have been widely adopted for fine-grained evaluation of large language models (LLMs) and vision-language models [34, 38], and increasingly tailor the criteria to each individual query rather than applying a generic rubric to all samples [35, 16, 4]. In text-to-image generation, a related line of work decomposes prompts into fine-grained questions to assess text-image alignment [29, 15]. However, rubric-based evaluation remains underexplored for physical commonsense in video generation. In this work, rubrics play two roles: they serve as the evaluation criteria of PhyRubric-Bench, and they guide an agentic annotator to label training data for PhyRubric-Judge.

    3 PhyRubric

    As illustrated in Fig. 2, PhyRubric fixes a rubric for each caption before any video is seen and shares it across all videos from that caption. This keeps the criteria identical across videos, so that scores from different generators are directly comparable and cannot be swayed by what a particular video happens to show. Moreover, a rubric reviewed by humans once can be reused for any number of videos, including those from future generators.

    3.1 Caption-Specific Rubric Formulation

    We evaluate generated videos along the two dimensions introduced by VideoPhy-2 [8], semantic adherence (SA) and physical commonsense (PC), each on a 1–5 scale. Unlike prior benchmarks, where annotators assign a holistic score to each dimension, we pair every caption with a rubric that specifies what a video must satisfy to be faithful and physically plausible for that caption. The rubric consists of two groups of items, one for SA and one for PC, and each score is derived from item-level verdicts rather than rated directly. A simplified rubric example is shown in Fig. 3.

    Semantic Adherence (SA). SA measures whether the video shows what the caption describes. Its rubric items are the visible facts the caption requires, in two tiers:

  • •

    Primary: the main objects and each event in the caption.

  • •

    Secondary: the remaining facts, including stated qualifiers (e.g., once, slowly, wooden), initial states implied by the caption, and the order of events.

    • Physical Commonsense (PC). This metric evaluates whether the events shown in the video follow physical commonsense. We define four severity levels for physical violations, inspired by the order in which infants acquire physical knowledge in developmental psychology [55, 6, 41]:

  • •

    Fatal: the scene is impossible as a whole, violating core object principles such as permanence, solidity, or continuity (e.g., objects passing through each other, or appearing or vanishing without cause).

  • •

    Core: the central interaction described by the caption does not happen or happens incorrectly (e.g., in reverse or through a broken mechanism).

  • •

    Major: a clear violation outside the central interaction, such as a missing secondary consequence (e.g., the lamp lights but the desk beneath it stays dark).

  • •

    Minor: a visual flaw that leaves the event intact, such as color or texture drift of untouched objects.

    • Each PC item is assigned one of these severity levels and one of ten violation types (e.g., permanence, solidity, causeless motion, process direction). Following the same developmental order, the ten types are grouped into L1 core object principles, L2 everyday dynamics, and L3 attribute experience (Suppl. Tab. 6). Each PC item is then judged by a pair of verifiable statements:

  • •

    Expect: what a physically correct video should show, specifying the moment, region, or event to inspect.

  • •

    Fail: the concrete visible signs that count as a violation, and the item fails only if one of these signs is observed.

    • Verdicts. An SA item is judged pass or fail. A PC item has a third verdict, not shown, which applies when the moment, region, or event specified by its Expect statement never appears in the video. Otherwise, the item fails if any sign in its Fail statement is observed, and passes if not. Note that not shown means the situation is absent, not that the expected behavior failed to occur. For example, for the caption “The key switch on the base of a desk lamp is turned, and the lamp lights” (Fig. 3), if the key is never turned in the video, P2 is not shown rather than failed, since the missing action is already penalized by the SA item S2. Since a fail can only be triggered by a listed sign, every negative verdict is grounded in a specific observation rather than an overall impression, and carries the severity and violation type of its item. Consistent with the nature of commonsense, PC items judge only the direction and order of change rather than its rate or extent, and never penalize a cause for being out of view (e.g., a heat source or power supply).

    Scoring Rules. Both scores lie on a 1–5 scale and are derived from the verdicts by fixed rules. For SA, a video judged entirely unrelated to the caption scores 1. Otherwise, it scores 5 if all items pass, 4 if only secondary items fail, 3 if exactly one primary item fails, and 2 if two or more primary items fail. For PC, let F be the set of failed items. A video with F=∅ scores 5; otherwise,

    PC=\max(1, \min_i∈Fc(sᵢ)-\max(0, h-1)),

    		(1)

    where sᵢ is the severity of item i, c(·) maps fatal, core, major, and minor to caps of 1, 2, 3, and 4, and h is the number of failed items of major severity or above. In words, the most severe failure sets the cap, and each additional failure of major severity or above lowers the score by one. Each rubric is checked to contain at least two primary and one secondary SA items and at least one PC item of every severity, so that every score from 1 to 5 is attainable.

    3.2 PhyRubric-Bench

    Suppl. Tab. 4 compares PhyRubric-Bench with prior benchmarks, which are dominated by mechanics. PhyRubric-Bench covers all five physical domains with 34 categories (Fig. 4), and every caption tests only physical commonsense and is paired with a human-verified rubric.

    Caption and rubric generation. Captions are drafted by Claude Fable 5.1 [2] and GPT-5.6 Sol [49] and refined by human reviewers until each describes a single causal event that is visible within about five seconds and has an explicitly stated outcome. Stating the outcome serves two purposes. (1) Fixed expectations: what should happen is determined before any video is seen, so the rubric can specify the expected events and violations rather than guess among plausible outcomes. (2) Diagnostic failures: if a model is told what should happen yet fails to render it, the failure reflects missing physical knowledge rather than creative freedom.

    In addition, captions include a person only when the human body itself is part of the physics, since current generators often produce distorted human bodies [66, 65, 46]. Each phenomenon is instantiated in three to five distinct scenes for diversity, yielding 1,192 captions, which are split into 245 for PhyRubric-Bench and 947 for PhyRubric-Train (Sec. 3.3) with no scene shared between the two. Each caption is then paired with a rubric, drafted by an LLM prompted with example rubrics from the same domain, checked automatically for format and score reachability, and revised by human reviewers until approved.

    Video generation and annotation. For evaluation, the 245 benchmark captions are rendered by ten text-to-video models, six of which are unseen during judge training, yielding 2,433 videos222 The remaining 17 of the 10×245 videos were not produced because the generators’ built-in safety filters declined the captions.. Each video is first pre-annotated item by item by our agentic annotator (Sec. 3.3), and human annotators then verify every verdict against the video to obtain the ground truth. Since the rubric already specifies what counts as a violation, annotators only need to check whether the listed signs appear, rather than judging physical plausibility themselves. More construction details and statistics are given in Suppl. Sec. A.2.

    3.3 PhyRubric-Train and PhyRubric-Judge

    Training data annotation. Human verification does not scale to thousands of videos, so we label the training set with the same agentic annotator used to pre-annotate PhyRubric-Bench, built on Claude Sonnet 5.5 [3]. Instead of a fixed set of frames, the annotator first scans a timestamped overview of the clip and then zooms in at full frame rate where and when it needs to, until each rubric item can be decided from frames that clearly show the relevant event. This matters because physical violations often involve small objects or brief moments that uniform sampling misses. For every item, it returns a verdict with timestamped evidence, and the scores follow from the verdicts by the rules in Sec. 3.1. Applied to the 947 training captions, each rendered by four generators, it yields PhyRubric-Train with 3,788 videos and 45.9K item-level verdicts. Suppl. Sec. A.4 details its protocol and reliability.

    Judge. The agentic annotator produces reliable labels but is impractical as a general-purpose evaluator: it relies on a proprietary model, makes repeated tool calls per video, and needs a rubric for every new caption. We therefore train PhyRubric-Judge, an open-source VLM, on PhyRubric-Train. Starting from Qwen3-VL-8B [5], we explore configurations that vary the rubric input, the output format, and the training objective (SFT or GRPO [54]). Our default judge takes only the caption and uniformly sampled frames, so that it applies to any new caption and receives the same input as existing judges. It outputs the SA score, whether PC is assessable, the PC score, and a diagnosis. The training targets come from PhyRubric-Train, with the diagnosis assembled from the item-level evidence: a summary of what the video shows, the missing caption facts, and each physical violation with its evidence. The judge thus learns not only what score to give but why (Suppl. Sec. C.3).

    4 Experiments

    4.1 Experimental Setup

    Video Generative Models. PhyRubric-Bench is rendered by ten video generators. Four of them are open-source T2V models that also render PhyRubric-Train: CogVideoX1.5-5B [64], HunyuanVideo-1.5-8B [62], LTX-Video-2B [22], and Wan2.2-T2V-A14B [59]. The other six are unseen during training and measure how well a judge generalizes to new generators: Wan2.2-TI2V-5B [59], LTX-2.3-22B [21], Cosmos-Predict2.5-2B and Cosmos-Predict2.5-14B [1], and the proprietary Seedance 2.5 [11] and Veo 3.1 [17]. All videos are five to six seconds long.

    Evaluation Metrics. Each video is rated on a 1–5 scale for SA and PC. We report the mean SA over all videos and the mean PC over assessable videos only. We also report the joint performance (JP), the percentage of all videos with SA≥4 and PC≥4, i.e., videos that are both faithful to the caption and physically plausible. Following VideoPhy-2 [8], we use JP as the primary metric. A high PC alone only indicates that what is shown is plausible (e.g., a nearly static video can easily appear plausible), so SA is needed to confirm that the model produces the described event.

    Implementation Details. For video generation, each open-source model is run with its official checkpoint and default sampling recipe, generating one video per caption with a fixed seed of 42. HunyuanVideo-1.5 and Wan2.2-T2V-A14B are rendered at 480p, CogVideoX1.5-5B at 768p, and the remaining open-source models at 704p. Seedance 2.5 and Veo 3.1 are accessed through their official APIs at 480p and 720p, respectively. Per-model settings are listed in Suppl. Sec. B.1. For PhyRubric-Judge, we fine-tune Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct [5] on PhyRubric-Train with LoRA (rank 16) [28] on all linear layers of the language model, keeping the vision encoder and projector frozen. The judge takes the caption and 16 uniformly sampled frames, each resized to at most 448×448. We train for 2 epochs (900 steps) with an effective batch size of 8 and a cosine learning rate schedule peaking at 10⁻⁴. At inference, the judge decodes greedily, and we additionally compute a soft score [42, 63] as the expected rating under the probabilities of the five score tokens (Suppl. Sec. B.2). All experiments are run on NVIDIA GH200 Superchips.

    4.2 Main Results

    Tab. 1 reports the results of ten video generators on PhyRubric-Bench across five physics domains. We summarize the main findings below.

    Physical commonsense remains far from solved. The two proprietary models lead by a wide margin: Seedance 2.5 achieves an average JP of 44.20% and Veo 3.1 36.20%, two to three times that of the strongest open-source model, HunyuanVideo-1.5-8B (14.93%). Even so, more than half of their videos are still not both faithful to the caption and physically plausible. Moreover, every open-source model has an average SA below 3, indicating that at least one primary element of the caption is typically missing from the generated video. Even among assessable videos, where the intended event does occur, their average PC never exceeds 3.5, suggesting that the event typically violates at least one expectation of major severity or above.

    Video generative models handle optics best but struggle with heat and acoustics. As shown in Tab. 1, Optics is the strongest domain for eight of the ten evaluated models, and ranks second (or tied for second) for the remaining two models, Seedance 2.5 and CogVideoX1.5-5B. In contrast, Heat and Acoustics are the weakest domains for most models. Even the proprietary models reach only 30.00% (Seedance 2.5) and 15.00% (Veo 3.1) JP on Acoustics, and two open-source models score 0.00% in this domain. We conjecture that optical phenomena (e.g., reflection and shadows) are visually salient and well represented in training data, whereas thermal processes involve gradual state changes and acoustic phenomena must be conveyed through indirect visual cues (e.g., sound-induced ripples on a liquid surface), both of which are harder to render.

    Semantic adherence is the main bottleneck, and physical errors are all-or-nothing. Fig. 5(a) shows the distribution of SA and PC scores. SA concentrates at 2 (50.8% of all videos), the score given when two or more primary elements of the caption are missing, while only 5.0% of videos receive a 4, the score for a video that misses only secondary details: most generated videos fail to depict the captioned event itself, before physics even comes into play. In contrast, once the event is fully shown, its physics is usually correct: as shown in Fig. 5(b), only 5.9% of videos show the event fully but violate physics (SA≥4, PC<4), compared with 16.9% that pass, meaning that 74.1% of fully shown events are rendered with plausible physics. Physical errors themselves are all-or-nothing: PC over assessable videos is bimodal, with 52.9% scoring 5, i.e., no violation at all, and 40.8% scoring 1 or 2, i.e., a fatal or core violation, whereas scores of 3 and 4, i.e., only major or minor violations, together account for 6.3%. This suggests that when current models do show the event, they either render its physics correctly or break it at the most basic level, and rarely get the core event right but slip on peripheral details.

    Models take a shortcut to high PC by not showing the event. Prior protocols rate PC on every video, so a video that never attempts the event leaves nothing for physics to contradict and receives a high PC. In PhyRubric, the PC items on the central event of such a video are judged not shown, so the video is marked unassessable and excluded from PC. We define the avoidance rate of a model as the share of its videos that never show the event. Such avoidance is common: 25.0% of all videos never show the event (Fig. 5(b)), and the avoidance rate ranges from 20.0% to 44.5% across open-source models, compared with 5.7% and 8.6% for Seedance 2.5 and Veo 3.1 (Fig. 5(c)). We regard avoidance as a failure of physical commonsense rather than merely of instruction following: every caption in PhyRubric-Bench states the outcome explicitly, so a model that still renders a static scene or a different event suggests that it does not know how the stated cause produces the stated effect. If avoided videos are scored as in prior protocols, the PC score of every open-source model rises by 0.16–0.59, and the gain grows with its avoidance rate (Fig. 5(c)). LTX-Video-2B, with the highest avoidance rate (44.5%), would then rank above Cosmos-Predict2.5-14B and Wan2.2-T2V-A14B. PC alone is most misleading for Cosmos-Predict2.5-2B: under prior protocols its PC would be second only to Seedance 2.5 and above Veo 3.1, yet its JP (6.69%) ranks eighth of ten, as it rarely depicts the event.

    4.3 Evaluation of PhyRubric-Judge

    We assess PhyRubric-Judge by its agreement with the human labels of PhyRubric-Bench. We apply each judge to every video in PhyRubric-Bench and report two metrics on its soft score: Pearson correlation (r) [50] with the human scores, and ROC-AUC [24] for distinguishing videos that humans rate as pass (score≥4) from those rated as fail, separately for SA and PC. Suppl. Sec. B.2 reports the results of all judges on the full set of metrics adopted by prior work.

    Baselines. We compare PhyRubric-Judge with four groups of judges. (1) Zero-shot VLMs: Qwen3-VL-8B, Qwen3-VL-32B, and Qwen3-VL-235B-A22B [5]. The 8B model is also the untrained starting point of our judge. (2) General video evaluators: VideoScore [26] and VideoScore2 [25], fine-tuned to rate generated videos along general quality dimensions. (3) Physics-specific evaluators: VideoCon-Physics [7] and VideoPhy-2-AutoEval [8], each fine-tuned on human annotations of its own benchmark. (4) Proprietary VLM: Gemini 4 Argon [18], a frontier closed-source model, prompted with the same instructions as our judge. Details are in the Suppl. Sec. B.3.

    PhyRubric-Judge aligns best with human judgments. As shown in Tab. 2, PhyRubric-Judge achieves the best agreement with human judgments on both SA and PC across all metrics. On SA, it reaches a correlation of 0.61, well above the best open-source baseline, Qwen3-VL-32B (0.49). PC is the harder dimension: open-source zero-shot VLMs perform close to chance (AUC 0.53–0.58), and even the strongest open-source evaluator, VideoPhy-2-AutoEval, reaches only r=0.23, despite being fine-tuned in two stages on 62K human annotations from VideoPhy and VideoPhy-2. In contrast, PhyRubric-Judge reaches 0.32 while being trained on only 3,600 automatically labeled videos. Notably, this 8B model is on par with the proprietary Gemini 4 Argon (r=0.60 on SA and 0.31 on PC), showing that rubric-grounded supervision enables a small open model to match a frontier proprietary model.

    PhyRubric-Judge generalizes to unseen generators and domains. PhyRubric-Train contains videos from only four of the ten generators. To test whether the judge learns physical commonsense rather than the artifacts of these four generators, Tab. 3 (a) compares its agreement on benchmark videos from these generators (Seen) and from the other six (Unseen). On unseen generators, PhyRubric-Judge loses only 0.03 in SA and 0.06 in PC correlation, and still outperforms every baseline. To test generalization across domains, Tab. 3 (b) trains five additional judges, each with one domain removed from PhyRubric-Train, and evaluates each on its held-out domain. SA correlation drops by at most 0.04, and PC correlation by at most 0.09 (on mechanics).

    4.4 Error Analysis

    To better understand the limitations of current T2V models, we categorize their failed items by the three levels and ten violation types in PhyRubric, with more analysis in Suppl. Sec. D.1.

    The physical commonsense of current T2V models is still limited at the most basic level. As shown in Fig. 6 (a), 41.6% of the violations belong to L1 (core object principles) and 50.7% to L2 (everyday dynamics), while only 7.6% belong to L3 (attribute experience). This indicates that current models rarely fail on fine attributes, but instead break principles that hold for any object, such as persistence over time, and the way common events unfold. Fig. 6 (b) shows that the two most frequent types, missing consequence (24.0%) and permanence & count (20.4%), together account for nearly half of all violations. A permanence & count violation occurs when an object appears from nothing, vanishes, teleports, duplicates, or merges with another during the video. For example, in Fig. 7 (a), the sauce becomes fully stirred and the spoon teleports to a new position between 1.50 s and 1.62 s, a severe violation that any viewer would notice at a glance. A missing consequence violation occurs when the trigger of an event is shown but its effect never follows, or occurs at the wrong time. In Fig. 7(b), the lights are on from the start, before the finger even reaches the button. Both videos have high visual quality, yet their obvious physical errors make them distinguishable from real videos.

    5 Conclusion

    We presented PhyRubric, a rubric-grounded framework for diagnostic evaluation of physical commonsense in T2V generation, which fixes a caption-specific rubric before any video is seen and derives every score from evidence-grounded item verdicts. We instantiated it as PhyRubric-Bench across five physical domains and scaled it up to PhyRubric-Train, on which we trained PhyRubric-Judge, an open-source judge that outperforms existing open-source judges, matches Gemini 4 Argon, and generalizes to unseen generators and domains. Our evaluation of T2V models reveals that physical commonsense remains far from solved, and our in-depth analysis provides actionable insights for developing future T2V models.
