which is Eq. (2). Conversely, homogeneity gives ρ(sx)=sρ(x) and sx/ρ(sx)=x/ρ(x). Substitution into Eq. (2) yields

f(sx)=α\log₂(sρ(x))u+Ψ (x/ρ(x))=f(x)+α\log₂(s)u.

□

The Realized Encoding

The deployed EquivFlow encoding is

f(x)=B\beginbmatrixℓ_τ(Y(x)) u^′(x) v^′(x)\endbmatrix+b,

(3)

where Y,u^′,v^′ are Rec. 709 luminance and CIE 1976 chromaticity. The toe-limited log luminance is

ℓ_τ(Y)=\begincases\log₂Y,&Y≥τ, \log₂τ+(Y/τ-1)/\ln2,&0≤Y<τ.\endcases

(4)

The frozen numerical values are

\resizebox32490785$B=\beginbmatrix0.0512156526&1.0503072513&0.1687983249 0.0553585156&-0.4965997474&0.3491496748 0.0499266056&0.0399719486&-1.0148571856\endbmatrix$,

\resizebox32490785$b=\beginbmatrix0.4599701209&0.6956425436&1.2171179097\endbmatrixᵀ, τ=0.0010543414867$.

Analytic inverse and transversality.

The scalar function ℓ_τ is strictly increasing on Y≥0, with range [t_\min,∞), where t_\min=\log₂τ-1/\ln2. Its inverse is

ℓ_τ⁻¹(t)=\begincases2ᵗ,&t≥\log₂τ, τ[1+\ln2 (t-\log₂τ)],&t_\min≤t<\log₂τ.\endcases

(5)

Moreover, the selected B is nonsingular: it has rank 3, \detB=0.10697, and spectral condition number 13.77. Thus, for a code z in the image of Eq. (3), one first computes q=B⁻¹(z-b), recovers Y=ℓ_τ⁻¹(q₁), and then converts (Y,q₂,q₃)=(Y,u^′,v^′) uniquely back to linear Rec. 709 RGB. The standard Yu^′v^′ inverse is unique on the admissible positive-color domain (Y>0,v^′>0), and the Rec. 709 RGB–XYZ matrix is nonsingular. Therefore Eq. (3) is injective on that domain.

This argument does not require the exposure and chromatic code directions to be orthogonal. Define the dual functional

λᵀ=e₁ᵀB⁻¹.

Then λᵀBe₁=1 and λᵀBe₂=λᵀBe₃=0. Consequently, λᵀ(z-b) recovers the luminance coordinate, while the chromatic plane span(Be₂,Be₃) lies in \kerλᵀ. This is the non-orthogonal direct-sum transversality realized by the fitted matrix.

Exactness domain.

Above the toe, scaling RGB by s leaves (u^′,v^′) unchanged and increments the first coordinate by \log₂s. Hence Eq. (1) holds whenever both Y and sY are at least τ, with α=\lVertBe₁\rVert₂ and u=Be₁/\lVertBe₁\rVert₂. The linear toe is deliberately finite at black and is not exactly log-equivariant when either endpoint lies below τ.

The implementation floors RGB components at 10⁻⁸ before computing u^′v^′, clamps inverse RGB to the nonnegative orthant, and clamps encoded codes to [0,1] at the VAE interface before mapping them to [-1,1]. Accordingly, analytic injectivity and equivariance refer to the mathematical encoding on the interior where these guards and code clipping are inactive; they are not claims of global invertibility or exact equivariance for the clipped VAE pipeline.

Appendix B Encoding Fitting and Selection

Relation to the main paper.

The main paper describes encoding fitting at the interface level: the closed-form parameters of its Eq. (3) are fitted by frozen-VAE round-trip measurements, and Figure 2 (Step 1) depicts that fitting as a single block. Concretely, this block is realized in two sub-stages. Stage 1 optimizes an auxiliary intermediate map through the frozen VAE by gradient descent; its round-trip component corresponds to main-paper Eq. (7) (see the normalization note below), and the main paper’s code-range requirement enters as the range penalty of the stage-1 objective, Eq. (6) below. Stage 2 produces the deployed encoding in closed form: the stage-1 targets are projected into the affine family of main-paper Eq. (3) by least squares (affine distillation), and one displacement scale is then chosen by the prespecified selection gates. The deployed parameters are therefore obtained as follows: B and b from the closed-form projection, the toe τ carried over from the stage-1 map and frozen, and the first-column scale from the frozen selection rule. Gradient optimization occurs only inside stage 1; the stage-1 map is scaffolding and is discarded after distillation.

Calibration data.

The encoding was fitted once through the frozen LTX video VAE. The fixed calibration pool contains 768 crops: four crops from each of 192 temporal windows. Each crop has 9 frames at 256×256. With seed 0, saturation is sampled uniformly from [.55,.80] and, with probability .5, hue is perturbed uniformly within [-40^∘,40^∘].

Stage 1: VAE-aware fitting targets.

Stage 1 optimizes an intermediate map g only to provide targets for affine distillation. Concretely, g is the fixed-form analytic map

g(x)=sₒᵤₜ⊙M₂{a⊙asinh(b⊙M₁x)+d}+bₒᵤₜ,

where Mᵢ=I+ΔMᵢ; its active tensors comprise the two 3×3 matrices; the three-channel a,b,d,sₒᵤₜ,bₒᵤₜ; an unconstrained three-vector normalized to the unit gauge u; and one log-scale whose exponential is α — 37 scalar parameters, of which u and α serve only the structural terms below. Its internal parameterization is not part of the deployed encoding. The final affine map instead obtains its realized exposure flow directly from Be₁.

The frozen VAE is kept in the computation graph: codes are clamped to [0,1], mapped to [-1,1], encoded and decoded in 32-bit floating point, and mapped back before analytic inversion. VAE parameters receive no gradient. One exposure from 𝔼_\rmfit={0,-4,-2,+2,+4} EV is sampled uniformly at each step.

For a VAE-round-tripped reconstruction x̂, the intermediate fitting objective is

L_fit=L_\log+Lᵤᵥ_Lᵣₜ+\underbraceL_eq+0.25Lₐₘₚ_L_struct+10L_range.

(6)

The three groups respectively measure VAE round-trip fidelity, regularize the exposure–chroma structure, and keep codes inside the useful VAE input range. The weights of L_\log, Lᵤᵥ, and L_eq are one. Specifically,

L_\log=mean\lVert\log(1+x̂)-\log(1+x)\rVert₂²,

and Lᵤᵥ is the mean Euclidean u^′v^′ error over pixels with ground-truth Y≥10⁻³. Thus the compact notation in the main paper denotes a masked per-pixel mean, rather than an unnormalized tensor norm. For e∈𝔼_fit, L_eq penalizes

meanₘ\lVertg(2ᵉx)-g(x)-eαu\rVert₂²,

where g is the intermediate fitting map, u is its learned unit gauge, and α>0 is its learned displacement scale. The term Lₐₘₚ penalizes the change with exposure of the code distance between an image and its chromatically perturbed counterpart. The same valid-luminance mask m=1[Y≥10⁻³] is used. Finally,

L_range=mean{ReLU(g(x)-0.95)²
+ReLU(0.05-g(x))²}.

We use AdamW for 15,000 steps with learning rate 2×10⁻³, weight decay 10⁻⁴, batch size 4, cosine decay to zero, unit gradient clipping, and seed 0.

Stage 2: affine distillation (closed form).

The distillation targets are the code vectors g(x) of the converged stage-1 map on 120,000 RGB samples at {0,-2,-4,-6,-8} EV (600,000 fitting rows); Eq. (3) is fitted to these targets by least squares. The -6 and -8 EV rows evaluate the fixed target map outside its optimization ladder; they do not extend the first-stage optimization. The toe is frozen, the first column of B is swept over c∈{.5,.75,1,1.5,2,2.5,3}, and the bias is recentered using 40,000 additional samples.

Since exposure moves the code along Be₁ with α=\lVertBe₁\rVert₂ (Eq. (1)), scaling that column by c rescales the per-stop displacement relative to the fixed chromatic columns, trading round-trip reconstruction against deep-exposure chromatic separation; Table 1 lists the gate thresholds and the two passing candidates of this sweep. The selected c is not a separate deployed parameter: it is absorbed into the frozen matrix of Eq. (3), whose printed first column already contains it.

Selection is performed before downstream task evaluation. Reconstruction uses a fixed 16-clip encoding-fit validation panel. OOD survival is the ratio of held-out chromaticity R² at -8 EV to that at EV 0 on a fixed 12-clip ARRI–UPIQ OOD survival panel. Grid identification is the four-fold texture-held-out classifier defined below. The projection score is a group-held-out linear probe on absolute top-24-PCA perturbation coordinates; the separation AUC uses the fraction of perturbation energy assigned to independently estimated luminance and chroma subspaces.

No downstream SDR-to-HDR prediction or task metric enters encoding selection; the selection and main-paper reconstruction values estimate different panels.

Encoding selection predates the downstream subset aggregation, but two of the 12 OOD-survival-panel clips also occur in the frozen ARRI subset of the test set. Thus no downstream output or metric is used for selection, but encoding selection and downstream evaluation are not strictly image-disjoint. We treat this gate as design selection and do not claim an untouched-image test for representation selection.

Chromatic-Loss Ablation

We rerun both fitting stages (stage-1 optimization and stage-2 affine distillation), the scale sweep, the frozen selection rule, and 6,500-step adapter training with the chromatic round-trip term Lᵤᵥ removed. All other loss terms and settings are fixed. This fit produces no candidate that passes the selection rule; for diagnostic downstream readout only, its best-reconstruction candidate is exported with the gate explicitly waived.

Removing Lᵤᵥ costs 1.73 dB PU21 and increases mean Δu^′v^′ from .0140 to .0219. The ablation identifies Lᵤᵥ as a load-bearing term in the EquivFlow fitting objective.

Appendix C SDR-to-HDR System Details

Data Construction

HDR targets and split.

The training corpus contains 5,780 crops from 1,015 parent sequences: 2,580 crops from 215 temporal windows extracted from 94 Tears of Steel shots, and 3,200 crops from 800 PolyHaven clips. The parent-disjoint split contains 5,388 training, 324 validation, and 68 test crops. Each clip is normalized by mapping the 75th percentile of its per-frame 99th-percentile luma to unity.

The two sources differ in provenance. PolyHaven renders are scene-referred and retain highlights above reference white. Tears of Steel is a finished 16-bit display grade that we linearize with the inverse sRGB transfer function; its grade has already compressed highlight information. We therefore refer to the combined data as linear Rec. 709 targets, not uniformly as scene-linear radiance.

SDR generation.

Each target has four offline SDR variants. Variant 0 is a clean lossless FFV1 render. Variants 1–3 use independently sampled degradation parameters. The loader selects the clean variant with probability 0.25 and otherwise selects uniformly among the three degraded variants, so each stored variant has marginal probability 0.25. The variant generator uses seed 42+sample index. No online exposure, contrast, blur, or codec augmentation is applied during adapter training.

All training variants use extended Reinhard with white point w=4 and no additional exposure offset. For linear luminance L,

Lₜ=(L(1+L/w²))/(1+L),
L=w²/2[(Lₜ-1)+√(1-Lₜ)²+4Lₜ/w²].(7)

The luminance ratio is applied to RGB, followed by per-channel clipping, sRGB OETF, and 8-bit quantization. The analytic inverse in Eq. (7) inverts the unclipped continuous luminance curve; clipping and quantization remain information-losing.

For degraded variants, sRGB contrast about 0.5 is sampled uniformly from [0.85,1.25]. Gaussian blur with σ∼U[1,3] is applied selectively to highlights above 0.98 and/or shadows below 0.02, each independently with probability 0.7. H.264 encoding uses yuv420p, integer CRF sampled from 18–32, and the medium preset.

Unseen tone curve.

The ACES-like evaluation condition applies

A(y)=clip (y(2.51y+0.03)/y(2.43y+0.59)+0.14,0,1)

(8)

as a luminance-preserving RGB ratio, followed by the same sRGB transfer and 8-bit quantization. This curve is not used to train either internal arm.

Adapter Training and Inference

The base model is the LTX-2.3 22B checkpoint ltx-2.3-22b-dev.safetensors; its transformer, VAE, and text encoder remain frozen. IC-LoRA reference tokens use clean (t=0) latents, participate in bidirectional attention, and are excluded from the denoising loss. Rank-32 modules use scale 32 and dropout 0. They are inserted into the q, k, v, and output projections of attn1 and attn2, and into ff.net.0.proj and ff.net.2.

Each arm is trained once for a fixed 6,500-step comparison budget, rather than a validation-selected checkpoint. We use AdamW at learning rate 2×10⁻⁴ with unit gradient clipping and a linear factor 1 → .1 over a 100,000-step horizon. Training uses four NVIDIA H100 80GB GPUs, per-GPU batch size 1, accumulation 1 (effective batch 4), BF16, gradient checkpointing, and seed 42. Noise follows a shifted logit-normal distribution with standard deviation 1, ε=10⁻³, a .1 uniform mixture, and the model’s sequence-dependent shift.

The positive prompt is “A high dynamic range cinematic scene with bright highlights and deep shadows.”; the negative prompt is “worst quality, inconsistent motion, blurry, jittery, distorted.” Inference uses seed 42, 30 steps, guidance 4, and spatiotemporal guidance 1 at block 28 in stg_v mode. All settings other than the conditioning contract and encoding are shared: EquivFlow conditions on the analytically inverse-tone-mapped proxy, whereas LogC3 uses the display-referred SDR directly.

Appendix D Evaluation Definitions

Common output domain.

All outputs are decoded to linear Rec. 709 before evaluation. PU21 uses 100 nits per normalized linear unit, clamps absolute luminance to [0.005,10,000] nits, applies the banding–glare PU21 encoding normalized to unit peak, and reports PSNR with peak 1.

For chromatic ΔC_TC_P, Rec. 709 is converted to Rec. 2020 and then to PQ ICtCp using the 10,000-nit convention. We use the ITP scaling (I,T,P)=(I,0.5C_T,C_P) and report the mean

720√(0.5ΔC_T)²+(ΔC_P)².

This omits the intensity difference by construction.

Luminance-independent chroma metrics.

Let r(x)=x/(∑_cx_c+ε), with ε=10⁻⁴ used only to avoid division by zero. Chroma L1 is mean|r(x̂)-r(x)|. Mean Δu^′v^′ is the Euclidean CIE 1976 chromaticity error over ground-truth pixels with Y≥10⁻³. LF drift first applies a spatial Gaussian with σ=8 to the chromaticity fields and measures the same masked error. Range drift further restricts evaluation to pixels whose SDR input is neither clipped nor null: all channels are below 254/255 and the maximum channel exceeds 3/255. The null region is replaced by the target field before Gaussian filtering to prevent invalid boundaries from leaking into the range mask.

Main-paper frozen-VAE probe.

Table 1 in the main paper uses no diffusion training. Its reconstruction column is the mean per-clip log-RGB PSNR after a frozen-VAE round trip on 16 deterministically sampled held-out validation clips (a panel distinct from the encoding-selection panel of Table 1). For the chromatic columns, 12 deterministic center-cropped clips from the ARRI–UPIQ OOD pool are evaluated at {0,-2,-4,-6,-8,-10} EV. Only latent tokens whose EV-0 ground-truth luminance is at least 10⁻³ are used. At every exposure and for each encoding separately, a StandardScaler followed by ridge regression with penalty 1 is refitted to predict u^′ and v^′. Five-fold GroupKFold by parent clip supplies held-out predictions; the reported R²_u^′v^′ is the mean of the two coordinate scores and surv₋ₖ=R²(-k)/R²(0). Because held-out R² is unbounded below and the numerator can exceed its EV-0 value, survival may be negative or exceed one. It measures relative linear recoverability, not chroma-energy amplification.

Cross-VAE probe.

The structural-portability test applies the same fixed encoding to each frozen host VAE over the exposure ladder {0,-2,-4,-6,-8}. Its chroma grid comprises 12 chromaticities (two radii, 0.03 and 0.06, at six equally spaced hue angles about D65) rendered with four luminance textures at base luminance 0.45. Grid identification is 12-way accuracy; chance is 1/12. At each host and exposure, a StandardScaler plus logistic regression (C=1) is evaluated by four-fold GroupKFold, holding out one luminance texture per fold. Thus the table’s grid readout is host- and exposure-specific.

For the exposure readout, a host-specific direction is the first right singular vector of all nonzero-EV latent differences. The scalar β(e) is their mean projection on that direction, and R²_β is the no-intercept linear fit of β(e) to EV. The reported Δu^′v^′₋₈ is the encoding round-trip chromaticity error at -8 EV. The prespecified non-collapse check uses 16 fixed clips (15 with a nonempty EV-0 luminance mask) and requires each foreign host’s round-trip Δu^′v^′ to be no more than twice the LTX value at both -6 and -8 EV. This is a within-subject collapse check, not a comparative superiority test.

EV-0-frozen readout.

The main paper notes that an EV-0-frozen readout degrades along each host’s exposure trajectory. This diagnostic fits the chroma-grid classifier at EV 0 and applies it unchanged at deeper exposures, instead of refitting per exposure as in the grid column of main-paper Table 4. Under the frozen readout, -8 EV grid accuracy falls to .208 (LTX), .083 (SD 2.1, chance level), .167 (Wan 2.1), and .250 (Wan 2.2) from EV-0 values of .979, .667, .958, and .979, while the per-exposure refitted readout remains high (main-paper Table 4). The latent coordinates therefore rotate or rescale along each host’s exposure trajectory even though exposure structure and chroma separability persist; the portability claim concerns the latter, not shared latent coordinates.

LEDiff radiometric alignment.

LEDiff is run with its official preprocessing and checkpoint. A single method-level scalar gain is fitted once on 24 fixed, parent-distinct training clips and then held fixed for every evaluation set. With luminance y, the gain is

g_\rmLEDiff=\exp (mean_y_\rmgt>10⁻⁴δ)=0.0294942,
δ=\log(y_\rmgt+10⁻⁴)-\log(y_\rmpred+10⁻⁴).

No test image, test ground truth, or per-clip gain enters this fit.

Qualitative selection and display.

For each evaluation set, the main-paper figure selects the evaluated crop with the largest EquivFlow–LumiVid ΔE_ITP margin; it therefore shows selected successes, not representative or median cases. ARRI and HDRTV4K are displayed in the full frame containing that crop, whereas UPIQ contains one evaluated crop. The inset is chosen as the darkest chroma-carrying target region that remains inside one reconstructed crop. A row-specific display gain is applied identically to every column and affects no reported metric. For HDRTV4K, only the evaluated quadrant contributes to quantitative results; the other quadrants are display context.

Appendix E Statistical Protocol and Full Results

Frozen evaluation subset.

The frozen 102-clip test subset of main-paper Table 2 was fixed before any subset aggregation was computed. Table 4 records the per-set selection rule.

Aggregation and inference.

Metrics are first averaged within each parent and then averaged with equal weight across parents. The chroma-decomposition panel uses the full HDRTV4K–UPIQ pool of 58 parents (36 HDRTV4K and 22 UPIQ). Confidence intervals are nonparametric parent-cluster bootstrap intervals from 10,000 resamples with seed 42. Pairwise tests are two-sided, parent-level paired Wilcoxon signed-rank tests. For the dataset-wise table, Holm correction is applied within each method pair and curve across three datasets and two primary metrics. For the chroma panel, correction is applied within each curve across its three primary metrics. There is one trained model per internal arm; bootstrap intervals characterize parent-level sampling uncertainty rather than variation across training runs.

Dataset-wise internal comparison.

Table 5 supplies the parent-level tests behind the dataset-wise statements in the main paper. Deltas are EquivFlow-LogC3, so positive PU21-PSNR and negative ΔC_TC_P favor EquivFlow. The UPIQ chromatic difference is significant under the training curve; HDRTV4K and UPIQ are significant under the unseen curve. ARRI does not separate under either curve, and HDRTV4K does not separate under the training curve.

Chroma-panel statistics.

Table 3 gives the paired differences underlying the main paper’s chroma panel for the fixed 6,500-step EquivFlow checkpoint. Units are parent scenes (n=58); each entry is EquivFlow-LogC3 with a 10,000-sample bootstrap 95% interval. The three primary metrics use Holm-corrected p_H. The two nested filtered forms of Δu^′v^′ are descriptive, use uncorrected p, and lie outside the correction family.

Interpretive boundary.

Under matched Reinhard, EquivFlow has higher aggregate-fidelity point estimates on the frozen subset. That aggregate advantage does not persist under the ACES-like swap. The result that remains consistent across the two tested curves is narrower: the full EquivFlow system has lower luminance-independent chromaticity error than the same-backbone LogC3 system. Because the arms also differ in reference reconstruction, these results attribute the effect to the complete conditioning system, not to the encoding alone.
item.content:encoded:
一句话：常见 log 类编码会在生成前抑制低亮度处的色差，造成「暗部塌陷」——这是编码问题不是模型问题。

要点：

  • 任务本身是病态的：SDR 转 HDR 要恢复被截断的高光、压死的暗部与量化痕迹，同时保住原内容
  • 作者把失败点定位到**信号如何穿过预训练 VAE**：常见的 log 类编码会在生成之前就抑制低亮度区域的色差，导致「暗部塌陷」
  • 因此提出 VAE 感知的 HDR 编码方式，而不是继续加更大的潜扩散先验

为什么值得看：HDR 是显示与渲染管线里最容易被「AI 后处理」搞坏的一环，而多数工作只顾换模型。这篇指出瓶颈在编码表示——这类「先改数据表示再谈模型」的诊断，对做 HDR 管线的人更有迁移价值。

中文摘要：SDR 到 HDR 的重建本身是病态问题：必须在恢复被截断的高光、被压死的暗部与量化伪影的同时保住原始内容。潜扩散模型能提供强生成先验，但作者发现其效果被一个更早的环节限制住——HDR 信号如何穿过预训练的 VAE。常见的 log 类编码会在生成发生之前就抑制低亮度区域的色差，造成所谓「暗部塌陷」。因此论文提出 VAE 感知的 HDR 编码方案，把问题从「换更强的生成模型」挪回到「先把信号编码对」。对显示与渲染管线而言，这个诊断比再刷一个指标更有用。

主题：AI Rendering

来源：arXiv·cs.CV（English）

原文发布：2026-11-11

本期推送：2026-11-13

Dark Matters: VAE-Aware HDR Encoding for SDR-to-HDR Video Reconstruction

Abstract

SDR-to-HDR reconstruction is an ill-posed problem in which clipped highlights, crushed shadows, and quantization artifacts must be recovered while preserving the original content. Latent diffusion models provide powerful generative priors for restoring missing detail, but their effectiveness is constrained by how HDR signals pass through the pretrained VAE. We find that common log-like encodings suppress low-luminance chromatic differences before generation, producing a dark-side collapse in the frozen-VAE latent. We introduce EquivFlow, a compact, invertible exposure-equivariant encoding that maps exposure changes to additive shifts while retaining a scale-independent chromatic component, without modifying the VAE. Encoding-level tests across pretrained image and video VAEs show that its exposure structure and deep-dark chroma transport persist across the tested hosts. Integrated into SDR-to-HDR video diffusion, EquivFlow delivers consistent chromatic-fidelity gains across the tested settings while retaining competitive reconstruction fidelity.

1STUDIO FREEWILLUSION Inc.

2Seoul National University

Introduction

The growing adoption of high-dynamic-range (HDR) displays and production workflows has increased the demand for converting existing standard-dynamic-range (SDR) content into HDR. This demand extends beyond conventional film and video remastering to a range of applications, including AI-assisted content creation workflows in which image or video assets are produced in SDR or otherwise limited-dynamic-range form and must be integrated into HDR production pipelines. SDR-to-HDR reconstruction is therefore becoming increasingly relevant across these application areas.

Dark-region fidelity is also a practical requirement in HDR mastering. Production quality control treats crushed blacks as a defect when underexposure removes intended shadow detail, texture, and depth [(Netflix n.d.)]. At the signal level, perceptual HDR coding allocates precision according to luminance-dependent visibility thresholds so that quantization artifacts remain uniformly small [(Miller, Nezamabadi, and Daly 2013)]. These practices motivate preserving not only shadow luminance but also low-luminance chromatic evidence before it enters the pretrained VAE.

Inverse tone mapping is an inherently ill-posed, one-to-many problem. A single SDR observation may correspond to multiple plausible HDR signals because highlight clipping removes intensity variation above the SDR range, while shadow crushing, quantization, and banding suppress subtle luminance and chromatic differences in dark regions. Deterministic tone expansion alone cannot uniquely recover this missing information. A successful SDR-to-HDR method must instead infer plausible detail in ambiguous regions while preserving the spatial and chromatic evidence that remains in the input.

Recent diffusion-based SDR-to-HDR methods address this ambiguity using pretrained generative models. Before generation, latent implementations encode HDR signals with a pretrained variational autoencoder (VAE). Recent systems first compress linear HDR with prescribed log-like transforms—LogC3 in LumiVid and Log-Gamma in DiffHDR—so that it lies within the pretrained VAE’s operating range [(Korem et al. 2026; Yu et al. 2026)]. The representation passed through the VAE can therefore affect which luminance and chromatic distinctions remain available to the reconstruction model.

Observation 1: latent chromatic structure collapses at low luminance.

Linear HDR signals are poorly matched to the bounded input range of pretrained VAEs; Figure 1 qualitatively illustrates how log-like chromatic trajectories contract in the frozen-VAE latent space at low exposure. Table 1 quantifies this behavior: LogC3 and Log-Gamma match or exceed EquivFlow in frozen-VAE round-trip reconstruction, yet retain less linearly recoverable chroma at -8 EV, with LogC3 unrecoverable there. These frozen-VAE representation and round-trip measurements diagnose what reaches the generative model; they are not downstream SDR-to-HDR reconstruction results.

Observation 2: exposure changes scale, not chromaticity.

In linear HDR, multiplicative exposure changes overall scale while leaving chromaticity unchanged. This suggests an encoding in which exposure becomes translation along a fixed code-space direction and a transverse chromatic component remains scale-independent. In our construction, this relation is exact above the luminance toe when both exposure endpoints remain above it.

These observations motivate EquivFlow, an invertible exposure-equivariant encoding optimized through the frozen target VAE. It adapts the representation to the VAE’s operating geometry without modifying the pretrained generative backbone.

Our contributions are:

(i) We identify and measure the loss of linearly recoverable chromatic structure in dark regions after frozen-VAE encoding, and show that the failure is asymmetric across exposure. (ii) We derive EquivFlow, an invertible, 13-parameter exposure-equivariant encoding with an analytic inverse, fitted through frozen-VAE round-trip measurements, and examine its structural behavior across multiple pretrained video VAEs. (iii) We integrate EquivFlow into SDR-to-HDR video diffusion and evaluate it against established baselines, obtaining consistent chromatic-fidelity gains across the tested settings while retaining competitive reconstruction fidelity.

Related Work

Inverse tone mapping and learning-based SDR-to-HDR.

Classical iTM expands observed SDR luminance using analytical or spatially adaptive operators [(Banterle et al. 2006; Rempel et al. 2007)], but cannot model content missing from the input. Learning-based methods instead predict saturated radiance with HDRCNN [(Eilertsen et al. 2017)], regress HDR through multi-scale features with ExpandNet [(Marnerides et al. 2018)], or decompose global mapping, local enhancement, and highlight generation with HDRTVNet [(Chen et al. 2021)]. These supervised feed-forward models motivate generative priors for severely underdetermined regions.

Diffusion-based SDR-to-HDR reconstruction.

Diffusion priors offer a way to synthesize plausible content where the SDR input carries no usable evidence. Existing methods incorporate such priors at different stages of reconstruction: Semantic-Aware Diffusion iTM completes saturated regions before merging estimated exposures [(Goswami et al. 2025)]; LEDiff generates and fuses exposure-dependent latents within an LDR latent coordinate system [(Wang et al. 2025)]; and gain-map diffusion predicts an SDR base and a gain map [(Guan et al. 2025)].

Many of these diffusion-based approaches build on latent diffusion models, which perform denoising in the latent space of a pretrained autoencoder rather than directly in pixel space [(Rombach et al. 2022)]. This formulation is particularly attractive for SDR-to-HDR reconstruction, as it enables the reuse of strong pretrained image or video priors while operating on compact perceptual representations. Adapting an SDR-pretrained latent diffusion model to HDR, however, also requires mapping HDR signals into a form compatible with its pretrained autoencoder. LumiVid addresses distribution alignment by applying a fixed LogC3 [(Brendel 2017)] transform before a frozen video VAE, thereby mapping scene-linear HDR signals closer to the pretrained latent distribution [(Korem et al. 2026)]. DiffHDR follows a related design using a fixed Log-Gamma transform with a frozen video VAE [(Yu et al. 2026)]. These designs highlight HDR encoding as an important component of latent diffusion pipelines for SDR-to-HDR reconstruction.

Luminance and chrominance.

Low-light enhancement methods have also emphasized how luminance interacts with color. HVI introduces a trainable color space that separates intensity from chromatic components and compresses low-intensity coordinates to suppress noise [(Yan et al. 2025)]. ICLR further improves luminance–chrominance interaction through dual-stream feature exchange and a covariance correction loss [(Xu et al. 2026)]. These methods show that restoration quality depends not only on network capacity, but also on how luminance and chromatic information are organized before feature extraction. This consideration becomes particularly important when signals undergo strong dynamic-range compression, since subtle chromatic distinctions in dark regions may be attenuated before later restoration stages can exploit them.

Method

Overview

Our method reconstructs scene-linear HDR video from a display-referred SDR observation through a frozen latent video diffusion model. It is defined by three choices. The SDR observation is first mapped to a scene-linear proxy by a fixed preprocessing convention, so that the observation and HDR target can be expressed in one scene-linear coordinate system. That space is then carried into the pretrained VAE by an invertible exposure-equivariant color encoding f_θ, which is what the generative model actually sees. Here, “encoding” denotes an invertible, pointwise reparameterization of scene-linear color rather than a transformation of scene content. The encoding is learned first, against the frozen VAE, so that subsequent adapter training operates in a code space already adapted to the bottleneck it must pass through.

Exposure Equivariance

The constraint is motivated by what the frozen VAE receives. Log-like encodings can shrink dark chromatic differences before the VAE sees them (Figure 1), leaving the generative prior conditioned on an already attenuated signal. We therefore seek an encoding in which exposure changes move codes predictably without reducing chromatic separations.

Exposure acts on scene-linear color by a positive scalar, x↦sx. We require the encoding to turn this multiplicative action into a translation along a fixed unit direction u of code space:

f_θ(sx)=f_θ(x)+α\log₂(s) u, \lVertu\rVert₂=1,

(1)

with α the code displacement per exposure stop.

Equation (1) gives exposure and chromaticity separate roles in the code. Along u the code travels with exposure; transverse to u it is untouched by any global scaling and therefore carries chromatic information. In particular, code differences are exposure-invariant, f_θ(sx)-f_θ(sy)=f_θ(x)-f_θ(y), so chromatic amplitude does not contract merely because luminance falls.

The requirement is restrictive enough to be characterized. A map satisfies Eq. (1) for all s>0 if and only if it decomposes as

f_θ(x)=α\log₂ρ(x) u+Ψ_θ (x/ρ(x)),

(2)

where ρ is positive and 1-homogeneous (ρ(sx)=sρ(x)) and Ψ_θ is defined on the chromaticity slice {x:ρ(x)=1}, with its image taken transverse to the exposure direction u. Taking Ψ_θ to be the restriction of f_θ to that slice and applying Eq. (1) with s=ρ(x) gives one direction; 1-homogeneity of ρ gives the other. The supplement states and proves this formally.

Equation (2) gives a practical template for the encoding. The function ρ chooses the brightness coordinate, Ψ_θ encodes the color remaining after brightness normalization, and α sets how far the code moves per exposure stop. Since the VAE accepts only a bounded input range, these choices are fixed as a measured operating point for the target VAE rather than set from color-science principles alone. The construction gives an invertible representation in which exposure and color have explicit roles before the representation is fitted to the target VAE.

Encoding Parameterization

Our encoding, EquivFlow, realizes Eq. (2) in closed form with 13 fitted parameters. We take ρ=Y, the Rec.709 luminance [(ITU-R 2015)], which is positive and 1-homogeneous, and coordinatize the chromaticity slice by the CIE 1976 coordinates (u^′,v^′)[(CIE 2024)], which are invariant under x↦sx by construction. Both roles of Eq. (2) are then linear, and the encoding is a single affine map of the feature triple φ(x)=(ℓ_τ(Y), u^′, v^′):

f_θ(x)=B φ(x)+b,

(3)

whose intensity coordinate is a toe-limited logarithm,

ℓ_τ(Y)=\begincases\log₂Y,&Y≥τ, [2.0pt] \log₂τ+\dfracY/τ-1\ln2,&Y<τ.\endcases

(4)

The fitted toe τ is required because \log₂ diverges as Y→0 while the code range is bounded; below it the intensity coordinate continues linearly with matched value and slope. This keeps the luminance coordinate finite near black without introducing a discontinuity at the toe.

Above the toe the encoding satisfies Eq. (1) exactly rather than approximately: u^′ and v^′ are unchanged by scaling and ℓ_τ(sY)=ℓ_τ(Y)+\log₂s, so f_θ(sx)=f_θ(x)+\log₂(s) Be₁. The flow direction and the per-stop budget are therefore read off the first column of B,

u=(Be₁)/(\lVertBe₁\rVert₂), α=\lVertBe₁\rVert₂,

(5)

so the exposure direction and per-stop displacement are determined by the first column of B. Inversion needs no learned decoder: solving the affine system gives φ=B⁻¹(z-b), from which Y=ℓ_τ⁻¹(φ₁) and (Y,u^′,v^′) maps back to linear Rec.709 in closed form, followed by the nonnegativity projection. The 13 parameters are the 9 entries of B, the 3 offsets b, and the toe τ.

VAE-Aware Optimization

Analytic invertibility does not imply survival through the pretrained bottleneck. The encoder is frozen and has its own operating geometry, so theclosed-form parameters of Eq. (3) are fitted against that geometry rather than from color-science principles alone. For the encoding f_θ, the relevant measurement is the frozen VAE round trip

x→f_θ(x)→D(E(f_θ(x)))→f_θ⁻¹(D(E(f_θ(x)))),

(6)

where E and D are the frozen encoder and decoder and the final inverse is followed by the nonnegativity projection.

Let x̂_θ denote the output of this round trip. For EquivFlow, we score VAE compatibility by the round-trip reconstruction loss

Lᵣₜ=\lVert\log(1+x̂_θ)-\log(1+x)\rVert₂²
+λᵤᵥ\lVertm(x)(q(x̂_θ)-q(x))\rVert₂².(7)

Here q(x)=(u^′(x),v^′(x)) and m(x) masks pixels above the dark-noise floor. The encoding is also required to keep codes in the VAE input range before hard clipping.

The EquivFlow encoding is an exactly exposure-equivariant closed form with an analytic inverse, fitted by frozen-VAE round-trip measurements before any task-level diffusion evaluation.

The fitted parameters belong to the VAE they were fitted against; how far one parameter set transfers to other frozen bottlenecks is measured in the experiments rather than assumed.

SDR-to-HDR Reconstruction

After fitting, the encoding is fixed. For supervised training and evaluation, each scene-linear HDR target x is rendered to a display-referred SDR observation by a fixed recipe: normalization, extended Reinhard tone mapping, per-channel clipping, the sRGB OETF [(IEC 1999)], and 8-bit quantization. The SDR observation is then mapped to a scene-linear proxy x̃ using a fixed Reinhard inverse-tone-mapping preprocessing convention. This proxy defines the conditioning coordinate used by the model, while clipped, crushed, and quantized content remains underdetermined. Because the preprocessing contract may affect performance, the experiments additionally evaluate tone-mapper variants rendered with Reinhard [(Reinhard et al. 2002)] and ACES-like [(Narkowicz 2016)] curves.

Both x and x̃ are mapped through the same encoding f_θ and encoded online by the frozen VAE. The target latent serves as the diffusion target, while the proxy latent is supplied as in-context conditioning.

At inference, the conditioned diffusion model predicts an HDR encoding latent. The frozen VAE decoder maps this latent to encoding space, after which the analytic inverse of f_θ maps the result to linear HDR:

x̂=f_θ⁻¹(D(ĥ)).

(8)

Diffusion backbone and IC-LoRA adaptation.

The reconstruction model uses an in-context LoRA conditioning scheme [(Huang et al. 2024)]. In our implementation, the SDR condition latent is formed from the scene-linear proxy after the same color encoding f_θ, rather than from raw SDR. It is prepended as clean reference tokens to the noised HDR target-token sequence; reference tokens receive zero timestep and are excluded from the denoising loss, which is evaluated only on the target portion. Only the low-rank adapter [(Hu et al. 2022)] is optimized; the VAE, diffusion backbone, and text encoder remain frozen.

Experiments

Datasets and Setup

Training corpus. All internal arms are trained on one corpus of 5,780 crops at 960×544 and 49 frames, drawn from 1,015 parent sequences: 215 windows from 94 Tears of Steel[(Blender Foundation 2012)] shots (2,580 crops) and 800 clips rendered from PolyHaven [(Poly Haven n.d.)] HDRI panoramas (3,200 crops). Splits are parent-disjoint, shot-level for Tears of Steel and asset-level for PolyHaven.

These are fixed derivatives of the cited public sources, not a newly introduced dataset or benchmark.

Training inputs. Training SDR inputs use the fixed Reinhard-based rendering protocol described in the Method section, followed by the same camera-style degradations for every internal arm: contrast scaling, band-selective blur, 8-bit quantization, and codec compression. Evaluation additionally includes ACES-like renderings.

Evaluation sets. We evaluate on ARRI’s official ALEXA Mini ProRes 4444 XQ sample reel M001R00H [(ARRI n.d.)], HDRTV4K [(Guo et al. 2023)], and UPIQ [(Mikhailiuk et al. 2021)], decoding every prediction to common linear Rec. 709 [(ITU-R 2015)] before scoring. ARRI contains 176 crops from 44 cinema-camera parents and is the brightest set. HDRTV4K contains 78 clips from 36 parents of mixed video and static content, including material from the source used by HDRTVNet++. UPIQ contains one 49-frame static clip for each of 22 calibrated image parents, so temporal metrics are undefined there. The main table reports a 102-clip test subset frozen before any aggregation was computed: the first 40 ARRI crops (10 parents), the first 40 HDRTV4K clips (19 parents), and all 22 UPIQ parents. The chromatic-decomposition panel is computed on the full HDRTV4K–UPIQ pool.

Baselines. The internal rows share the training split above, the frozen LTX-2.3 22B backbone and VAE [(HaCohen et al. 2024; Lightricks 2026)], IC-LoRA adapter [(Huang et al. 2024)], inference settings, and scorer. We report the protocol from the Method section: canonical Reinhard inputs and one unseen tone mapper, ACES-like. LogC3 is the matched internal baseline: it is retrained on the same corpus and degradation protocol with the same backbone, conditioning method, and scorer. The two internal arms differ in the HDR representation and in its paired reference contract: EquivFlow conditions on the inverse-tone-mapped scene-linear proxy of the Method section, which is part of the contribution, while LogC3 is trained under raw-SDR conditioning, the official contract of LumiVid.

LumiVid is reported separately because it is the closest architectural predecessor: a pretrained video diffusion model adapted for SDR-to-HDR through a fixed LogC3 interface. HDRTVNet++ [(Chen et al. 2023)] and LEDiff [(Wang et al. 2025)] are external system baselines that differ in architecture, training data, and budget. LEDiff uses its official preprocessing and one method-level radiometric gain fitted on a frozen 24-clip training subset, without access to test images or per-clip ground truth.

Main Results

Quantitative results. Table 2 evaluates the frozen test subset under the training Reinhard curve and an unseen ACES-like curve, with the target and evaluated clips held fixed. PU21-PSNR [(Mantiuk and Azimi 2021)] measures aggregate HDR reconstruction, while ΔC_TC_P, the chromatic component of ΔE_ITP[(ITU-R 2019)], measures perceptual chromatic error at absolute luminance. Under the training curve, EquivFlow leads the matched LogC3 control on both quantities across all three sets. Under the unseen curve, it retains the chromatic lead throughout, while LogC3 takes the aggregate PU21-PSNR lead. The consistent result is therefore improved chromatic fidelity across tone curves; aggregate reconstruction depends more strongly on the SDR rendering. Parent-level tests support the matched-pair chromatic difference on UPIQ under the training curve and on HDRTV4K and UPIQ under the unseen curve; the smaller ARRI subset does not separate under the training curve. Remaining preregistered metrics and full statistical details are reported in the supplement.

Baseline comparison. LumiVid is the closest architectural predecessor and therefore the most direct external comparison. EquivFlow has lower chromatic error in every column and higher aggregate fidelity in all but the HDRTV4K ACES-like case. It also leads LEDiff and HDRTVNet++ on both reported quantities wherever a comparison is available; HDRTVNet++ is withheld on HDRTV4K because that set is same-domain. These remain system-level comparisons because architecture, training data, radiometric convention, and budget differ.

Chromatic decomposition. To test whether the main-table chromatic trend depends on one metric, Table 3 evaluates the matched pair using raw chroma amplitude, exposure-invariant CIE 1976 chromaticity, and PQ-encoded ICtCp [(ITU-R 2018)]. Every metric favors EquivFlow under both tone curves, with a larger margin under the unseen curve. This consistency supports the chromatic-fidelity reading across the tested metrics and curves.

Qualitative results. Figure 4 shows the highest-margin EquivFlow–LumiVid example from each evaluation set, so the rows show selected successes rather than typical cases. In the magnified dark regions, EquivFlow remains closer to the target’s color and local structure, while the comparison outputs show stronger saturation, hue, or shadow-level deviations. These examples complement, but do not replace, the dataset-level quantitative comparisons above.

Representation Analysis

Table 1 tests representation behavior before diffusion by passing each published encoding through the same frozen VAE without a fitted head. The log-like encodings reconstruct well but lose linearly recoverable chroma as exposure falls, whereas EquivFlow preserves it; reconstruction quality is therefore not a proxy for dark-exposure chroma retention. This divergence is consistent with exposure–chroma coupling and matches the downstream widening of the chromatic margin under the unseen tone curve (Tables 2 and 3). We next examine the supporting design choices.

Cross-VAE transfer test.EquivFlow’s exposure structure is tested on frozen LTX, Stable Diffusion 2.1 [(Rombach et al. 2022; Stability AI 2022)], Wan 2.1 T2V-1.3B [(Team Wan et al. 2025)], and Wan 2.2 TI2V-5B [(Wan Team 2025)] VAEs; only LTX was used during fitting. On the three foreign hosts, the exposure-linked latent displacement remains nearly linear and chromaticity readout stays above chance at deep exposure. All three foreign hosts pass the frozen roundtrip non-collapse rule in that regime.

Portability here concerns the exposure structure, not the latent coordinates themselves: an EV-0-frozen readout degrades along each host’s exposure trajectory, and absolute round-trip quality varies substantially across hosts.

Conclusion

We introduced EquivFlow, a VAE-aware HDR encoding motivated by the loss of recoverable chromatic structure under darkening in common log-like representations. Its compact, invertible, pointwise construction maps exposure changes to code-space translations while preserving a scale-independent chromatic component, without modifying the pretrained VAE or diffusion backbone. Representation analyses across pretrained image and video VAEs confirm the persistence of this structure, and integration into SDR-to-HDR video diffusion yields consistent chromatic-fidelity gains across the tested datasets and tone curves while retaining competitive reconstruction fidelity. Together, these results establish VAE-aware encoding as an effective interface for adapting pretrained latent generative models to HDR reconstruction. Future work will examine this design across broader VAE families and reconstruction settings.

（参考文献见原文。）

Supplementary Material

Appendix A Exposure-Equivariant Encodings

This section states the general characterization used in the main paper and then verifies the properties of the realized encoding. Let f:ℝ_>0³→ℝᵈ be a code map, let u∈ℝᵈ be a unit vector, and let α>0. We say that f is exposure-equivariant along u if, for every color x∈ℝ_>0³ and every exposure scale s>0,

f(sx)=f(x)+α\log₂(s)u.

(1)

Proposition 1 (characterization).

Let ρ:ℝ_>0³→ℝ_>0 be any positive 1-homogeneous function, ρ(sx)=sρ(x), and define

ℂ_ρ={c∈ℝ_>0³:ρ(c)=1}.

A map f satisfies Eq. (1) if and only if there exists a map Ψ:ℂ_ρ→ℝᵈ such that

f(x)=α\log₂ρ(x)u+Ψ (x/ρ(x)).

(2)

This characterization alone does not assert injectivity; transversality and injectivity of the chromatic component are additional requirements.

Proof.

Assume Eq. (1). For c∈ℂ_ρ, define Ψ(c)=f(c). For arbitrary x, set c=x/ρ(x). Homogeneity gives ρ(c)=1 and x=ρ(x)c. Hence

f(x)=f(c)+α\log₂ρ(x)u=Ψ(c)+α\log₂ρ(x)u,

which is Eq. (2). Conversely, homogeneity gives ρ(sx)=sρ(x) and sx/ρ(sx)=x/ρ(x). Substitution into Eq. (2) yields

f(sx)=α\log₂(sρ(x))u+Ψ (x/ρ(x))=f(x)+α\log₂(s)u.

□

The Realized Encoding

The deployed EquivFlow encoding is

f(x)=B\beginbmatrixℓ_τ(Y(x)) u^′(x) v^′(x)\endbmatrix+b,

(3)

where Y,u^′,v^′ are Rec. 709 luminance and CIE 1976 chromaticity. The toe-limited log luminance is

ℓ_τ(Y)=\begincases\log₂Y,&Y≥τ, \log₂τ+(Y/τ-1)/\ln2,&0≤Y<τ.\endcases

(4)

The frozen numerical values are

\resizebox32490785$B=\beginbmatrix0.0512156526&1.0503072513&0.1687983249 0.0553585156&-0.4965997474&0.3491496748 0.0499266056&0.0399719486&-1.0148571856\endbmatrix$,

\resizebox32490785$b=\beginbmatrix0.4599701209&0.6956425436&1.2171179097\endbmatrixᵀ, τ=0.0010543414867$.

Analytic inverse and transversality.

The scalar function ℓ_τ is strictly increasing on Y≥0, with range [t_\min,∞), where t_\min=\log₂τ-1/\ln2. Its inverse is

ℓ_τ⁻¹(t)=\begincases2ᵗ,&t≥\log₂τ, τ[1+\ln2 (t-\log₂τ)],&t_\min≤t<\log₂τ.\endcases

(5)

Moreover, the selected B is nonsingular: it has rank 3, \detB=0.10697, and spectral condition number 13.77. Thus, for a code z in the image of Eq. (3), one first computes q=B⁻¹(z-b), recovers Y=ℓ_τ⁻¹(q₁), and then converts (Y,q₂,q₃)=(Y,u^′,v^′) uniquely back to linear Rec. 709 RGB. The standard Yu^′v^′ inverse is unique on the admissible positive-color domain (Y>0,v^′>0), and the Rec. 709 RGB–XYZ matrix is nonsingular. Therefore Eq. (3) is injective on that domain.

This argument does not require the exposure and chromatic code directions to be orthogonal. Define the dual functional

λᵀ=e₁ᵀB⁻¹.

Then λᵀBe₁=1 and λᵀBe₂=λᵀBe₃=0. Consequently, λᵀ(z-b) recovers the luminance coordinate, while the chromatic plane span(Be₂,Be₃) lies in \kerλᵀ. This is the non-orthogonal direct-sum transversality realized by the fitted matrix.

Exactness domain.

Above the toe, scaling RGB by s leaves (u^′,v^′) unchanged and increments the first coordinate by \log₂s. Hence Eq. (1) holds whenever both Y and sY are at least τ, with α=\lVertBe₁\rVert₂ and u=Be₁/\lVertBe₁\rVert₂. The linear toe is deliberately finite at black and is not exactly log-equivariant when either endpoint lies below τ.

The implementation floors RGB components at 10⁻⁸ before computing u^′v^′, clamps inverse RGB to the nonnegative orthant, and clamps encoded codes to [0,1] at the VAE interface before mapping them to [-1,1]. Accordingly, analytic injectivity and equivariance refer to the mathematical encoding on the interior where these guards and code clipping are inactive; they are not claims of global invertibility or exact equivariance for the clipped VAE pipeline.

Appendix B Encoding Fitting and Selection

Relation to the main paper.

The main paper describes encoding fitting at the interface level: the closed-form parameters of its Eq. (3) are fitted by frozen-VAE round-trip measurements, and Figure 2 (Step 1) depicts that fitting as a single block. Concretely, this block is realized in two sub-stages. Stage 1 optimizes an auxiliary intermediate map through the frozen VAE by gradient descent; its round-trip component corresponds to main-paper Eq. (7) (see the normalization note below), and the main paper’s code-range requirement enters as the range penalty of the stage-1 objective, Eq. (6) below. Stage 2 produces the deployed encoding in closed form: the stage-1 targets are projected into the affine family of main-paper Eq. (3) by least squares (affine distillation), and one displacement scale is then chosen by the prespecified selection gates. The deployed parameters are therefore obtained as follows: B and b from the closed-form projection, the toe τ carried over from the stage-1 map and frozen, and the first-column scale from the frozen selection rule. Gradient optimization occurs only inside stage 1; the stage-1 map is scaffolding and is discarded after distillation.

Calibration data.

The encoding was fitted once through the frozen LTX video VAE. The fixed calibration pool contains 768 crops: four crops from each of 192 temporal windows. Each crop has 9 frames at 256×256. With seed 0, saturation is sampled uniformly from [.55,.80] and, with probability .5, hue is perturbed uniformly within [-40^∘,40^∘].

Stage 1: VAE-aware fitting targets.

Stage 1 optimizes an intermediate map g only to provide targets for affine distillation. Concretely, g is the fixed-form analytic map

g(x)=sₒᵤₜ⊙M₂{a⊙asinh(b⊙M₁x)+d}+bₒᵤₜ,

where Mᵢ=I+ΔMᵢ; its active tensors comprise the two 3×3 matrices; the three-channel a,b,d,sₒᵤₜ,bₒᵤₜ; an unconstrained three-vector normalized to the unit gauge u; and one log-scale whose exponential is α — 37 scalar parameters, of which u and α serve only the structural terms below. Its internal parameterization is not part of the deployed encoding. The final affine map instead obtains its realized exposure flow directly from Be₁.

The frozen VAE is kept in the computation graph: codes are clamped to [0,1], mapped to [-1,1], encoded and decoded in 32-bit floating point, and mapped back before analytic inversion. VAE parameters receive no gradient. One exposure from 𝔼_\rmfit={0,-4,-2,+2,+4} EV is sampled uniformly at each step.

For a VAE-round-tripped reconstruction x̂, the intermediate fitting objective is

L_fit=L_\log+Lᵤᵥ_Lᵣₜ+\underbraceL_eq+0.25Lₐₘₚ_L_struct+10L_range.

(6)

The three groups respectively measure VAE round-trip fidelity, regularize the exposure–chroma structure, and keep codes inside the useful VAE input range. The weights of L_\log, Lᵤᵥ, and L_eq are one. Specifically,

L_\log=mean\lVert\log(1+x̂)-\log(1+x)\rVert₂²,

and Lᵤᵥ is the mean Euclidean u^′v^′ error over pixels with ground-truth Y≥10⁻³. Thus the compact notation in the main paper denotes a masked per-pixel mean, rather than an unnormalized tensor norm. For e∈𝔼_fit, L_eq penalizes

meanₘ\lVertg(2ᵉx)-g(x)-eαu\rVert₂²,

where g is the intermediate fitting map, u is its learned unit gauge, and α>0 is its learned displacement scale. The term Lₐₘₚ penalizes the change with exposure of the code distance between an image and its chromatically perturbed counterpart. The same valid-luminance mask m=1[Y≥10⁻³] is used. Finally,

L_range=mean{ReLU(g(x)-0.95)²
+ReLU(0.05-g(x))²}.

We use AdamW for 15,000 steps with learning rate 2×10⁻³, weight decay 10⁻⁴, batch size 4, cosine decay to zero, unit gradient clipping, and seed 0.

Stage 2: affine distillation (closed form).

The distillation targets are the code vectors g(x) of the converged stage-1 map on 120,000 RGB samples at {0,-2,-4,-6,-8} EV (600,000 fitting rows); Eq. (3) is fitted to these targets by least squares. The -6 and -8 EV rows evaluate the fixed target map outside its optimization ladder; they do not extend the first-stage optimization. The toe is frozen, the first column of B is swept over c∈{.5,.75,1,1.5,2,2.5,3}, and the bias is recentered using 40,000 additional samples.

Since exposure moves the code along Be₁ with α=\lVertBe₁\rVert₂ (Eq. (1)), scaling that column by c rescales the per-stop displacement relative to the fixed chromatic columns, trading round-trip reconstruction against deep-exposure chromatic separation; Table 1 lists the gate thresholds and the two passing candidates of this sweep. The selected c is not a separate deployed parameter: it is absorbed into the frozen matrix of Eq. (3), whose printed first column already contains it.

Selection is performed before downstream task evaluation. Reconstruction uses a fixed 16-clip encoding-fit validation panel. OOD survival is the ratio of held-out chromaticity R² at -8 EV to that at EV 0 on a fixed 12-clip ARRI–UPIQ OOD survival panel. Grid identification is the four-fold texture-held-out classifier defined below. The projection score is a group-held-out linear probe on absolute top-24-PCA perturbation coordinates; the separation AUC uses the fraction of perturbation energy assigned to independently estimated luminance and chroma subspaces.

No downstream SDR-to-HDR prediction or task metric enters encoding selection; the selection and main-paper reconstruction values estimate different panels.

Encoding selection predates the downstream subset aggregation, but two of the 12 OOD-survival-panel clips also occur in the frozen ARRI subset of the test set. Thus no downstream output or metric is used for selection, but encoding selection and downstream evaluation are not strictly image-disjoint. We treat this gate as design selection and do not claim an untouched-image test for representation selection.

Chromatic-Loss Ablation

We rerun both fitting stages (stage-1 optimization and stage-2 affine distillation), the scale sweep, the frozen selection rule, and 6,500-step adapter training with the chromatic round-trip term Lᵤᵥ removed. All other loss terms and settings are fixed. This fit produces no candidate that passes the selection rule; for diagnostic downstream readout only, its best-reconstruction candidate is exported with the gate explicitly waived.

Removing Lᵤᵥ costs 1.73 dB PU21 and increases mean Δu^′v^′ from .0140 to .0219. The ablation identifies Lᵤᵥ as a load-bearing term in the EquivFlow fitting objective.

Appendix C SDR-to-HDR System Details

Data Construction

HDR targets and split.

The training corpus contains 5,780 crops from 1,015 parent sequences: 2,580 crops from 215 temporal windows extracted from 94 Tears of Steel shots, and 3,200 crops from 800 PolyHaven clips. The parent-disjoint split contains 5,388 training, 324 validation, and 68 test crops. Each clip is normalized by mapping the 75th percentile of its per-frame 99th-percentile luma to unity.

The two sources differ in provenance. PolyHaven renders are scene-referred and retain highlights above reference white. Tears of Steel is a finished 16-bit display grade that we linearize with the inverse sRGB transfer function; its grade has already compressed highlight information. We therefore refer to the combined data as linear Rec. 709 targets, not uniformly as scene-linear radiance.

SDR generation.

Each target has four offline SDR variants. Variant 0 is a clean lossless FFV1 render. Variants 1–3 use independently sampled degradation parameters. The loader selects the clean variant with probability 0.25 and otherwise selects uniformly among the three degraded variants, so each stored variant has marginal probability 0.25. The variant generator uses seed 42+sample index. No online exposure, contrast, blur, or codec augmentation is applied during adapter training.

All training variants use extended Reinhard with white point w=4 and no additional exposure offset. For linear luminance L,

Lₜ=(L(1+L/w²))/(1+L),
L=w²/2[(Lₜ-1)+√(1-Lₜ)²+4Lₜ/w²].(7)

The luminance ratio is applied to RGB, followed by per-channel clipping, sRGB OETF, and 8-bit quantization. The analytic inverse in Eq. (7) inverts the unclipped continuous luminance curve; clipping and quantization remain information-losing.

For degraded variants, sRGB contrast about 0.5 is sampled uniformly from [0.85,1.25]. Gaussian blur with σ∼U[1,3] is applied selectively to highlights above 0.98 and/or shadows below 0.02, each independently with probability 0.7. H.264 encoding uses yuv420p, integer CRF sampled from 18–32, and the medium preset.

Unseen tone curve.

The ACES-like evaluation condition applies

A(y)=clip (y(2.51y+0.03)/y(2.43y+0.59)+0.14,0,1)

(8)

as a luminance-preserving RGB ratio, followed by the same sRGB transfer and 8-bit quantization. This curve is not used to train either internal arm.

Adapter Training and Inference

The base model is the LTX-2.3 22B checkpoint ltx-2.3-22b-dev.safetensors; its transformer, VAE, and text encoder remain frozen. IC-LoRA reference tokens use clean (t=0) latents, participate in bidirectional attention, and are excluded from the denoising loss. Rank-32 modules use scale 32 and dropout 0. They are inserted into the q, k, v, and output projections of attn1 and attn2, and into ff.net.0.proj and ff.net.2.

Each arm is trained once for a fixed 6,500-step comparison budget, rather than a validation-selected checkpoint. We use AdamW at learning rate 2×10⁻⁴ with unit gradient clipping and a linear factor 1 → .1 over a 100,000-step horizon. Training uses four NVIDIA H100 80GB GPUs, per-GPU batch size 1, accumulation 1 (effective batch 4), BF16, gradient checkpointing, and seed 42. Noise follows a shifted logit-normal distribution with standard deviation 1, ε=10⁻³, a .1 uniform mixture, and the model’s sequence-dependent shift.

The positive prompt is “A high dynamic range cinematic scene with bright highlights and deep shadows.”; the negative prompt is “worst quality, inconsistent motion, blurry, jittery, distorted.” Inference uses seed 42, 30 steps, guidance 4, and spatiotemporal guidance 1 at block 28 in stg_v mode. All settings other than the conditioning contract and encoding are shared: EquivFlow conditions on the analytically inverse-tone-mapped proxy, whereas LogC3 uses the display-referred SDR directly.

Appendix D Evaluation Definitions

Common output domain.

All outputs are decoded to linear Rec. 709 before evaluation. PU21 uses 100 nits per normalized linear unit, clamps absolute luminance to [0.005,10,000] nits, applies the banding–glare PU21 encoding normalized to unit peak, and reports PSNR with peak 1.

For chromatic ΔC_TC_P, Rec. 709 is converted to Rec. 2020 and then to PQ ICtCp using the 10,000-nit convention. We use the ITP scaling (I,T,P)=(I,0.5C_T,C_P) and report the mean

720√(0.5ΔC_T)²+(ΔC_P)².

This omits the intensity difference by construction.

Luminance-independent chroma metrics.

Let r(x)=x/(∑_cx_c+ε), with ε=10⁻⁴ used only to avoid division by zero. Chroma L1 is mean|r(x̂)-r(x)|. Mean Δu^′v^′ is the Euclidean CIE 1976 chromaticity error over ground-truth pixels with Y≥10⁻³. LF drift first applies a spatial Gaussian with σ=8 to the chromaticity fields and measures the same masked error. Range drift further restricts evaluation to pixels whose SDR input is neither clipped nor null: all channels are below 254/255 and the maximum channel exceeds 3/255. The null region is replaced by the target field before Gaussian filtering to prevent invalid boundaries from leaking into the range mask.

Main-paper frozen-VAE probe.

Table 1 in the main paper uses no diffusion training. Its reconstruction column is the mean per-clip log-RGB PSNR after a frozen-VAE round trip on 16 deterministically sampled held-out validation clips (a panel distinct from the encoding-selection panel of Table 1). For the chromatic columns, 12 deterministic center-cropped clips from the ARRI–UPIQ OOD pool are evaluated at {0,-2,-4,-6,-8,-10} EV. Only latent tokens whose EV-0 ground-truth luminance is at least 10⁻³ are used. At every exposure and for each encoding separately, a StandardScaler followed by ridge regression with penalty 1 is refitted to predict u^′ and v^′. Five-fold GroupKFold by parent clip supplies held-out predictions; the reported R²_u^′v^′ is the mean of the two coordinate scores and surv₋ₖ=R²(-k)/R²(0). Because held-out R² is unbounded below and the numerator can exceed its EV-0 value, survival may be negative or exceed one. It measures relative linear recoverability, not chroma-energy amplification.

Cross-VAE probe.

The structural-portability test applies the same fixed encoding to each frozen host VAE over the exposure ladder {0,-2,-4,-6,-8}. Its chroma grid comprises 12 chromaticities (two radii, 0.03 and 0.06, at six equally spaced hue angles about D65) rendered with four luminance textures at base luminance 0.45. Grid identification is 12-way accuracy; chance is 1/12. At each host and exposure, a StandardScaler plus logistic regression (C=1) is evaluated by four-fold GroupKFold, holding out one luminance texture per fold. Thus the table’s grid readout is host- and exposure-specific.

For the exposure readout, a host-specific direction is the first right singular vector of all nonzero-EV latent differences. The scalar β(e) is their mean projection on that direction, and R²_β is the no-intercept linear fit of β(e) to EV. The reported Δu^′v^′₋₈ is the encoding round-trip chromaticity error at -8 EV. The prespecified non-collapse check uses 16 fixed clips (15 with a nonempty EV-0 luminance mask) and requires each foreign host’s round-trip Δu^′v^′ to be no more than twice the LTX value at both -6 and -8 EV. This is a within-subject collapse check, not a comparative superiority test.

EV-0-frozen readout.

The main paper notes that an EV-0-frozen readout degrades along each host’s exposure trajectory. This diagnostic fits the chroma-grid classifier at EV 0 and applies it unchanged at deeper exposures, instead of refitting per exposure as in the grid column of main-paper Table 4. Under the frozen readout, -8 EV grid accuracy falls to .208 (LTX), .083 (SD 2.1, chance level), .167 (Wan 2.1), and .250 (Wan 2.2) from EV-0 values of .979, .667, .958, and .979, while the per-exposure refitted readout remains high (main-paper Table 4). The latent coordinates therefore rotate or rescale along each host’s exposure trajectory even though exposure structure and chroma separability persist; the portability claim concerns the latter, not shared latent coordinates.

LEDiff radiometric alignment.

LEDiff is run with its official preprocessing and checkpoint. A single method-level scalar gain is fitted once on 24 fixed, parent-distinct training clips and then held fixed for every evaluation set. With luminance y, the gain is

g_\rmLEDiff=\exp (mean_y_\rmgt>10⁻⁴δ)=0.0294942,
δ=\log(y_\rmgt+10⁻⁴)-\log(y_\rmpred+10⁻⁴).

No test image, test ground truth, or per-clip gain enters this fit.

Qualitative selection and display.

For each evaluation set, the main-paper figure selects the evaluated crop with the largest EquivFlow–LumiVid ΔE_ITP margin; it therefore shows selected successes, not representative or median cases. ARRI and HDRTV4K are displayed in the full frame containing that crop, whereas UPIQ contains one evaluated crop. The inset is chosen as the darkest chroma-carrying target region that remains inside one reconstructed crop. A row-specific display gain is applied identically to every column and affects no reported metric. For HDRTV4K, only the evaluated quadrant contributes to quantitative results; the other quadrants are display context.

Appendix E Statistical Protocol and Full Results

Frozen evaluation subset.

The frozen 102-clip test subset of main-paper Table 2 was fixed before any subset aggregation was computed. Table 4 records the per-set selection rule.

Aggregation and inference.

Metrics are first averaged within each parent and then averaged with equal weight across parents. The chroma-decomposition panel uses the full HDRTV4K–UPIQ pool of 58 parents (36 HDRTV4K and 22 UPIQ). Confidence intervals are nonparametric parent-cluster bootstrap intervals from 10,000 resamples with seed 42. Pairwise tests are two-sided, parent-level paired Wilcoxon signed-rank tests. For the dataset-wise table, Holm correction is applied within each method pair and curve across three datasets and two primary metrics. For the chroma panel, correction is applied within each curve across its three primary metrics. There is one trained model per internal arm; bootstrap intervals characterize parent-level sampling uncertainty rather than variation across training runs.

Dataset-wise internal comparison.

Table 5 supplies the parent-level tests behind the dataset-wise statements in the main paper. Deltas are EquivFlow-LogC3, so positive PU21-PSNR and negative ΔC_TC_P favor EquivFlow. The UPIQ chromatic difference is significant under the training curve; HDRTV4K and UPIQ are significant under the unseen curve. ARRI does not separate under either curve, and HDRTV4K does not separate under the training curve.

Chroma-panel statistics.

Table 3 gives the paired differences underlying the main paper’s chroma panel for the fixed 6,500-step EquivFlow checkpoint. Units are parent scenes (n=58); each entry is EquivFlow-LogC3 with a 10,000-sample bootstrap 95% interval. The three primary metrics use Holm-corrected p_H. The two nested filtered forms of Δu^′v^′ are descriptive, use uncorrected p, and lie outside the correction family.

Interpretive boundary.

Under matched Reinhard, EquivFlow has higher aggregate-fidelity point estimates on the frozen subset. That aggregate advantage does not persist under the ACES-like swap. The result that remains consistent across the two tested curves is narrower: the full EquivFlow system has lower luminance-independent chromaticity error than the same-backbone LogC3 system. Because the arms also differ in reference reconstruction, these results attribute the effect to the complete conditioning system, not to the encoding alone.

item.title: 前馈三维重建只认透视相机：Camera3R 要解决鱼眼、全景这类「非透视」输入 ｜ Camera3R: Feed-Forward 3D Reconstruction from Heterogeneous Camera Models
item.description:
一句话：基础重建模型都在透视数据集上训练，换到非透视相机就泛化不动——这挡住了实际部署。

要点：

  • 现状：非约束多视图的前馈三维重建（3R）是热点，已有多个架构与范式不同的基础模型
  • 共同短板：它们都在大规模**透视（perspective）**数据集上训练，即便算力充足，也普遍难以泛化到非透视图像
  • 这篇针对「异构相机模型」做前馈重建，直接面向鱼眼、全景等非透视输入的实际部署

为什么值得看：游戏与 XR 里的相机不只有针孔：鱼眼、全景、畸变镜头都要进管线。重建模型把「透视」写死在训练分布里，等于把这些输入排除在外——这条是把适用范围从「实验室相机」扩到「真实相机」。

中文摘要：从无约束多视图图像做前馈三维重建已成为 3D 视觉的重要方向，也出现了多种架构与范式各异的基础重建模型。但它们有一个共同短板：训练数据几乎都是大规模透视（perspective）图像，因此即便投入了大量算力，这些模型在非透视图像上仍普遍泛化不佳，直接限制了实际部署。Camera3R 针对异构相机模型做前馈重建，目标是把适用范围从「针孔相机」扩展到鱼眼、全景等真实设备。对引擎与 XR 管线来说，相机模型从来不止一种，这条补的正是被训练分布排除掉的那部分输入。

主题：AI Rendering

来源：arXiv·cs.CV（English）

原文发布：2026-11-11

本期推送：2026-11-13

Camera3R: Feed-Forward 3D Reconstruction
from Heterogeneous Camera Models

Abstract

Feed-forward 3D reconstruction (3R) from unconstrained multi-view images has recently emerged as a prominent research direction in 3D computer vision. Various foundational reconstruction models have been proposed with different architectures and reconstruction paradigms. Despite being trained on large-scale perspective datasets with substantial computational resources, these models generally struggle to generalize to non-perspective images. This limitation hinders their deployment in applications involving arbitrary, unknown, and potentially heterogeneous camera models. To build on the capabilities of existing reconstruction models with minimal retraining, we propose Camera3R, a low-rank adaptation framework that efficiently extends perspective-pretrained 3R networks to any other camera models. Extensive experiments demonstrate that, with only 0.5% additional parameters and less than a day of training, Camera3R adapts a foundational 3D reconstruction model to non-perspective cameras while fully preserving its original performance on perspective inputs. Code is available at https://github.com/android-xr/camera3r.

1 Introduction

Three-dimensional (3D) visual mapping of an environment is a fundamental component in many spatial applications, ranging from autonomous navigation to extended reality systems. Decision-making within these applications rests on the fidelity of the map, e.g., accuracy of estimated points (and position and orientation of the platform), as well as completeness, or coverage, of the environment as observed by a set of cameras. In practice, the two metrics are not independently optimizable, but are coupled through sensing trade-offs. For a fixed sensing budget, a reduction in field-of-view (FoV) increases the angular resolution, which often results in higher fidelity estimates. On the other hand, an increase in FoV naturally improves environmental coverage, but typically introduces non-trivial lens distortion and measurement noise that degrade per-point accuracy. This trade-off motivates the use of multiple cameras, e.g., combinations of perspective and fisheye or panoramic (360∘) cameras, within a mixed-camera system whose cameras provide complementary fidelity and coverage.

While mixed-camera systems offer the potential to balance map fidelity and environmental coverage in 3D reconstruction, existing feed-forward 3D reconstruction models [26, 29, 15] cannot fully exploit the non-perspective or heterogeneous camera inputs. Despite being trained on large-scale datasets comprising tens of millions of images, these models cannot generalize to images captured by wide-FoV or mixed cameras. This failure mode can be attributed to a covariate shift between the training and deployment imaging platforms: The training data used by current feed-forward reconstruction models is predominantly composed of perspective images. In contrast, images captured by different camera models exhibit varying fields of view, resolutions, and distortion profiles, leading to heterogeneous photometric and spatial sampling statistics. Consequently, these models do not directly transfer to mixed-camera streams, limiting their potential to provide high-fidelity maps with broad environmental coverage, despite their strong generalization across diverse 3D scenes.

A natural response to this limitation is to train separate 3D reconstruction models tailored to each camera type or imaging configuration, and subsequently register their outputs and combine them into a single map. However, such an approach would incur substantial operational overhead, and is poorly suited to spatial applications, which are often constrained by compute, memory, and overall system complexity. A key insight is that, despite differences in photometric and spatial sampling statistics due to the image formation process, images of the same 3D scene captured by different camera models should correspond to a single consistent environmental map. In other words, the heterogeneity in camera models may alter the observations, but not the underlying 3D structures being reconstructed. This intuition motivates our central thesis of whether a single feed-forward 3D reconstruction model trained primarily on images captured by perspective cameras can be systematically extended to operate on heterogeneous camera inputs without retraining from scratch.

To this end, we introduce Camera3R, a framework that enables a single feed-forward model to ingest images captured by multiple camera types to produce a consistent map. The crux of our method lies in selective adaptation to inputs during inference time through a mixture of experts. We assume access to a pretrained feed-forward model and that images can originate from a broad categorization of perspective, fisheye, and panoramic cameras. We associate each camera model with an expert, each parameterized by a set of weights. We begin by freezing the pretrained model; as it is pretrained on large-scale datasets of perspective images, we consider it an expert in itself. We surmise that the pretrained model has already learned sufficiently expressive features to model diverse 3D scenes and that the same features can be efficiently modulated, rather than relearned, to extend the pretrained model to accommodate alternative camera types. Accordingly, we introduce low-rank adaptation (LoRA) [11] to the network layers to yield experts for fisheye and panoramic cameras. However, it remains a question as to how much capacity should be allocated to each camera type to model specific distortions and viewing statistics. To address this, we employ a rank-truncation scheme that redistributes capacity by allocating higher ranks to layer-expert pairs based on need, allowing us to leverage the existing knowledge to its full extent while adding minimal overhead in parameters to the model. The result is an efficient model unified across cameras that can be trained with an order of magnitude less data than the base model itself.

In most spatial applications, the origin of the camera data stream is known; therefore, expert selection based on camera identity is sufficient to adaptively run inference on each image. Nonetheless, to accommodate general usage, we propose to learn a camera router which determines the expert to use for modulating latent features. Hence, at test time, we do not assume access to camera metadata and can handle inputs of any single camera type, as well as a collection of images originating from a mixture of heterogeneous cameras. This design naturally enables backward compatibility, where the generalizability and performance of existing feed-forward 3D reconstruction models are preserved. At the same time, new cameras can be introduced into an existing platform to improve both map fidelity and environmental coverage, and be accommodated without disruption to established workflows. We evaluate our method on multiple 3D reconstruction datasets, spanning indoor and outdoor environments. In single-camera settings, our method achieves a significant improvement over the baseline methods and fully preserves performance on perspective images. We further demonstrate that, in mixed-camera scenarios, our approach can handle a collection of images originating from any of the cameras from a heterogeneous set without prior knowledge of their identity to yield consistent and high-fidelity reconstructions. Our method is applied to three different feed-forward 3D reconstruction models to demonstrate its generalizability.

Our contributions are as follows: (1) We extend existing feed-forward 3D reconstruction models pretrained on perspective imagery to operate on fisheye and panoramic camera inputs through a mixture-of-experts framework with adaptive routing. (2) We introduce an adaptive capacity allocation mechanism that selectively allocates LoRA-based adaptation capacity across experts and layers, significantly reducing the parameter overhead. (3) We achieve state-of-the-art performance in both single-camera and mixed-camera reconstruction settings across multiple indoor and outdoor datasets. (4) To the best of our knowledge, we are the first to enable joint feed-forward 3D reconstruction from heterogeneous perspective, fisheye, and panoramic images in a single forward pass.

2 Related Work

Feed-Forward 3D Reconstruction. Recent progress in 3D reconstruction has been strongly impacted by the introduction of unified, feed-forward foundational models that infer camera poses and scene geometry from unconstrained images in a single forward pass. The trend can be traced back to DUSt3R [27], which directly predicts dense point maps from image pairs. MASt3R [17] further advances the framework by improving reconstruction quality through explicit feature matching. Spann3R [25] subsequently extends this pairwise paradigm to image collections by aggregating information with spatial memory and directly regressing global point maps without optimization-based global alignment. VGGT [26] pioneered a unified, general-purpose framework that predicts camera parameters, depth maps, point maps, and point tracks from multiple images in a single forward pass with an alternating-attention transformer architecture. π³[29] introduces a permutation-equivariant formulation that eliminates performance dependence on a fixed reference view and input order. MapAnything [15] incorporates optional geometric inputs for flexible metric reconstruction. These works collectively mark a shift towards unified, feed-forward visual-geometry foundational models for general-purpose 3D reconstruction.

Feed-Forward 3D Reconstruction for Non-Perspective Images. Despite their strong performance on standard perspective imagery, these foundational reconstruction models generally fail on non-perspective inputs. Some recent works have developed reconstruction models for non-perspective images. PanoVGGT [9] and Argus [19] achieve feed-forward reconstruction from panoramic images based on VGGT. Wid3R [13] employs spherical harmonics for ray representations to handle perspective, fisheye, and panoramic inputs in reconstruction models, but does not demonstrate reconstructions from mixed-camera sequences. These approaches either specialize in a particular camera model or rely on known camera types during inference. Furthermore, they do not explicitly address mixed-camera input sequences or guarantee backward compatibility on perspective images. CAM3R [10] extends the pairwise reconstruction to camera-agnostic settings by predicting per-pixel rays and radial distances, using a ray-aware global alignment stage to combine pairwise predictions across views. Fisheye3R [4] formulates the task of generalizing reconstruction models to fisheye cameras as an adaptation problem and introduces calibration tokens [7] to extend perspective-pretrained reconstruction networks [26, 29, 15] to fisheye cameras without performance degradation on perspective inputs, but the scope is limited to the fisheye domain. In contrast, our work extends foundational multi-view reconstruction models to handle perspective, fisheye, and panoramic inputs simultaneously in a single forward propagation, accepting sequences with unknown and heterogeneous camera models, while ensuring backward compatibility on perspective data.

Low-Rank Adaptation and Adaptive Rank Allocation. Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) [11] is a parameter-efficient finetuning strategy originally proposed to adapt large language models. Instead of updating the entire set of model parameters, LoRA freezes the backbone and injects lightweight learnable low-rank matrices into selected layers for efficient adaptation, reducing the number of trainable parameters while preserving the original model’s knowledge.
