一句话：DMD 要额外训一个 fake-score 网络并追着生成器更新，训练显存与算力都被吃掉。

要点：

  • 少步采样是压低流式视频生成成本的直接手段，而 Distribution Matching Distillation（DMD）用一个**独立的 fake-score 网络**来监督少步生成器
  • 这个设计的代价：额外训练显存与算力，而且该网络必须持续追赶不断变化的生成器
  • 这篇把 APEX 扩展到流式视频：用**条件平移**在生成器内部估计生成分布的速度场——原条件选生成，平移后的条件选「假」估计

为什么值得看：实时生成内容进管线的关键就是步数。把蒸馏的「裁判」从外部网络搬回生成器内部，省下的是训练与部署两头的成本，这对要做实时流式生成的团队直接可用。

中文摘要：少步采样是降低流式视频生成成本最直接的手段。Distribution Matching Distillation（DMD）的做法是用一个独立的 fake-score 网络来监督少步生成器，代价是额外的训练显存与算力，而且这个网络必须持续追赶不断变化的生成器。这篇把 APEX 扩展到流式视频场景：不再外挂打分网络，而是用「条件平移」在生成器内部估计生成分布的速度场——原始文本条件用于选择生成，平移后的条件用于选择「假」的估计，从而在同一模型内完成蒸馏监督。对追求实时流式生成的管线，这同时省下了训练与部署两端的开销。

主题：AI Rendering

来源：arXiv·cs.CV（English）

原文发布：2026-11-11

本期推送：2026-11-13

Few-Step Streaming Video
Generation via Condition Shifting

Abstract

Few-step sampling reduces the cost of streaming video generation. Distribution Matching Distillation (DMD) supervises few-step generators with a separate fake-score network, which adds training memory and computation and must track the evolving generator. We extend APEX to streaming video by using condition shifting to estimate the velocity field of the generated distribution within the generator. The original text condition selects generation, while a shifted condition selects fake estimation using the same parameters. This removes the independent fake network while retaining S2-Avatar’s frozen reference teacher, Self-Replay Forcing, and perceptual regularization. We evaluate APEX on 180-second videos using three backbone evaluations per block and a one-step spatial Refiner, with a 70-case human study and a 320-case StreamAV-Bench comparison. Compared with S2-Avatar, APEX achieves higher video instruction fulfillment on the Progressive track (3.856 versus 3.831) and higher visual aesthetics across both tracks (0.641898 versus 0.632606). Human raters favor APEX most strongly on instruction following, with +30.0% net preference, followed by consistency and video quality at +4.3% each. Motion quality favors S2-Avatar, audiovisual synchronization is predominantly tied, and usability is unchanged. Separate measurements under matched training settings show 4.4% lower peak allocated GPU memory per GPU and 9.2% shorter mean iteration time than DMD.

††footnotetext: *Co-first authorship. ‡Corresponding authors.

1 Introduction

Diffusion and flow models produce high-quality videos through repeated network evaluations [(Brooks et al., 2024, Google DeepMind, 2025, Wan et al., 2025, Seedance et al., 2026)]. Streaming generation incurs this cost for every new block, making few-step sampling particularly valuable for long sequences. Distillation reduces the number of evaluations [(Song et al., 2023, Salimans and Ho, 2022, Zheng et al., 2025b)], while the resulting generator must preserve visual quality, maintain characters and scenes, and respond to changing instructions. shows APEX video examples of object interaction and storytelling.

Distribution Matching Distillation (DMD) supervises generated samples through the difference between reference and generated-distribution scores [(Yin et al., 2024b, Yin et al., 2024a)]. A frozen pretrained teacher supplies the reference estimate, while a separate fake-score network learns from current generator outputs. For large video backbones, maintaining this auxiliary network adds training memory and computation. Its estimate must also track the generator as the output distribution changes, requiring coordination of their optimization settings and updates. This motivates learning the fake estimate within the generator.

TwinFlow [(Cheng et al., 2026)] and the original APEX[(Liu et al., 2026c)] show how generation and distribution estimation can share a network. We extend APEX’s condition shifting to streaming video: the original text condition selects generation, and its shifted version selects a fake estimator trained on outputs for the same prompt. The two roles share model parameters and, by default, optimizer states, while a separate frozen pretrained teacher provides the same reference guidance as in S2-Avatar.

Streaming video requires the estimator to track outputs generated with a causal history. We integrate condition shifting into S2-Avatar’s Self-Replay Forcing (SRF), which trains on replayed segments of the model’s own generated sequences [(Zhang et al., 2026c)]. The shared fake estimator is fitted to these replay outputs, and its clean-latent predictions are compared with those of the frozen teacher to construct a detached correction for the generator. We retain S2’s replay procedure and perceptual regularization, as described in .

We evaluate APEX on 180-second videos through a 70-case human study and all 320 StreamAV-Bench scenarios. Relative to S2-Avatar, APEX receives positive net human preference for instruction following, consistency, and video quality, and achieves higher video instruction-fulfillment scores and visual aesthetics on both benchmark tracks. A separate measurement under matched training settings shows 4.4% lower peak allocated GPU memory and 9.2% shorter mean iteration time than DMD. Instruction-following preference also remains positive at 2 backbone NFE. also reports audiovisual synchronization, motion quality, and usability.

The paper makes three contributions to few-step streaming video generation:

  • 1.

    Shared-network estimation through condition shifting. We learn the fake velocity within the generator while retaining a frozen reference teacher and removing the independent fake network.

  • 2.

    Integration with Self-Replay Forcing. We apply condition-shifted estimation to the outputs of S2’s Self-Replay Forcing, retaining its replay procedure and perceptual regularization.

  • 3.

    Video quality and training efficiency. We evaluate 180-second generation on 70 paired cases and all 320 StreamAV-Bench scenarios, alongside training-cost and sampling comparisons.

    • 2 Preliminaries

    We use x for a data latent, z for Gaussian noise, c for projected text, and F_θ for a velocity predictor. The operator \mathop\color[rgb]1,0,0sg denotes stop-gradient, and defines the video context.

    Continuous Generative Models.

    Conditional diffusion [(Ho et al., 2020, Song et al., 2020)] and flow matching [(Lipman et al., 2022)] transport Gaussian noise z∼p_z=ℕ(0,I) to data x∼pᵣ(·|c). For t∈[0,1], we use the linear interpolation path of optimal transport (OT) flow matching:

    xₜ=tz+(1-t)x .

    		(1)

    Sampling transports noise x₁=z to data x₀=x along the probability-flow ODE:

    dxₜ/dt=v(xₜ,t,c) .

    		(2)

    Flow matching learns this velocity field by regressing to the known target uᵣ(x,z):=z-x:

    L_FM(θ)=𝔼_x, c, z, t[∥F_θ(xₜ,t,c)-uᵣ(x,z)∥²] .

    		(3)

    The expectation uses paired data (x,c), independent z∼p_z, and t∼U(0,1). The population minimizer is the conditional mean velocity vᵣ^*(xₜ,t,c)=𝔼[z-x|xₜ,t,c]. Sampling integrates from t=1 to t=0 with numerical ODE solvers [(Karras et al., 2022)], such as the first-order Euler method.

    Few-Step Generation.

    Consistency and interval-mapping methods support few-step sampling [(Song et al., 2023, Wang et al., 2024, Zheng et al., 2025b, Sun and Lin, 2025, Geng et al., 2025)]. The one-step Euler map is G_θ(z,c)=z-F_θ(z,1,c), with no destination-time input to the velocity predictor.

    Distribution Matching.

    For a fixed condition, let p_θ be the distribution of G_θ(z,c) and pᵣ the reference distribution. Their noised marginals at time t have scores s_i,t(y):=∇_y\logp_i,t(y) for i∈{r,θ}. DMD [(Yin et al., 2024b)] estimates the reverse-KL gradient using their score difference at the same noised generated sample. It uses a pretrained reference score and an auxiliary fake-score network trained on current outputs. expresses this score difference through marginal velocities under the OT path.

    TwinFlow [(Cheng et al., 2026)] learns both velocities within one model, using positive time for the real trajectory and negative time for the fake trajectory. APEX selects the fake estimator through the condition input. Our video implementation shares the generator and fake estimator and retains S2’s frozen teacher for the reference prediction. relates the GAN gradient to a weighted score difference.

    2.1 Autoregressive Video Generation and Self-Replay Forcing

    We express S2-Avatar’s causal predictor and Self-Replay Forcing procedure [(Zhang et al., 2026c)] in APEX notation. For block i, let xⁱ denote the video latent and cⁱ its text representation. The context hⁱ contains the reference image, the preceding video states, and any accompanying audio. The diffusion time tᵢ∈(0,1] is its noise level, with larger values indicating more noise. The clean prediction is

    x̂₀ⁱ=x_tᵢⁱ-tᵢF_θ(x_tᵢⁱ,tᵢ,cⁱ|hⁱ).

    		(4)

    A block-wise causal mask lets each block attend to its own tokens, conditions, and preceding video blocks.

    Self-Replay Forcing.

    Following S2 [(Zhang et al., 2026c)], we generate a detached autoregressive rollout [(Huang et al., 2026a)] and re-noise a sampled segment with diffusion forcing (DF) [(Chen et al., 2024)]. One differentiable causal pass processes this segment, with each block reading preceding blocks at their replay noise levels. This allows cross-block gradients within the segment while keeping the external history and original rollout detached. We retain S2’s teacher and perceptual regularization [(Zhang et al., 2026d)] and replace DMD’s fake estimator [(Yin et al., 2024b, Yin et al., 2024a)] through condition shifting in .

    3 Condition Shifting for Streaming Video Generation

    We apply APEX’s condition shifting [(Liu et al., 2026c)] to the fake estimator in S2’s Self-Replay Forcing framework. The generator and fake estimator share parameters θ, with a frozen teacher F_φ providing S2’s reference prediction and guidance. compares DMD and APEX during training.

    3.1 Condition Shifting on Generated Video

    The network generates under cⁱ and estimates the fake velocity from these outputs under c_shiftⁱ=-cⁱ. We negate projected text before the transformer blocks, with positive diffusion times in both calls.

    The N evaluated blocks x_θ^1:N include replay outputs and any detached prefix from . We detach them and re-noise at a scoring time t^′∈(0,1) with fresh Gaussian noise ε^′∼p_z:

    x_θ^1:N,\mathop\color[rgb]1,0,0sg:=\mathop\color[rgb]1,0,0sg(x_θ^1:N), x_θ,t^′^1:N,\mathop\color[rgb]1,0,0sg:=(1-t^′)x_θ^1:N,\mathop\color[rgb]1,0,0sg+t^′ε^′.

    		(5)

    We draw a single scoring time t^′ for all generated blocks in a sequence, separately from the replay times tᵢ used to produce the clean predictions. With reference-image and audio conditions fixed and omitted from the notation, the shifted-condition network predicts the fake velocity from the re-noised video latents:

    v̂_θ,t^′^1:N:=F_θ(x_θ,t^′^1:N,\mathop\color[rgb]1,0,0sg,t^′,c_shift^1:N).

    		(6)

    To learn the velocity field of the generated samples, we use the following flow-matching loss with causal attention over the current and preceding noisy blocks, without an additional clean-video stream:

    L_fake(θ)=𝔼 [MSE (v̂_θ,t^′^1:N,ε^′-x_θ^1:N,\mathop\color[rgb]1,0,0sg)].

    		(7)

    Here MSE is the mean squared error with S2’s video weighting and averaging. Detaching the generated sequence and regression target restricts this update to the shifted-condition prediction.

    3.2 A Detached Correction from the Velocity Difference

    We form the generator correction from the frozen teacher’s x̂_0,r^1:N and fake clean-latent predictions at the same noisy video and scoring time, retaining S2’s conditioning, guidance, and DMD target [(Zhang et al., 2026c, Yin et al., 2024b, Yin et al., 2024a)]. Here r marks the teacher prediction and θ the fake estimate.

    x̂_0,θⁱ=x_θ,t^′^i,\mathop\color[rgb]1,0,0sg-t^′v̂_θ,t^′ⁱ, v̂_r,t^′ⁱ:=(x_θ,t^′^i,\mathop\color[rgb]1,0,0sg-x̂_0,rⁱ)/(t^′).

    		(8)

    Their clean-latent difference is proportional to the velocity difference at the same scoring time:

    x̂_0,rⁱ-x̂_0,θⁱ=t^′d̂_t^′ⁱ, d̂_t^′ⁱ:=v̂_θ,t^′ⁱ-v̂_r,t^′ⁱ.

    		(9)

    We normalize this clean-latent difference as in to obtain d̃_t^′^1:N and add it to the current output, giving the generator a detached regression target for the replay predictions:

    L_score(θ)=𝔼 [MSE (x_θ^1:N,\mathop\color[rgb]1,0,0sg (x_θ^1:N+d̃_t^′^1:N))].

    		(10)

    We hold the target fixed, including estimator predictions and normalization. Gradients therefore pass through replay outputs and their connected causal representations within the active segment.

    Under the OT path, velocity estimates induce score estimates satisfying

    d̂_t^′ⁱ=-(t^′)/(1-t^′)(ŝ_θ,t^′ⁱ-ŝ_r,t^′ⁱ).

    		(11)

    Interpreting these induced estimates as true conditional scores requires calibrated fields under common conditioning. derives the gradient of and discusses its score interpretation.

    3.3 Shared-Parameter Updates

    Following S2, the generator objective combines distribution matching and perceptual regularization:

    L(θ)=L_score(θ)+L_perc(θ).

    		(12)

    Generator updates alternate with fake estimation in on shared parameters θ, retaining S2’s perceptual regularization [(Zhang et al., 2026c, Zhang et al., 2026d)] and keeping φ frozen. By default, these updates share AdamW states, with separate states evaluated in . At inference, the original projected text selects generation with the chosen few-step schedule, followed by the common one-step spatial Refiner.

    4 Evaluation

    We evaluate 180-second streaming generation on ten StreamAV-Bench metrics and five human-preference dimensions, complemented by absolute ratings, usability, and training-cost and sampling comparisons.

    4.1 Setting

    Training data and model.

    We reuse S2-Avatar’s complete training data and preparation pipeline [(Zhang et al., 2026c)], including filtering and annotation, for livestreams, talking heads, film and television, solo dance, and 2D/3D animation, as summarized in . APEX uses its causal audiovisual backbone and Self-Replay Forcing, sharing parameters and, by default, AdamW states for generator and fake updates.

    Inference.

    Unless otherwise specified, both models use 3 backbone denoising function evaluations (NFE) per generated block, excluding KV-cache encoding and updates. The common one-step 2× spatial Refiner is counted separately. StreamAV-Bench outputs have resolution 1344×768.

    StreamAV-Bench.

    Following the experimental setup of Vidu S2 [(Zhang et al., 2026c)], we use all 160 Progressive and 160 Interactive scenarios of StreamAV-Bench [(Liu et al., 2026f)]. The metrics cover instruction fulfillment (VIF, AIF), visual quality and aesthetics (VQ, VA), audio quality (AQ, PQ), audiovisual alignment and synchronization (AVAlign, AVSync), and subject and background consistency (SC, BC). All metrics are higher-is-better except AVSync, which measures temporal offset error in seconds. The 12-model comparison uses Progressive cases for VIF, AIF, SC, and BC, and both tracks for the remaining metrics.

    Human evaluation.

    We invited experts with backgrounds in art or aesthetics to provide preference ratings for 70 pairs of image-to-video (I2V) sequences across five dimensions: consistency, instruction following, audiovisual synchronization, video quality, and motion quality. Good/Same/Bad (GSB) denote wins, ties, and losses relative to S2-Avatar at 3 NFE. Net preference is 100(G-B)/70, retaining ties in the denominator. Usability requires Mean Opinion Scores (MOS) above 2 for both instruction following and synchronization.

    4.2 Results

    Qualitative comparison.

    compares 3-NFE I2V outputs using the same reference images and timestamps. APEX retains both bags late in one sequence and moves the tube toward the other hand for the applying instruction in another, illustrating object persistence and a prompt-directed change in hand pose.

    Benchmark results.

    APEX ranks first on VA, VIF, and AIF and second on VQ among the 12 models with available results in . In , VIF, AIF, and VA improve on both tracks, with Progressive VIF and AIF increasing by 0.025 and 0.067. VQ rises on Progressive (+0.049) but falls on Interactive (-0.070), yielding -0.011 overall. BC shows the opposite track-level pattern. AQ, AVAlign, and SC decrease on both tracks, pooled PQ is effectively unchanged, and pooled AVSync error rises from 1.319 to 1.341 s. These results show instruction and aesthetic gains alongside visual and audiovisual trade-offs.

    Human evaluation.

    and show the strongest preference for instruction following: 22 wins, 47 ties, and 1 loss yield +30.0% net preference, with MOS of 4.17 versus 3.99. Consistency and video quality each receive +4.3%, corresponding to three net wins. Audiovisual synchronization is tied in 69 of 70 pairs, with one loss (-1.4%) and MOS of 4.23 versus 4.26. Motion quality favors S2-Avatar (-8.6%). Both models meet the usability criterion for 62 of 70 evaluated I2V sequences (88.6%).

    4.3 Training and Sampling Comparisons

    Additional preference evaluations use separate rounds of 70 paired 180-second I2V sequences, each against S2-Avatar at 3 NFE with the same Refiner. groups results by comparison round.

    Training cost.

    In a separate measurement under matched training settings (), peak allocated memory decreases from 102.7 to 98.2 GiB per GPU, saving 4.5 GiB (4.4%) relative to DMD. Mean iteration time decreases from 35.9 to 32.6 s, a reduction of 3.3 s (9.2%), while retaining the frozen teacher.

    Two-step generation.

    Against S2-Avatar at 3 NFE, APEX at 2 NFE receives +27.1% instruction preference (22 wins, 45 ties, 3 losses), while S2-Avatar at 2 NFE receives +2.9% in a separate paired round, as shown in . APEX’s other margins are negative: -2.9% for consistency and video quality, and -7.1% for synchronization and motion quality. compares APEX at 2 NFE with S2-Avatar at 3 NFE, showing broadly similar character appearance with differences in pose and fine detail.

    Timestep sampling.

    We vary the sampling of replay times tᵢ over (0.75,0.9375,0.99), leaving the scoring-time schedule for t^′ unchanged. The default uses equal weights, whereas DF4 and DF10 use (4,1,1) and (10,1,1), raising the probability of drawing the lowest noise level from 1/3 to 2/3 and 5/6. Sampled times are sorted along the replay segment before the differentiable pass. Default sampling has the highest instruction preference at both budgets in , reaching +27.1% at 2 NFE and +21.4% at 3 NFE. Other dimensions vary across both inference budgets, with no consistent advantage from favoring lower-noise replay.

    Optimizer configurations.

    reports results for shared optimizer states at 3 NFE and separate generator/fake optimizer states at 2 NFE. Both configurations use AdamW with shared model parameters, achieving instruction-following net preferences of +21.4% and +14.3%, respectively.

    5 Conclusion

    APEX integrates condition-shifted fake estimation into S2’s Self-Replay Forcing, sharing generator and fake parameters while retaining the frozen teacher. It improves instruction fulfillment and visual aesthetics, with positive human preference for instruction following at both 3 and 2 backbone NFE. Matched measurements show lower peak allocated GPU memory and shorter mean iteration time. Motion quality and audiovisual synchronization remain trade-offs, while APEX and S2-Avatar achieve the same usability rate.

    Appendix A Related Work

    A.1 Consistency and Trajectory-Based Generation

    Diffusion [(Ho et al., 2020, Song et al., 2020, Karras et al., 2022)] and flow matching [(Lipman et al., 2022)] generate samples by integrating a learned velocity field from noise to data. Embedded Representation Warmup [(Liu et al., 2025a)] improves training efficiency by aligning early model layers with a pretrained encoder before full generative training. Consistency and trajectory-based methods train the model to predict over a time interval, allowing generation with fewer network evaluations. Consistency Models (CMs) [(Song et al., 2023, Lu and Song, 2024)] learn to map points on the same trajectory to a common endpoint. Score-regularized continuous-time consistency (rCM) combines consistency training with score-based distribution matching for large-scale diffusion distillation [(Zheng et al., 2025b)]. MeanFlow [(Geng et al., 2025)] predicts the average velocity over an interval, while Transition Models (TiM) [(Wang et al., 2025)] learn the transition between its endpoints. DuMo [(Sun et al., 2026b)] jointly predicts local velocity and a flow map with two heads on a shared backbone. UCGM [(Sun et al., 2025b)] interpolates between generative training objectives.

    A.2 Distribution Matching and Adversarial Training

    Few-step generation also benefits from direct feedback on the generated distribution.

    External correction signals can come from auxiliary score models, as in distribution matching [(Yin et al., 2024b, Yin et al., 2024a)], or from discriminators used in adversarial refiners [(Kim et al., 2023, Sauer et al., 2024, Zheng et al., 2025a)]. Additional networks increase memory use and update cost. Some early distillation methods also use precomputed teacher-student pairs for regularization, while DMD2 removes that paired-data requirement [(Yin et al., 2024a)]. Direct Discriminative Optimization (DDO) [(Zheng et al., 2025a)] expresses the GAN discriminator as a likelihood ratio constructed from the target and a fixed reference model.

    TwinFlow [(Cheng et al., 2026)] learns real and fake trajectories within a shared model and uses their velocity discrepancy to construct an internal correction signal. LLaDA-Image Turbo [(Chen et al., 2026a)] adapts TwinFlow-based distillation to support image generation in two to four sampling steps.

    APEX[(Liu et al., 2026c)] follows this line and separates the branches through condition shifting. The shifted condition selects the fake estimator for samples generated with the original prompt. In , our video formulation shares generator and fake parameters while retaining S2’s frozen reference teacher.

    Intrinsic Distribution Matching (IDM) [(Liu et al., 2026a)] adds feature mean and standard deviation matching to DMD using the generator’s exponential moving average (EMA) copy.

    Few-step score identity distillation (SiD) [(Zhou et al., 2025)] also studies how conditioning affects distribution matching. Its Zero-CFG strategy removes text conditioning from the fake-score network, while Anti-CFG applies negative classifier-free guidance by combining conditional and unconditional predictions. These strategies modify the fake-score estimate. APEX fits the fake velocity under shifted text.

    Fake-Score-network-Free DMD (FSF-DMD) [(Kim et al., 2026a)] replaces the auxiliary fake-score network with a generator-induced endpoint pseudo-velocity. APEX instead learns the fake velocity through flow matching on generated samples under a shifted condition. TBSM [(Sun et al., 2026a)] constructs regression targets from attraction to real samples and repulsion from generated samples under an energy-distance objective; its correction is defined by sample interactions rather than a real/fake velocity difference.

    A.3 Causal Streaming Video

    Autoregressive video diffusion has been studied through asynchronous generation [(Sun et al., 2025a)], progressive prediction [(Xie et al., 2025)], and causal generation with cache sharing [(Gao et al., 2025a)]. MAGI-1 studies autoregressive generation at scale [(Teng et al., 2025)], while SkyReels-V2 targets extended video generation [(Chen et al., 2025)]. FIFO-Diffusion [(Kim et al., 2024)] and StreamingT2V [(Henschel et al., 2025)] also investigate extending video generation beyond a short clip. Later predictions depend on generated history.

    CausVid distills bidirectional video diffusion into an autoregressive model [(Yin et al., 2025)]; diagonal distillation provides another streaming autoregressive formulation [(Liu et al., 2026d)]. Causal Forcing and Causal Forcing++ study few-step autoregressive distillation for real-time interaction [(Zhu et al., 2026a, Zhao et al., 2026b)]. Causal-rCM unifies Teacher Forcing and Self Forcing in a streaming distillation recipe [(Zheng et al., 2026)]. LPM studies video-based character performance [(Zeng et al., 2026)], providing a setting for distribution matching in autoregressive models that animate characters.

    S2-Avatar [(Zhang et al., 2026c)] combines bidirectional reference-conditioned training, causal adaptation with Teacher and Diffusion Forcing, and Self-Replay Forcing. Diffusion Forcing [(Chen et al., 2024)] exposes the model to noisy historical states, while Self Forcing [(Huang et al., 2026a)] trains with autoregressive histories generated by the current model. S2’s replay procedure retains cross-block gradients inside a sampled trajectory segment without retaining the full rollout graph. APEX uses this video setting to learn the fake estimator within the generator while retaining S2’s causal replay procedure and reference teacher. FlowCPO [(Han et al., 2026)] studies offline preference alignment using fixed preferred and dispreferred samples. Preference optimization and latent refinement are separate from the APEX correction.

    A.4 Historical Context and Long Video Generation

    History-Guided Video Diffusion studies conditioning on past video [(Song et al., 2025)], while Grounded Forcing separates persistent semantics from recent dynamics [(Chen et al., 2026b)]. LongLive [(Yang et al., 2025a)] and Rolling Forcing [(Liu et al., 2025b)] target real-time long video generation; Infinity-RoPE investigates action control under autoregressive self-rollout [(Yesiltepe et al., 2026)]. UltraViCo [(Zhao et al., 2026a)] addresses length extrapolation by suppressing attention dispersion beyond the training window, providing a complementary approach to extending video duration. These works motivate evaluating instruction response and motion quality alongside visual appearance as a stream grows longer.

    Memory design provides a complementary approach. SWIFT uses prompt-adaptive memory [(Tan et al., 2026)], IAMFlow studies identity-aware memory [(Liu et al., 2026e)], and FramePack compresses the input-frame context for next-frame prediction [(Zhang and Agrawala, 2025)]. Deep Forcing uses sink states and compression [(Yi et al., 2025)]; Rolling Sink studies the gap between limited training horizons and open-ended testing [(Li et al., 2026b)]. MemRoPE uses evolving memory tokens for extended generation [(Kim et al., 2026b)]. Attention sinks were also studied for streaming language models [(Xiao et al., 2024)]; S2 adopts sink blocks within its video context design [(Zhang et al., 2026d, Zhang et al., 2026c)]. APEX retains this context design for its shared model. Quant VideoGen [(Xi et al., 2026)] reduces autoregressive history-storage costs through two-bit KV-cache quantization, using semantic-aware smoothing and progressive residual quantization. ViewRope [(Xiang et al., 2026)] instead injects camera-ray geometry into rotary position embeddings and selects relevant historical frames to improve spatial consistency in camera-controlled video world models. These methods address history storage and retrieval, complementing APEX’s focus on the training cost of distribution estimation.

    For streaming video understanding, ChronoReplay [(Hu et al., 2026a)] organizes heterogeneous spatial supervision into chronological episodes, while Supervising the Visible State[(Hu et al., 2026b)] separates supervision of temporal state from adaptive selection of visual evidence. These studies provide complementary context for the role of temporal supervision and historical evidence in streaming video understanding.

    A.5 Audio-Driven and Interactive Video

    Audio-driven character generation includes portrait animation with Hallo3 [(Cui et al., 2025)], body animation with OmniAvatar [(Gan et al., 2025)], and cinematic video with Wan-S2V [(Gao et al., 2025b)]. StableAvatar studies extended audio-driven generation [(Tu et al., 2025)]. Live Avatar [(Huang et al., 2025)], SoulX-FlashTalk [(Shen et al., 2025)], and AptAvatar [(Zhang et al., 2026a)] address real-time or long-form avatar generation. AvatarForcing specifically studies one-step streaming talking avatars [(Cui et al., 2026)]. Joint audio and video generation is studied by OmniForcing [(Su et al., 2026b)], Hallo-Live [(Li et al., 2026a)], and Omni-LiveAvatar [(Zhu et al., 2026b)]. TurboT2VA [(Yang et al., 2026)] extends consistency distillation to joint video-audio generation with modality-specific normalization and a progressive curriculum that introduces distribution matching after consistency training. This connects few-step distillation to audiovisual synchronization, although its joint-generation setting differs from the causal replay setting studied here. Comparisons must distinguish joint audio generation from video generation conditioned on fixed external audio.

    S2’s evaluation also includes external systems such as PixVerse R1 [(PixVerse, 2026)], HappyOyster [(Alibaba, 2026)], Odyssey-2 [(Odyssey, 2025)], and HeyGen [(HeyGen, 2026)]. Their inclusion in S2 provides evaluation context; the APEX evidence here consists of the internal I2V comparison and the completed StreamAV-Bench run in . Comparisons must match references, audio, duration, and resolution.

    A.6 Efficient Video Inference

    Sampling steps are one component of generation cost. TurboDiffusion accelerates video diffusion [(Zhang et al., 2025h)], and TurboServe addresses efficient streaming service [(Jiang et al., 2026)]. Pyramidal Flow Matching studies efficient video generation across scales [(Jin et al., 2025)]; the present experiments account separately for the low-resolution backbone and one-step high-resolution spatial Refiner.

    Efficient attention methods can be organized into hardware-efficient, sparse, compact, and linear approaches [(Zhang et al., 2025b)]. Sparse VideoGen [(Xi et al., 2025)] exploits spatial and temporal attention-head patterns, while Sparse VideoGen2 [(Yang et al., 2025b)] uses semantic-aware token permutation to identify and group important attention blocks. SVG-EAR [(Zhou et al., 2026)] complements sparse computation with parameter-free centroid compensation and error-aware routing for skipped blocks.

    S2’s attention implementation draws on several families of efficient operators. SageAttention and SageAttention2 use low-bit attention [(Zhang et al., 2025e, Zhang et al., 2025a)]; SageAttention2++ improves its implementation [(Zhang et al., 2025g)], and SageAttention3 explores FP4 inference and low-bit training [(Zhang et al., 2025d)]. SageBwd further studies trainable low-bit attention [(Zhang et al., 2026b)]. SpargeAttention studies sparse attention without additional training [(Zhang et al., 2025f)], while SpargeAttention2 uses trainable masking and distillation [(Zhang et al., 2026e)]. SLA and SLA2 combine sparse and linear attention. SLA2 incorporates learnable routing together with quantization-aware training [(Zhang et al., 2025c, Zhang et al., 2026f)].

    At the linear-layer level, 6Bit-Diffusion [(Su et al., 2026a)] dynamically allocates NVFP4 and INT8 precision according to quantization sensitivity and reuses temporally stable block residuals. Speculative Decoding for Autoregressive Video Generation [(Hu and Zhang, 2026)] uses a smaller model to draft video blocks and a quality router to decide which blocks require regeneration by the larger target model. Both affect inference computation, a separate consideration from the number of networks maintained during distillation.

    S2 also draws on block-level low-bit computation [(Zhang et al., 2025i)] and Ulysses-style parallelism [(Jacobs et al., 2023)]. These operators, precision choices, and parallel schedules can change latency at the same NFE. The training-cost comparison in measures APEX and DMD under matched settings.

    A.7 Streaming Video Editing

    StreamDiffusionV2 studies dynamic interactive video generation [(Feng et al., 2025)]. LiveEdit [(Wang et al., 2026)], JoyAI-Video-Edit [(Xiao et al., 2026)], and SANA-Streaming [(Zhao et al., 2026c)] address streaming video editing. These methods use an incoming video’s motion and structure, which differs from I2V conditioning.

    Interactive streaming evaluation.

    StreamEval [(StreamEval Team, 2026)] evaluates timed interactions across avatar dialogue, avatar performance, world generation, instruction editing, and reference editing, measuring task execution, state consistency, visual fidelity, and audiovisual coordination. Our reported benchmark results use StreamAV-Bench [(Liu et al., 2026f)] and do not include StreamEval measurements.

    Visual text evaluation.

    VTR-Bench [(Huang et al., 2026b)] evaluates visual text fidelity separately from scene and motion requirements in video. UltraText Bench [(Liu et al., 2026b)] evaluates dense bilingual text in individual images, providing complementary background on visual text rendering. Neither is evaluated here.

    Appendix B Theoretical Analysis and Proofs

    We derive the OT score-velocity identity and the frozen-target gradient in . The endpoint formulation in compares clean-latent and velocity losses algebraically. The score identities fix conditioning; the replay gradient differentiates connected predictions with the target fixed. These results do not establish long-horizon stability or an exact KL gradient for the joint video trajectory.

    B.1 Setup

    We use bold lowercase letters for vectors like x,z,v and bold uppercase letters for matrices and operators like F. The identity matrix is denoted by I, and 0 represents the zero vector.

    For x,z∈ℝᵈ, let pᵣ(x) be the data distribution and p_z(z)=ℕ(0,I) the standard Gaussian prior.

    For conditional generation, c denotes the projected text representation, and pᵣ(x|c) is the conditional data distribution. Additional video conditions h are held fixed and suppressed, as is c when unambiguous. Throughout this appendix, we work with the Optimal Transport (OT) interpolation path defined by:

    xₜ=tz+(1-t)x, t∈[0,1],

    		(13)

    This satisfies the boundary conditions: x₀=x (pure data) and x₁=z (pure noise). All score identities and time weights below are used for t∈(0,1). The per-sample FM target is constant along this path:

    uᵣ(x,z):=z-x.

    		(14)

    The population real-data velocity is the conditional mean of this target:

    vᵣ^*(xₜ,t):=𝔼[uᵣ(x,z)|xₜ,t].

    		(15)

    The score function is s_r,t(xₜ):=∇_xₜ\logp_r,t(xₜ), where p_r,t(xₜ) is the marginal density of xₜ at time t.

    A star marks a population conditional mean, distinct from a network estimate.

    We write F_θ for the velocity estimate F_θ(xₜ,t,c)∈ℝᵈ when its inputs are clear.

    The operator \mathop\color[rgb]1,0,0sg(·) denotes stop-gradient. For θ∈ℝ^P and a vector output q∈ℝᵈ, J_θq:=∂q/∂θ∈ℝ^d×P, so the chain rule uses its transpose to map output derivatives to parameter gradients.

    For video, branch r is the guided frozen-teacher reference and branch θ is the shared fake estimate. Teacher parameters are φ. Hats mark network estimates; unadorned scores are exact.

    Throughout this paper, F_θ(y,t,c) denotes a velocity prediction with no destination-time argument. The one-step map G_θ(z,c)=z-F_θ(z,1,c) and S2’s clean-latent conversion use this same parameterization.

    We define the endpoint predictor that maps a velocity estimate to its implied clean sample:

    fˣ(F,xₜ,t):=xₜ-t·F.

    		(16)

    This is motivated by the OT path: if xₜ=tz+(1-t)x and F≈z-x, then fˣ(F,xₜ,t)≈x.

    B.2 Score-Velocity Duality under OT Path

    The OT path gives a score-velocity identity for both real and generated endpoint distributions.

    Proposition B.1 (Score-Velocity Duality) .

    Let xₜ=tz+(1-t)x for t∈(0,1), with independent draws z∼ℕ(0,I) and x∼pᵣ. Write p_r,t for the density of xₜ. The optimal least-squares velocity is

    vᵣ^*(xₜ,t):=𝔼[uᵣ(x,z)|xₜ,t].

    		(17)

    Then the score function s_r,t(xₜ):=∇_xₜ\logp_r,t(xₜ) along the OT path satisfies

    s_r,t(xₜ)=-(xₜ+(1-t)vᵣ^*(xₜ,t))/(t).

    		(18)

    Proof B.2 .

    Step 1: Rewrite as an additive Gaussian observation model. Define x^′:=(1-t)x. Then the OT path becomes an additive Gaussian observation of the scaled endpoint:

    xₜ=x^′+tz, z∼ℕ(0,I).

    Conditioned on x^′, the likelihood is xₜ|x^′∼ℕ(x^′,t²I), since xₜ-x^′=tz and z∼ℕ(0,I) implies tz∼ℕ(0,t²I), with the noise covariance determined by the sampled diffusion time.

    Step 2: Apply Tweedie’s formula to recover the posterior mean. At fixed t, Tweedie’s formula [(Efron, 2011)] recovers the posterior mean of the scaled endpoint x^′=(1-t)x from the marginal score of xₜ=x^′+tz:

    𝔼[x^′|xₜ]=xₜ+t² ∇_xₜ\logp_r,t(xₜ)=xₜ+t² s_r,t(xₜ).

    		(19)

    Since x^′=(1-t)x, we recover the conditional expectation of the original clean endpoint x:

    𝔼[x|xₜ]=1/1-t𝔼[x^′|xₜ]
    =1/1-t[xₜ+t² s_r,t(xₜ)]
    =(xₜ+t² s_r,t(xₜ))/(1-t).(20)

    Step 3: Express the conditional mean of z. From the OT path xₜ=tz+(1-t)x, solving for the noise gives:

    z=xₜ-(1-t)x/t.

    Taking expectations conditioned on xₜ and substituting the mean endpoint gives:

    𝔼[z|xₜ]=𝔼 [xₜ-(1-t)x/t \middle| xₜ]

item.title: 流式多参考视频生成：TaoMate-R1 给「建立场景」和「延续场景」各配一个 LoRA，冻结主干 ｜ TaoMate-R1: Temporal Role Specialization for Streaming Multi-Reference Video Generation
item.description:
一句话：先按指定人物与物体建场景，再在指令变化下持续生成——两个阶段的任务性质并不一样。

要点：

  • 任务定义：流式多参考视频生成先用指定的人与物建立场景，然后在**指令不断变化**的情况下继续生成
  • TaoMate-R1 的做法是按时间角色分工：在**冻结的主干**上，为「场景建立」与「场景延续」各挂一组独立的低秩适配器
  • 每个适配器既负责自己角色的去噪，也负责上下文写入，并通过 Self Gradient Forcing 联合训练这两个角色

为什么值得看：「开局建立身份、之后保持身份」是实时生成内容最难的部分：同一个人在镜头转开后还能不能是同一个人。按角色拆适配器而不是整模型微调，是低成本的工程解法。

中文摘要：流式多参考视频生成的任务形态是：先用指定的人物与物体建立一个场景，然后在指令持续变化的情况下把它延续下去。两个阶段的性质其实不同——前者要「建对身份」，后者要「长期保持身份」。TaoMate-R1 因此按时间角色做分工：在一个冻结的主干上，为场景建立与场景延续分别挂一组独立的低秩适配器；每个适配器既执行自己角色的去噪，也执行对应的上下文写入，再通过 Self Gradient Forcing 把两个角色联合训练起来。相比整模型微调，这种拆法更省，也更适合流式场景下的持续生成。

主题：AI Rendering

来源：arXiv·cs.CV（English）

原文发布：2026-11-11

本期推送：2026-11-13

TaoMate-R1: Temporal Role Specialization for Streaming Multi-Reference Video Generation

Abstract

Streaming multi-reference video generation establishes a scene from specified people and objects, then continues it under changing instructions. We introduce TaoMate-R1, a streaming multi-reference generator that organizes adaptation parameters through temporal role specialization. It assigns separate low-rank adapters to scene establishment and continuation on a frozen backbone. Each adapter performs both denoising and context writing for its role; Self Gradient Forcing jointly trains the roles through the history they construct. This allocation contrasts with operation-based specialization, which separates denoising from context writing across all chunks. A fixed-replay gradient analysis characterizes the update directions admitted by the two sharing schemes. On 32 multi-reference cases, we compare the schemes at the same two-adapter budget. Across ten approximately two-minute streams with changing instructions and shared teacher-audio conditioning, TaoMate-R1 reduces the mean boundary luminance jump from 1.96 to 0.613, with higher boundary feature similarity. It also achieves higher mean CLIP and DINO temporal similarity across short interactions, long streams, and public reference compositions. These results support grouping adaptation parameters by scene establishment and continuation for streaming multi-reference generation. Our code and model are released at https://github.com/TaoLiveAIGC/TaoMate-H3.

Qijun Gan*, Chenwei Zhang*, Xinyang Li, Meiguang Jin†, Junfeng Ma

Alibaba Group
{ganqijun.gqj, meiguang.jmg}@taobao.com

††footnotetext: *Equal contribution. †Corresponding author.

1  Introduction

Multi-reference video generation specifies the people and objects in a scene through images. Models such as Phantom, VACE, and MiniMax-H3 compose these visual conditions into video clips [1, 2, 3]. Streaming extends the task to an evolving scene: a presenter introduces a cup, puts it away, and picks up a bag as new instructions arrive. The desired behavior combines change with persistence. The current instruction determines the interaction, while the generated past determines its starting state.

The opening and subsequent chunks therefore solve different conditional tasks. At the opening, the generator chooses how reference appearances are realized through pose, placement, and initial motion. During continuation, those realized choices become part of the conditioning: a hand holding a cup constrains where the next action begins. This asymmetry motivates studying whether these tasks should receive independent adaptation.

Autoregressive diffusion and student-rollout training make generated history available during learning [4, 5]. Self Gradient Forcing (SGF) also lets later predictions supervise the computations that write this history [6]. SGF+ separates denoising and context-writing parameters to accommodate differences between their gradient contributions [7]. This is an operation-based partition: each operation shares parameters across the entire stream. We investigate a temporal-role partition at the same two-adapter budget, grouping generation and writing by whether they establish or continue a scene. The distinction concerns which computations learn together (Fig.1).

We introduce TaoMate-R1, which implements temporal role specialization with an opening adapter at absolute chunk zero and a continuation adapter for every later chunk. Within each role, denoising and context writing share the same low-rank parameters on a frozen backbone. Instruction changes update the continuation conditions while preserving its adapter and generated history. We train both roles with SGF: historical-context gradients return to the role that wrote the corresponding representation. The opening role thus learns both the first chunk and its persistent video anchor; the continuation role learns subsequent predictions and recent audiovisual context.

We characterize this design through a local analysis of parameter sharing. At a common initialization and fixed replay, the two partitions preserve the same common gradient component but admit different specialization directions. The analysis also isolates continuation-only windows, where the comparison depends on alignment between continuation’s generation and writing gradients. These relations describe the optimization consequences of tying parameters and provide a precise basis for comparing the two assignments.

Our experiments compare TaoMate-R1’s Temporal split with Shared and Operation split on the same H3 backbone. Across 32 cases, TaoMate-R1 achieves higher mean CLIP and DINO temporal similarity than Operation split on short interactions, long instruction-driven streams, and public reference compositions. The clearest difference occurs at instruction boundaries in ten approximately two-minute streams: TaoMate-R1 has a mean luminance jump of 0.613, compared with 1.96 for Operation split, and higher adjacent-frame feature similarity. We examine these differences with case-paired statistics and background-appearance visualizations, then place the generator’s results alongside external reference-conditioned systems. The contributions are:

  • \blacktriangleright

    TaoMate-R1, a streaming multi-reference generator that assigns independent adapters to scene establishment and continuation, shares denoising and context writing within each role, and trains them jointly through SGF.

  • \blacktriangleright

    A local gradient characterization of temporal and operation-based sharing, including the dependence on generation–writing alignment in continuation-only training windows.

  • \blacktriangleright

    A comparison across 32 multi-reference cases showing higher mean temporal similarity across three interaction settings and reduced instruction-boundary discontinuities on long streams.

    • 2  Related Work

    Multi-Reference Generation and Control.

    Reference images specify visual attributes and associate them with entities. ConsisID separates facial structure from identity detail [8]; Video Alchemist binds reference features to entity words [9]; and Movie Weaver combines prompt anchors with reference-order embeddings [10]. Phantom aligns visual and textual reference representations [1], VACE integrates image, video, and mask conditions [2], and MiniMax-H3 supports multi-reference audiovisual generation [3]. Spatiotemporal control specifies where and when these entities appear: DreamVideo-2 uses bounding-box trajectories [11], AlcheMinT uses interval-dependent rotary embeddings [12], and MultiShotMaster combines shot-aware encoding with reference grounding [13]. For interactive streams, FlowAct-R2 aligns evolving conditions with planned behavior [14], while ReferStream introduces arriving subjects through contextualized reference latents and cache injection [15]. These methods organize visual conditions; our study concerns the adaptation parameters used to realize them across an ongoing scene.

    Causal Generation and Generated-History Training.

    Diffusion Forcing uses token-wise noise levels for causal generation [16]; CausVid distills a bidirectional teacher into a few-step causal model [4]; and SkyReels-V2 extends videos with nondecreasing frame-wise noise schedules [17]. History retention supplies persistent appearance and recent motion: StreamingT2V combines initial-chunk cues with preceding-chunk features [18], FramePack compresses context according to historical importance [19], and LongLive combines a frame sink with local attention [20]. LongLive-RAG retrieves earlier latents [21], while FilmWeaver separates cross-shot keyframes from recent within-shot memory [22]. Training with generated predecessors addresses the context distribution encountered at inference, from Scheduled Sampling [23] to Self Forcing’s student rollouts [5] and Rolling Forcing’s jointly denoised windows [24]. SGF additionally propagates supervision through historical context writers [6]. We adopt this training framework and study parameter sharing under a fixed history-retention policy.

    Parameter Specialization.

    Specialization allocates independent parameters to computations with different learning demands. DreamVideo composes identity and motion adapters [25], while eDiff-I and Wan2.2 specialize denoisers by diffusion-noise interval [26, 27]. SGF+ separates denoising and context-writing parameters to address gradient differences between these operations [7]. TaoMate-R1 groups the same operations by temporal role, using independent low-rank adapters [28] for scene establishment and continuation. Our comparison with operation-based sharing holds the two-adapter budget fixed and examines the resulting generation and continuity measurements.

    3  TaoMate-R1

    TaoMate-R1 is a streaming multi-reference generator built on temporal role specialization: it groups generation and context writing by their role in the stream (Fig.2).

    3.1 Preliminaries

    Generation and Context Writing.

    A streaming diffusion model alternates between generating a chunk and encoding it as history. For external conditions q_b and retained keys and values H_
    ẑ_b=G_θ(ε_b,q_b,H_(1)
    h_b=W_θ(ẑ_b,q_b,H_

    The retained part of h_b conditions subsequent predictions.

    Generated-History Supervision.

    SGF trains historical representations on student-generated rollouts [6]. Recorded historical latent inputs remain fixed during differentiation, while later losses propagate through their KV-writing computations. Generation and writing therefore contribute separate paths to the same objective. Sharing their parameters sums these contributions into one update; independent parameters allocate them to separate updates. Our method specifies this sharing relation for the opening and continuation of a stream.

    3.2 Problem Formulation

    Let ℝ_b denote the reference images active at chunk b, c_b its instruction, and z_b=(z_bᵛ,z_bᵃ) its audiovisual latents. These specify q_b=(ℝ_b,c_b) in Eq.1. The retained history H_
    p(z_0:B-1|ℝ_0:B-1,c_0:B-1)(2)
    =p_θ_first(z₀|ℝ₀,c₀)∏_b=1^B-1p_θ_cont(z_b|ℝ_b,c_b,H_

    Establishment occurs once, at absolute chunk b=0. Changes in instructions or active references become conditions for continuation within the existing scene.

    The references and generated history provide different kinds of information. Reference images identify entities and their appearances; history records how those entities have been realized together in the current scene. At the opening, the model establishes their spatial arrangement, poses, and interaction state from the supplied conditions. Continuation inherits this realization and predicts its evolution under the current instruction. For example, presenting a new object changes the active references while the presenter and room remain part of the ongoing scene. The temporal role thus follows the stream’s established state: changing an instruction updates the interaction goal while retaining the history from which the next action begins.

    The long-stream evaluation additionally supplies cached audio states and removal-segment end-frame conditions.

    3.3 Temporal Role Specialization

    The opening and continuation adapters use independent LoRA updates [28] on a shared frozen backbone:

    r(b)=\begincasesfirst,&b=0, cont,&b>0,\endcases θ_b=θ_base+Δθ_r(b).

    		(3)

    Both inherit the LoRA weights of the same trained autoregressive generator and are optimized jointly. Their weights, AdamW moments, and exponential moving averages are copied into independent states. For each adapted layer, Θᵣ=Θ₀+BᵣAᵣ, with fixed LoRA scaling absorbed into the factors. Both adapters use rank and scaling 128 on the attention QKV/output and feed-forward projections, covering 208 linear layers.

    The selected θ_b governs both G and W in Eq.1. Thus, a temporal role adapts its synthesis mapping together with the context representation it leaves for future predictions.

    This grouping specifies which learning signals shape the same adaptation. For establishment, generation realizes the references in an initial scene and writing represents that scene for subsequent predictions. For continuation, generation evolves the interaction and writing updates the context available to the next chunk. Within-role sharing combines these contributions according to their conditional task. Operation-based specialization instead combines opening and continuation signals within each operation. The same generation and writing calls are therefore grouped along different axes: temporal role in TaoMate-R1 and computational operation in SGF+.

    At inference, the history retains the opening video KVs as a persistent appearance anchor and the latest two audiovisual chunks’ KVs as recent interaction context. For b>0,

    H_

    		(4)

    Overlapping entries are counted once; opening audio remains only in the recent window. Reference conditions remain available independently of this history, and temporal positions remain absolute. Thus, the opening role writes the persistent anchor, while continuation supplies the rolling interaction context. All three parameter-sharing configurations use this retention policy.

    3.4 Joint Training with Context Gradients

    Student Rollouts and Distribution Matching.

    We train TaoMate-R1’s two roles using student rollouts [5] and SGF’s context gradients [6]. Let I={s,…,e} denote a sampled training window, with its preceding prefix held fixed as conditioning. We request five or ten chunks with probabilities 0.8 and 0.2, truncated by source length. The prefix is encoded from cached clean teacher latents; references and text remain fixed within an example. Nominal opening and continuation chunks contain 39 and 34 frames at 24 fps. A gradient-free rollout uses one initial-to-clean evaluation per chunk and records the prediction noise, generated latents, context, and actual writer input z̃_b, including the training context perturbation. Both computations use the adapter selected by the absolute chunk index.

    Distribution-matching distillation [29] supervises the generated audiovisual content. A frozen real-score model and a learned fake-score model evaluate the same corrupted student sequence, producing a detached direction d_b. Let ẑ_b,realᵐ and ẑ_b,fakeᵐ be their clean estimates for modality m. We use the normalized direction

    d_bᵐ=sg [(ẑ_b,fakeᵐ-ẑ_b,realᵐ)/(\max (mean|ẑ_bᵐ-ẑ_b,realᵐ|,ε))].

    		(5)

    We set ε=10⁻⁸. For a prediction ẑ_b replayed with its recorded inputs, we optimize

    L_b=1/2∑_m∈{v,a}λₘ∥ẑ_bᵐ-sg(ẑ_bᵐ-d_bᵐ)∥ₘₑₐₙ².

    		(6)

    Here sg stops gradients, λᵥ=1, λₐ=0.1, and the squared norm averages over that modality’s latent elements. The window objective is L=|I|⁻¹∑_b∈IL_b. Both roles share a single fake-score model, trained on detached student outputs. The fake score receives velocity-regression updates every iteration; generator updates occur every fifth iteration.

    Historical Credit Assignment.

    Replay losses accumulate context gradients on shared historical KV variables. We realize SGF’s context-gradient reconstruction by differentiating each historical writer once in reverse temporal order, with its recorded latent input held fixed. The accumulated gradient returns to the adapter selected by that writer’s absolute chunk index and propagates through its preceding KVs. This assigns both synthesis and historical credit to the appropriate temporal role:

    ∇_ΔθᵣL=∑_b∈Iᵣg_bᵍᵉⁿ+∑_j∈Jᵣ((∂hⱼ)/(∂Δθᵣ))^⊤h̄ⱼ.

    		(7)

    Here Iᵣ and Jᵣ index role r’s supervised predictions and differentiable historical writers within the effective window. The direct gradient g_bᵍᵉⁿ is taken through the current denoiser from L_b/|I|. The writer Jacobian holds its recorded latent input and incoming KVs fixed; h̄ⱼ includes all downstream prediction and writer paths under the window-averaged objective.

    A historical representation influences the objective through direct reads by later denoisers and through context written by intervening chunks. The reverse pass accumulates these routes before differentiating the corresponding writer. For a recorded writer input, the context computation and its contribution to an earlier representation are

    hⱼ=W_θⱼ(sg(z̃ⱼ),qⱼ,H_(8)
    h̄ᵢ\mathrel+=((∂hⱼ)/(∂hᵢ))^⊤h̄ⱼ, s≤i(9)

    The same accumulated signal supplies the writer term in Eq.7. Its parameter update belongs to the role that produced the representation, connecting independently adapted opening and continuation computations through their shared generated history.

    When the effective window includes the opening, continuation losses supervise its context representation through Δθ_first. For s>0, the opening is fixed conditioning and receives no update. Algorithm 1 summarizes the rollout and reverse context-gradient pass.

    Optimization and Inference.

    We use AdamW with generator/fake-score learning rates 5×10⁻⁵/10⁻⁵, β=(0,0.999), weight decay 0.01, gradient clipping at 1, global batch 16, and seed 42. Training perturbs noninitial writer inputs up to noise level 0.15; writing still uses clean time, and replay retains the sampled perturbation. Inference uses unperturbed context and three Euler evaluations per chunk. With u_b,0=ε_b and velocity prediction v_θ_bᵐ, each evaluation updates

    u_b,k+1ᵐ=u_b,kᵐ+(σₖᵐ-σₖ₊₁ᵐ)(10)
    ·v_θ_bᵐ(u_b,k,q_b,H_

    For uᵢ=1-i/49, the noise schedule is σᵢᵐ=γₘuᵢ/[1+(γₘ-1)uᵢ], with γᵥ=12, γₐ=3 and retained indices (0,16,33,49). The selected role remains active throughout denoising and clean-context writing.

    3.5 Local Gradient Analysis of Parameter Sharing

    To compare the partitions in Figure 1(b), introduce four virtual adapter copies, one per temporal-role–operation pair: x=(θ_firstG,θ_firstW,θ_contG,θ_contW). Temporal role specialization ties generation and writing within each temporal role; SGF+’s operation split ties opening and continuation within each operation [7].

    Consider a fixed replay at the common adapter initialization, holding the sampled rollout, historical latent inputs, prediction noise, and distribution-matching targets fixed. Let g_rG and g_rW denote the gradient contributions through generation and writing for temporal role r. The contrasts retained by the two assignments are

    v_T=(g_firstG+g_firstW)-(g_contG+g_contW),(11)
    v_O=(g_firstG+g_contG)-(g_firstW+g_contW).

    For a fixed norm ρ of the four-block parameter update, let D_T and D_O be the largest first-order loss decreases admitted by temporal and operation sharing. Orthogonal projection gives

    D_T²-D_O²=ρ²/4(∥v_T∥²-∥v_O∥²).

    		(12)

    Both assignments retain the common gradient while preserving a different specialization direction. Temporal role specialization admits the larger local decrease when the establishment–continuation contrast exceeds the denoising–writing contrast in norm. For a window starting after chunk zero, the opening belongs to the fixed prefix, so g_firstG=g_firstW=0 and

    D_T²-D_O²=ρ²⟨g_contG,g_contW⟩.

    		(13)

    In this case, aligned generation and writing gradients favor sharing within continuation; opposing gradients favor operation separation. The relations characterize a fixed replay’s local update geometry; our experiments compare the resulting trained generators.

    4  Experiments

    We evaluate TaoMate-R1 through parameter-sharing comparisons on a common streaming backbone, followed by system-level generation results.

    4.1 Experimental Setup

    Cases and Parameter-Sharing Configurations.

    We evaluate 32 cases: ten short person–object interactions, ten approximately two-minute streams with twenty successive instructions each, and twelve public reference compositions from MultiRef-Compass [30]. Short and public clips are approximately ten seconds long. On the H3 backbone, Shared uses one rank-128 adapter for generation and writing across all chunks. Operation split uses two rank-128 adapters, separating generation from writing following SGF+. TaoMate-R1 implements Temporal split with two rank-128 adapters, separating opening from continuation. The two splits have the same adapter budget; their grouping of computations is the variable of interest. All three configurations use the same training cohort, reference inputs, instructions, history-retention policy, and three-evaluation Euler solver. Short and public cases generate native audio; long cases follow cached teacher-audio trajectories and use end-frame conditions for object-removal segments. The training cohort contains 2,196 examples of 4–15 seconds, covering 1,969 object-preserving, 119 object-removal, and 108 object-introduction interactions. Training excludes first- and last-frame image conditions. For long evaluation streams, each product presentation is followed by removal, with the person-and-scene reference supplied as the removal segment’s end-frame condition.

    Metrics and Aggregation.

    CLIP and DINOv2 measure whole-frame reference similarity and temporal similarity between successive 1 Hz samples [31, 32]. Full-prompt CLIP and ViCLIP assess text alignment; VABench measures realism and five-question case-level visual QA [33]. At instruction changes, CLIP and DINO compare adjacent boundary frames; Luma is the absolute difference in their mean grayscale intensity (0–255). Scores use equal case weights; paired bootstrapping resamples cases while retaining each complete stream and its matched model outputs. We draw 100,000 paired resamples and report unadjusted percentile 95% intervals.

    4.2 Effect of the Specialization Axis

    The same-backbone block of Table1 compares all three assignments. TaoMate-R1 achieves an aggregate DINO temporal similarity of 0.934, compared with 0.928 for Operation split and 0.914 for Shared.

    Table2 separates short interactions, long changing-instruction streams, and public reference compositions. TaoMate-R1 obtains the highest mean CLIP and DINO temporal similarity in all three groups. On short interactions, it also leads in DINO reference similarity, reaching 0.545 versus 0.531 for Operation split. Its CLIP and DINO temporal similarities are 0.970 and 0.975, compared with 0.969 and 0.972 for Operation split, while Operation split has higher visual QA (0.900 versus 0.880).

    On long streams, TaoMate-R1 reaches CLIP and DINO temporal similarities of 0.956 and 0.921, compared with 0.948 and 0.914 for Operation split. The paired difference in DINO temporal similarity (TaoMate-R1 minus Operation split) is +0.00730 (95% interval [-0.00958,0.0227]). Operation split has higher DINO reference similarity (0.486 versus 0.478). Its QA of 1.00 and TaoMate-R1’s 0.980 correspond to 50 and 49 correct answers across five questions per case. On public reference compositions, TaoMate-R1 leads all four reported metrics, with DINO reference similarity of 0.207, CLIP and DINO temporal similarities of 0.948 and 0.911, and visual QA of 0.983.

    Interaction Settings and Shared Adaptation.

    Both two-adapter configurations improve DINO temporal similarity over Shared in every evaluated group. At the same adapter budget, TaoMate-R1 further increases the temporal means across all three settings, supporting the assignment of adaptation capacity by opening and continuation. The aggregate score combines twenty-two short or public cases with ten long streams under equal case weighting; the subgroup results show higher temporal means for TaoMate-R1 within each group. Reference similarity and visual QA vary by setting, indicating that higher temporal similarity does not imply uniformly better reference matching or visual QA.

    Figure3 examines background appearance in fixed foliage and vase crops over a 119-second stream. Views at 0, 60, and 119 seconds show the evolution of leaf and ceramic tones. The overlays average per-pixel CIE Lab distances from each video’s initial frame over the full stream at 1 Hz. TaoMate-R1 shows smaller appearance changes than Operation split in these regions, complementing the whole-frame temporal measurements.

    Interaction Dynamics.

    Figure4 compares the three sharing schemes at matched timestamps within two changing-instruction streams. In the bag sequence, all three configurations present the referenced item at 72 and 74 s. At 76 s, TaoMate-R1 moves it toward the instructed screen-right side, Shared moves it screen-left, and Operation split still holds it centrally. In the second sequence, Shared and TaoMate-R1 proceed from the notebook to the folded umbrella; Operation split remains empty-handed at 106 and 108 s. The TaoMate-R1 frames show evolving hand poses and object states within the retained scene. Together with the background views, these sequences make both components of streaming interaction visible: carrying out a new action and preserving the scene in which it unfolds.

    4.3 Continuity across Instruction Changes

    Table3 compares adjacent frames at the same instruction boundaries in the ten long streams. TaoMate-R1 obtains CLIP and DINO boundary similarities of 0.991 and 0.990, compared with 0.979 and 0.973 for Operation split. Its mean luminance jump is 0.613 versus 1.96, a reduction of 1.35 gray levels, or 68.7%. Shared obtains boundary similarities of 0.979 and 0.978 and a mean luminance jump of 1.86.

    The case-paired analysis gives a difference (TaoMate-R1 minus Operation split) of +0.0177 in DINO boundary similarity (95% interval [0.00820,0.0288]) and -1.35 in luminance jump ([-1.58,-1.12]). Luminance jumps decrease in all ten streams, and CLIP and DINO boundary similarities each increase in nine streams. These transition-level gains are more consistent across cases than the sequence-level DINO temporal difference.

    Continuity under Changing Conditions.

    An instruction change introduces a new interaction goal while the preceding scene remains the starting state for continuation. Boundary measurements evaluate the immediate transition from the last frame under one instruction to the first under the next. Sequence-level temporal scores also include the intervening within-instruction evolution. Together, they show higher temporal-similarity means over the full streams, with the clearest paired evidence at instruction changes. The background views in Fig.3 extend this analysis to retained scene appearance over the complete stream. These observations support temporal specialization for maintaining scene continuity as interaction goals change.

    4.4 Generation Quality

    Reference-Conditioned Systems.

    The external-system block of Table1 compares MiniMax-H3 [3], VACE [2], SkyReels-V3 [34], and Phantom [1]. For the long cases, these systems generate each instruction segment independently and concatenate the resulting clips; our autoregressive variants retain history across instruction changes. TaoMate-R1 leads in mean DINO reference similarity, both temporal similarity metrics, realism, and visual QA. VACE leads in CLIP reference and full-prompt CLIP scores, and MiniMax-H3 in ViCLIP.

    Qualitative Comparisons.

    Figure5 shows four reference-conditioned interactions. In the gallery scene, MiniMax-H3 and TaoMate-R1 depict both cartoon characters interacting with a guitar. VACE renders live-action participants, while SkyReels-V3 and Phantom depict Santa as a small held figure. In the scarf scene, our output includes an additional guitar. The continuous-interaction rows show cosmetics-bag and closed-umbrella presentation within the established scene. At 72 s, our stream depicts the sage-green bag alongside the presenter in the established room.

    Long-Stream System Comparison.

    Table4 compares continuous generation with independently generated instruction clips on the ten long cases. TaoMate-R1 achieves DINO temporal similarity of 0.921, compared with 0.812–0.848 for the clip-generation systems. At segment boundaries, DINO similarity is 0.990 versus 0.589–0.831, and the mean luminance jump is 0.613 versus 9.12–14.3. These results compare the complete generation protocols; the same-backbone comparisons above isolate the choice of adaptation assignment.

    Figure6 arranges frame columns sampled every 0.5 s along a timeline. Independent clip joins produce bands in head height, body scale, and background appearance, while the continuous stream maintains more stable presenter and table geometry.

    The time-column representation relates these bands to changes in scene composition. A change in camera framing or subject scale shifts several horizontal structures together, producing a discontinuity across the sampled timeline. In the continuous stream, the table edge and background patterns trace more continuous paths through successive instructions. This connects the boundary scores in Table4 to visible scene properties such as presenter scale and background placement. Together, the visual comparisons examine reference-conditioned interactions in Fig.5, localized background appearance in Fig.3, and scene-level continuity in Fig.6.

    Audiovisual Measurements.

    On the 22 native-audio cases, TaoMate-R1 has higher mean AV alignment than Operation split (4.77 versus 4.59). Operation split has higher audio QA (0.809 versus 0.736) and lower Desync (0.282 versus 0.445), showing a different ordering for audio content and synchronization.

    5  Conclusion

    We presented TaoMate-R1, a streaming multi-reference generator that groups denoising and context writing by scene establishment and continuation, with SGF coupling the roles through generated history. A local gradient analysis characterizes the directions retained by this grouping and by operation-based sharing. On the H3 backbone, TaoMate-R1 achieves higher mean CLIP and DINO temporal similarity across the three evaluated interaction settings at the same two-adapter budget. It also reduces discontinuities at instruction boundaries in long streams. The resulting comparison makes the specialization axis an explicit design variable in streaming multi-reference generation.

    （参考文献见原文。）
item.content:encoded:
一句话：先按指定人物与物体建场景，再在指令变化下持续生成——两个阶段的任务性质并不一样。

要点：

  • 任务定义：流式多参考视频生成先用指定的人与物建立场景，然后在**指令不断变化**的情况下继续生成
  • TaoMate-R1 的做法是按时间角色分工：在**冻结的主干**上，为「场景建立」与「场景延续」各挂一组独立的低秩适配器
  • 每个适配器既负责自己角色的去噪，也负责上下文写入，并通过 Self Gradient Forcing 联合训练这两个角色

为什么值得看：「开局建立身份、之后保持身份」是实时生成内容最难的部分：同一个人在镜头转开后还能不能是同一个人。按角色拆适配器而不是整模型微调，是低成本的工程解法。

中文摘要：流式多参考视频生成的任务形态是：先用指定的人物与物体建立一个场景，然后在指令持续变化的情况下把它延续下去。两个阶段的性质其实不同——前者要「建对身份」，后者要「长期保持身份」。TaoMate-R1 因此按时间角色做分工：在一个冻结的主干上，为场景建立与场景延续分别挂一组独立的低秩适配器；每个适配器既执行自己角色的去噪，也执行对应的上下文写入，再通过 Self Gradient Forcing 把两个角色联合训练起来。相比整模型微调，这种拆法更省，也更适合流式场景下的持续生成。

主题：AI Rendering

来源：arXiv·cs.CV（English）

原文发布：2026-11-11

本期推送：2026-11-13

TaoMate-R1: Temporal Role Specialization for Streaming Multi-Reference Video Generation

Abstract

Streaming multi-reference video generation establishes a scene from specified people and objects, then continues it under changing instructions. We introduce TaoMate-R1, a streaming multi-reference generator that organizes adaptation parameters through temporal role specialization. It assigns separate low-rank adapters to scene establishment and continuation on a frozen backbone. Each adapter performs both denoising and context writing for its role; Self Gradient Forcing jointly trains the roles through the history they construct. This allocation contrasts with operation-based specialization, which separates denoising from context writing across all chunks. A fixed-replay gradient analysis characterizes the update directions admitted by the two sharing schemes. On 32 multi-reference cases, we compare the schemes at the same two-adapter budget. Across ten approximately two-minute streams with changing instructions and shared teacher-audio conditioning, TaoMate-R1 reduces the mean boundary luminance jump from 1.96 to 0.613, with higher boundary feature similarity. It also achieves higher mean CLIP and DINO temporal similarity across short interactions, long streams, and public reference compositions. These results support grouping adaptation parameters by scene establishment and continuation for streaming multi-reference generation. Our code and model are released at https://github.com/TaoLiveAIGC/TaoMate-H3.

Qijun Gan*, Chenwei Zhang*, Xinyang Li, Meiguang Jin†, Junfeng Ma

Alibaba Group
{ganqijun.gqj, meiguang.jmg}@taobao.com

††footnotetext: *Equal contribution. †Corresponding author.

1  Introduction

Multi-reference video generation specifies the people and objects in a scene through images. Models such as Phantom, VACE, and MiniMax-H3 compose these visual conditions into video clips [1, 2, 3]. Streaming extends the task to an evolving scene: a presenter introduces a cup, puts it away, and picks up a bag as new instructions arrive. The desired behavior combines change with persistence. The current instruction determines the interaction, while the generated past determines its starting state.

The opening and subsequent chunks therefore solve different conditional tasks. At the opening, the generator chooses how reference appearances are realized through pose, placement, and initial motion. During continuation, those realized choices become part of the conditioning: a hand holding a cup constrains where the next action begins. This asymmetry motivates studying whether these tasks should receive independent adaptation.

Autoregressive diffusion and student-rollout training make generated history available during learning [4, 5]. Self Gradient Forcing (SGF) also lets later predictions supervise the computations that write this history [6]. SGF+ separates denoising and context-writing parameters to accommodate differences between their gradient contributions [7]. This is an operation-based partition: each operation shares parameters across the entire stream. We investigate a temporal-role partition at the same two-adapter budget, grouping generation and writing by whether they establish or continue a scene. The distinction concerns which computations learn together (Fig.1).

We introduce TaoMate-R1, which implements temporal role specialization with an opening adapter at absolute chunk zero and a continuation adapter for every later chunk. Within each role, denoising and context writing share the same low-rank parameters on a frozen backbone. Instruction changes update the continuation conditions while preserving its adapter and generated history. We train both roles with SGF: historical-context gradients return to the role that wrote the corresponding representation. The opening role thus learns both the first chunk and its persistent video anchor; the continuation role learns subsequent predictions and recent audiovisual context.

We characterize this design through a local analysis of parameter sharing. At a common initialization and fixed replay, the two partitions preserve the same common gradient component but admit different specialization directions. The analysis also isolates continuation-only windows, where the comparison depends on alignment between continuation’s generation and writing gradients. These relations describe the optimization consequences of tying parameters and provide a precise basis for comparing the two assignments.

Our experiments compare TaoMate-R1’s Temporal split with Shared and Operation split on the same H3 backbone. Across 32 cases, TaoMate-R1 achieves higher mean CLIP and DINO temporal similarity than Operation split on short interactions, long instruction-driven streams, and public reference compositions. The clearest difference occurs at instruction boundaries in ten approximately two-minute streams: TaoMate-R1 has a mean luminance jump of 0.613, compared with 1.96 for Operation split, and higher adjacent-frame feature similarity. We examine these differences with case-paired statistics and background-appearance visualizations, then place the generator’s results alongside external reference-conditioned systems. The contributions are:

  • \blacktriangleright

    TaoMate-R1, a streaming multi-reference generator that assigns independent adapters to scene establishment and continuation, shares denoising and context writing within each role, and trains them jointly through SGF.

  • \blacktriangleright

    A local gradient characterization of temporal and operation-based sharing, including the dependence on generation–writing alignment in continuation-only training windows.

  • \blacktriangleright

    A comparison across 32 multi-reference cases showing higher mean temporal similarity across three interaction settings and reduced instruction-boundary discontinuities on long streams.

    • 2  Related Work

    Multi-Reference Generation and Control.

    Reference images specify visual attributes and associate them with entities. ConsisID separates facial structure from identity detail [8]; Video Alchemist binds reference features to entity words [9]; and Movie Weaver combines prompt anchors with reference-order embeddings [10]. Phantom aligns visual and textual reference representations [1], VACE integrates image, video, and mask conditions [2], and MiniMax-H3 supports multi-reference audiovisual generation [3]. Spatiotemporal control specifies where and when these entities appear: DreamVideo-2 uses bounding-box trajectories [11], AlcheMinT uses interval-dependent rotary embeddings [12], and MultiShotMaster combines shot-aware encoding with reference grounding [13]. For interactive streams, FlowAct-R2 aligns evolving conditions with planned behavior [14], while ReferStream introduces arriving subjects through contextualized reference latents and cache injection [15]. These methods organize visual conditions; our study concerns the adaptation parameters used to realize them across an ongoing scene.

    Causal Generation and Generated-History Training.

    Diffusion Forcing uses token-wise noise levels for causal generation [16]; CausVid distills a bidirectional teacher into a few-step causal model [4]; and SkyReels-V2 extends videos with nondecreasing frame-wise noise schedules [17]. History retention supplies persistent appearance and recent motion: StreamingT2V combines initial-chunk cues with preceding-chunk features [18], FramePack compresses context according to historical importance [19], and LongLive combines a frame sink with local attention [20]. LongLive-RAG retrieves earlier latents [21], while FilmWeaver separates cross-shot keyframes from recent within-shot memory [22]. Training with generated predecessors addresses the context distribution encountered at inference, from Scheduled Sampling [23] to Self Forcing’s student rollouts [5] and Rolling Forcing’s jointly denoised windows [24]. SGF additionally propagates supervision through historical context writers [6]. We adopt this training framework and study parameter sharing under a fixed history-retention policy.

    Parameter Specialization.

    Specialization allocates independent parameters to computations with different learning demands. DreamVideo composes identity and motion adapters [25], while eDiff-I and Wan2.2 specialize denoisers by diffusion-noise interval [26, 27]. SGF+ separates denoising and context-writing parameters to address gradient differences between these operations [7]. TaoMate-R1 groups the same operations by temporal role, using independent low-rank adapters [28] for scene establishment and continuation. Our comparison with operation-based sharing holds the two-adapter budget fixed and examines the resulting generation and continuity measurements.

    3  TaoMate-R1

    TaoMate-R1 is a streaming multi-reference generator built on temporal role specialization: it groups generation and context writing by their role in the stream (Fig.2).

    3.1 Preliminaries

    Generation and Context Writing.

    A streaming diffusion model alternates between generating a chunk and encoding it as history. For external conditions q_b and retained keys and values H_

    h_b=W_θ(ẑ_b,q_b,H_

    The retained part of h_b conditions subsequent predictions.

    Generated-History Supervision.

    SGF trains historical representations on student-generated rollouts [6]. Recorded historical latent inputs remain fixed during differentiation, while later losses propagate through their KV-writing computations. Generation and writing therefore contribute separate paths to the same objective. Sharing their parameters sums these contributions into one update; independent parameters allocate them to separate updates. Our method specifies this sharing relation for the opening and continuation of a stream.

    3.2 Problem Formulation

    Let ℝ_b denote the reference images active at chunk b, c_b its instruction, and z_b=(z_bᵛ,z_bᵃ) its audiovisual latents. These specify q_b=(ℝ_b,c_b) in Eq.1. The retained history H_
