    =p_θ_first(z₀|ℝ₀,c₀)∏_b=1^B-1p_θ_cont(z_b|ℝ_b,c_b,H_

    Establishment occurs once, at absolute chunk b=0. Changes in instructions or active references become conditions for continuation within the existing scene.

    The references and generated history provide different kinds of information. Reference images identify entities and their appearances; history records how those entities have been realized together in the current scene. At the opening, the model establishes their spatial arrangement, poses, and interaction state from the supplied conditions. Continuation inherits this realization and predicts its evolution under the current instruction. For example, presenting a new object changes the active references while the presenter and room remain part of the ongoing scene. The temporal role thus follows the stream’s established state: changing an instruction updates the interaction goal while retaining the history from which the next action begins.

    The long-stream evaluation additionally supplies cached audio states and removal-segment end-frame conditions.

    3.3 Temporal Role Specialization

    The opening and continuation adapters use independent LoRA updates [28] on a shared frozen backbone:

    r(b)=\begincasesfirst,&b=0, cont,&b>0,\endcases θ_b=θ_base+Δθ_r(b).

    		(3)

    Both inherit the LoRA weights of the same trained autoregressive generator and are optimized jointly. Their weights, AdamW moments, and exponential moving averages are copied into independent states. For each adapted layer, Θᵣ=Θ₀+BᵣAᵣ, with fixed LoRA scaling absorbed into the factors. Both adapters use rank and scaling 128 on the attention QKV/output and feed-forward projections, covering 208 linear layers.

    The selected θ_b governs both G and W in Eq.1. Thus, a temporal role adapts its synthesis mapping together with the context representation it leaves for future predictions.

    This grouping specifies which learning signals shape the same adaptation. For establishment, generation realizes the references in an initial scene and writing represents that scene for subsequent predictions. For continuation, generation evolves the interaction and writing updates the context available to the next chunk. Within-role sharing combines these contributions according to their conditional task. Operation-based specialization instead combines opening and continuation signals within each operation. The same generation and writing calls are therefore grouped along different axes: temporal role in TaoMate-R1 and computational operation in SGF+.

    At inference, the history retains the opening video KVs as a persistent appearance anchor and the latest two audiovisual chunks’ KVs as recent interaction context. For b>0,

    H_

    		(4)

    Overlapping entries are counted once; opening audio remains only in the recent window. Reference conditions remain available independently of this history, and temporal positions remain absolute. Thus, the opening role writes the persistent anchor, while continuation supplies the rolling interaction context. All three parameter-sharing configurations use this retention policy.

    3.4 Joint Training with Context Gradients

    Student Rollouts and Distribution Matching.

    We train TaoMate-R1’s two roles using student rollouts [5] and SGF’s context gradients [6]. Let I={s,…,e} denote a sampled training window, with its preceding prefix held fixed as conditioning. We request five or ten chunks with probabilities 0.8 and 0.2, truncated by source length. The prefix is encoded from cached clean teacher latents; references and text remain fixed within an example. Nominal opening and continuation chunks contain 39 and 34 frames at 24 fps. A gradient-free rollout uses one initial-to-clean evaluation per chunk and records the prediction noise, generated latents, context, and actual writer input z̃_b, including the training context perturbation. Both computations use the adapter selected by the absolute chunk index.

    Distribution-matching distillation [29] supervises the generated audiovisual content. A frozen real-score model and a learned fake-score model evaluate the same corrupted student sequence, producing a detached direction d_b. Let ẑ_b,realᵐ and ẑ_b,fakeᵐ be their clean estimates for modality m. We use the normalized direction

    d_bᵐ=sg [(ẑ_b,fakeᵐ-ẑ_b,realᵐ)/(\max (mean|ẑ_bᵐ-ẑ_b,realᵐ|,ε))].

    		(5)

    We set ε=10⁻⁸. For a prediction ẑ_b replayed with its recorded inputs, we optimize

    L_b=1/2∑_m∈{v,a}λₘ∥ẑ_bᵐ-sg(ẑ_bᵐ-d_bᵐ)∥ₘₑₐₙ².

    		(6)

    Here sg stops gradients, λᵥ=1, λₐ=0.1, and the squared norm averages over that modality’s latent elements. The window objective is L=|I|⁻¹∑_b∈IL_b. Both roles share a single fake-score model, trained on detached student outputs. The fake score receives velocity-regression updates every iteration; generator updates occur every fifth iteration.

    Historical Credit Assignment.

    Replay losses accumulate context gradients on shared historical KV variables. We realize SGF’s context-gradient reconstruction by differentiating each historical writer once in reverse temporal order, with its recorded latent input held fixed. The accumulated gradient returns to the adapter selected by that writer’s absolute chunk index and propagates through its preceding KVs. This assigns both synthesis and historical credit to the appropriate temporal role:

    ∇_ΔθᵣL=∑_b∈Iᵣg_bᵍᵉⁿ+∑_j∈Jᵣ((∂hⱼ)/(∂Δθᵣ))^⊤h̄ⱼ.

    		(7)

    Here Iᵣ and Jᵣ index role r’s supervised predictions and differentiable historical writers within the effective window. The direct gradient g_bᵍᵉⁿ is taken through the current denoiser from L_b/|I|. The writer Jacobian holds its recorded latent input and incoming KVs fixed; h̄ⱼ includes all downstream prediction and writer paths under the window-averaged objective.

    A historical representation influences the objective through direct reads by later denoisers and through context written by intervening chunks. The reverse pass accumulates these routes before differentiating the corresponding writer. For a recorded writer input, the context computation and its contribution to an earlier representation are

    hⱼ=W_θⱼ(sg(z̃ⱼ),qⱼ,H_(8)
    h̄ᵢ\mathrel+=((∂hⱼ)/(∂hᵢ))^⊤h̄ⱼ, s≤i(9)

    The same accumulated signal supplies the writer term in Eq.7. Its parameter update belongs to the role that produced the representation, connecting independently adapted opening and continuation computations through their shared generated history.

    When the effective window includes the opening, continuation losses supervise its context representation through Δθ_first. For s>0, the opening is fixed conditioning and receives no update. Algorithm 1 summarizes the rollout and reverse context-gradient pass.

    Optimization and Inference.

    We use AdamW with generator/fake-score learning rates 5×10⁻⁵/10⁻⁵, β=(0,0.999), weight decay 0.01, gradient clipping at 1, global batch 16, and seed 42. Training perturbs noninitial writer inputs up to noise level 0.15; writing still uses clean time, and replay retains the sampled perturbation. Inference uses unperturbed context and three Euler evaluations per chunk. With u_b,0=ε_b and velocity prediction v_θ_bᵐ, each evaluation updates

    u_b,k+1ᵐ=u_b,kᵐ+(σₖᵐ-σₖ₊₁ᵐ)(10)
    ·v_θ_bᵐ(u_b,k,q_b,H_

    For uᵢ=1-i/49, the noise schedule is σᵢᵐ=γₘuᵢ/[1+(γₘ-1)uᵢ], with γᵥ=12, γₐ=3 and retained indices (0,16,33,49). The selected role remains active throughout denoising and clean-context writing.

    3.5 Local Gradient Analysis of Parameter Sharing

    To compare the partitions in Figure 1(b), introduce four virtual adapter copies, one per temporal-role–operation pair: x=(θ_firstG,θ_firstW,θ_contG,θ_contW). Temporal role specialization ties generation and writing within each temporal role; SGF+’s operation split ties opening and continuation within each operation [7].

    Consider a fixed replay at the common adapter initialization, holding the sampled rollout, historical latent inputs, prediction noise, and distribution-matching targets fixed. Let g_rG and g_rW denote the gradient contributions through generation and writing for temporal role r. The contrasts retained by the two assignments are

    v_T=(g_firstG+g_firstW)-(g_contG+g_contW),(11)
    v_O=(g_firstG+g_contG)-(g_firstW+g_contW).

    For a fixed norm ρ of the four-block parameter update, let D_T and D_O be the largest first-order loss decreases admitted by temporal and operation sharing. Orthogonal projection gives

    D_T²-D_O²=ρ²/4(∥v_T∥²-∥v_O∥²).

    		(12)

    Both assignments retain the common gradient while preserving a different specialization direction. Temporal role specialization admits the larger local decrease when the establishment–continuation contrast exceeds the denoising–writing contrast in norm. For a window starting after chunk zero, the opening belongs to the fixed prefix, so g_firstG=g_firstW=0 and

    D_T²-D_O²=ρ²⟨g_contG,g_contW⟩.

    		(13)

    In this case, aligned generation and writing gradients favor sharing within continuation; opposing gradients favor operation separation. The relations characterize a fixed replay’s local update geometry; our experiments compare the resulting trained generators.

    4  Experiments

    We evaluate TaoMate-R1 through parameter-sharing comparisons on a common streaming backbone, followed by system-level generation results.

    4.1 Experimental Setup

    Cases and Parameter-Sharing Configurations.

    We evaluate 32 cases: ten short person–object interactions, ten approximately two-minute streams with twenty successive instructions each, and twelve public reference compositions from MultiRef-Compass [30]. Short and public clips are approximately ten seconds long. On the H3 backbone, Shared uses one rank-128 adapter for generation and writing across all chunks. Operation split uses two rank-128 adapters, separating generation from writing following SGF+. TaoMate-R1 implements Temporal split with two rank-128 adapters, separating opening from continuation. The two splits have the same adapter budget; their grouping of computations is the variable of interest. All three configurations use the same training cohort, reference inputs, instructions, history-retention policy, and three-evaluation Euler solver. Short and public cases generate native audio; long cases follow cached teacher-audio trajectories and use end-frame conditions for object-removal segments. The training cohort contains 2,196 examples of 4–15 seconds, covering 1,969 object-preserving, 119 object-removal, and 108 object-introduction interactions. Training excludes first- and last-frame image conditions. For long evaluation streams, each product presentation is followed by removal, with the person-and-scene reference supplied as the removal segment’s end-frame condition.

    Metrics and Aggregation.

    CLIP and DINOv2 measure whole-frame reference similarity and temporal similarity between successive 1 Hz samples [31, 32]. Full-prompt CLIP and ViCLIP assess text alignment; VABench measures realism and five-question case-level visual QA [33]. At instruction changes, CLIP and DINO compare adjacent boundary frames; Luma is the absolute difference in their mean grayscale intensity (0–255). Scores use equal case weights; paired bootstrapping resamples cases while retaining each complete stream and its matched model outputs. We draw 100,000 paired resamples and report unadjusted percentile 95% intervals.

    4.2 Effect of the Specialization Axis

    The same-backbone block of Table1 compares all three assignments. TaoMate-R1 achieves an aggregate DINO temporal similarity of 0.934, compared with 0.928 for Operation split and 0.914 for Shared.

    Table2 separates short interactions, long changing-instruction streams, and public reference compositions. TaoMate-R1 obtains the highest mean CLIP and DINO temporal similarity in all three groups. On short interactions, it also leads in DINO reference similarity, reaching 0.545 versus 0.531 for Operation split. Its CLIP and DINO temporal similarities are 0.970 and 0.975, compared with 0.969 and 0.972 for Operation split, while Operation split has higher visual QA (0.900 versus 0.880).

    On long streams, TaoMate-R1 reaches CLIP and DINO temporal similarities of 0.956 and 0.921, compared with 0.948 and 0.914 for Operation split. The paired difference in DINO temporal similarity (TaoMate-R1 minus Operation split) is +0.00730 (95% interval [-0.00958,0.0227]). Operation split has higher DINO reference similarity (0.486 versus 0.478). Its QA of 1.00 and TaoMate-R1’s 0.980 correspond to 50 and 49 correct answers across five questions per case. On public reference compositions, TaoMate-R1 leads all four reported metrics, with DINO reference similarity of 0.207, CLIP and DINO temporal similarities of 0.948 and 0.911, and visual QA of 0.983.

    Interaction Settings and Shared Adaptation.

    Both two-adapter configurations improve DINO temporal similarity over Shared in every evaluated group. At the same adapter budget, TaoMate-R1 further increases the temporal means across all three settings, supporting the assignment of adaptation capacity by opening and continuation. The aggregate score combines twenty-two short or public cases with ten long streams under equal case weighting; the subgroup results show higher temporal means for TaoMate-R1 within each group. Reference similarity and visual QA vary by setting, indicating that higher temporal similarity does not imply uniformly better reference matching or visual QA.

    Figure3 examines background appearance in fixed foliage and vase crops over a 119-second stream. Views at 0, 60, and 119 seconds show the evolution of leaf and ceramic tones. The overlays average per-pixel CIE Lab distances from each video’s initial frame over the full stream at 1 Hz. TaoMate-R1 shows smaller appearance changes than Operation split in these regions, complementing the whole-frame temporal measurements.

    Interaction Dynamics.

    Figure4 compares the three sharing schemes at matched timestamps within two changing-instruction streams. In the bag sequence, all three configurations present the referenced item at 72 and 74 s. At 76 s, TaoMate-R1 moves it toward the instructed screen-right side, Shared moves it screen-left, and Operation split still holds it centrally. In the second sequence, Shared and TaoMate-R1 proceed from the notebook to the folded umbrella; Operation split remains empty-handed at 106 and 108 s. The TaoMate-R1 frames show evolving hand poses and object states within the retained scene. Together with the background views, these sequences make both components of streaming interaction visible: carrying out a new action and preserving the scene in which it unfolds.

    4.3 Continuity across Instruction Changes

    Table3 compares adjacent frames at the same instruction boundaries in the ten long streams. TaoMate-R1 obtains CLIP and DINO boundary similarities of 0.991 and 0.990, compared with 0.979 and 0.973 for Operation split. Its mean luminance jump is 0.613 versus 1.96, a reduction of 1.35 gray levels, or 68.7%. Shared obtains boundary similarities of 0.979 and 0.978 and a mean luminance jump of 1.86.

    The case-paired analysis gives a difference (TaoMate-R1 minus Operation split) of +0.0177 in DINO boundary similarity (95% interval [0.00820,0.0288]) and -1.35 in luminance jump ([-1.58,-1.12]). Luminance jumps decrease in all ten streams, and CLIP and DINO boundary similarities each increase in nine streams. These transition-level gains are more consistent across cases than the sequence-level DINO temporal difference.

    Continuity under Changing Conditions.

    An instruction change introduces a new interaction goal while the preceding scene remains the starting state for continuation. Boundary measurements evaluate the immediate transition from the last frame under one instruction to the first under the next. Sequence-level temporal scores also include the intervening within-instruction evolution. Together, they show higher temporal-similarity means over the full streams, with the clearest paired evidence at instruction changes. The background views in Fig.3 extend this analysis to retained scene appearance over the complete stream. These observations support temporal specialization for maintaining scene continuity as interaction goals change.

    4.4 Generation Quality

    Reference-Conditioned Systems.

    The external-system block of Table1 compares MiniMax-H3 [3], VACE [2], SkyReels-V3 [34], and Phantom [1]. For the long cases, these systems generate each instruction segment independently and concatenate the resulting clips; our autoregressive variants retain history across instruction changes. TaoMate-R1 leads in mean DINO reference similarity, both temporal similarity metrics, realism, and visual QA. VACE leads in CLIP reference and full-prompt CLIP scores, and MiniMax-H3 in ViCLIP.

    Qualitative Comparisons.

    Figure5 shows four reference-conditioned interactions. In the gallery scene, MiniMax-H3 and TaoMate-R1 depict both cartoon characters interacting with a guitar. VACE renders live-action participants, while SkyReels-V3 and Phantom depict Santa as a small held figure. In the scarf scene, our output includes an additional guitar. The continuous-interaction rows show cosmetics-bag and closed-umbrella presentation within the established scene. At 72 s, our stream depicts the sage-green bag alongside the presenter in the established room.

    Long-Stream System Comparison.

    Table4 compares continuous generation with independently generated instruction clips on the ten long cases. TaoMate-R1 achieves DINO temporal similarity of 0.921, compared with 0.812–0.848 for the clip-generation systems. At segment boundaries, DINO similarity is 0.990 versus 0.589–0.831, and the mean luminance jump is 0.613 versus 9.12–14.3. These results compare the complete generation protocols; the same-backbone comparisons above isolate the choice of adaptation assignment.

    Figure6 arranges frame columns sampled every 0.5 s along a timeline. Independent clip joins produce bands in head height, body scale, and background appearance, while the continuous stream maintains more stable presenter and table geometry.

    The time-column representation relates these bands to changes in scene composition. A change in camera framing or subject scale shifts several horizontal structures together, producing a discontinuity across the sampled timeline. In the continuous stream, the table edge and background patterns trace more continuous paths through successive instructions. This connects the boundary scores in Table4 to visible scene properties such as presenter scale and background placement. Together, the visual comparisons examine reference-conditioned interactions in Fig.5, localized background appearance in Fig.3, and scene-level continuity in Fig.6.

    Audiovisual Measurements.

    On the 22 native-audio cases, TaoMate-R1 has higher mean AV alignment than Operation split (4.77 versus 4.59). Operation split has higher audio QA (0.809 versus 0.736) and lower Desync (0.282 versus 0.445), showing a different ordering for audio content and synchronization.

    5  Conclusion

    We presented TaoMate-R1, a streaming multi-reference generator that groups denoising and context writing by scene establishment and continuation, with SGF coupling the roles through generated history. A local gradient analysis characterizes the directions retained by this grouping and by operation-based sharing. On the H3 backbone, TaoMate-R1 achieves higher mean CLIP and DINO temporal similarity across the three evaluated interaction settings at the same two-adapter budget. It also reduces discontinuities at instruction boundaries in long streams. The resulting comparison makes the specialization axis an explicit design variable in streaming multi-reference generation.

    （参考文献见原文。）

item.title: 4D 场景理解被切成两派：UGG 把 RGB 视频与深度/相机位姿放进同一个生成框架 ｜ UGG: Unified Generative Geometry Model
item.description:
一句话：前馈模型只做几何预测、生成模型只做画面合成；两派各缺一半。

要点：

  • 问题定位：理解 4D 场景要求模型从部分观测里同时抓住**几何、外观与动态**
  • 现状分裂：一派是直接预测几何的前馈模型，另一派是做视觉合成的生成模型——各自只覆盖一半
  • UGG 提出统一框架，联合建模 RGB 视频与深度、相机位姿等几何表示

为什么值得看：几何与外观分开做，就会在「几何对了但画不出来」「画得像但空间是错的」之间来回。统一到一个生成框架里，才有可能同时服务于重建与渲染两侧的需求。

中文摘要：理解 4D 场景是视觉智能的核心挑战，要求模型能从部分观测中同时捕获场景的几何、外观与动态。现有方法分成两派：一派是直接预测几何的前馈模型，另一派是做视觉合成的生成模型，各自只覆盖其中一面。UGG 因此提出统一框架，把 RGB 视频与深度、相机位姿等几何表示放在一起联合建模，试图让「几何正确」与「画得出来」在同一模型内同时成立。对需要同时拿到可用几何与可用画面的引擎侧应用，这个方向比单点突破更贴近需求。

主题：AI Rendering

来源：arXiv·cs.CV（English）

原文发布：2026-11-11

本期推送：2026-11-13

UGG: Unified Generative Geometry Model

Abstract

Understanding 4D scenes is a core challenge in visual intelligence, requiring models to jointly capture scene geometry, appearance, and dynamics from partial observations. However, existing approaches are subdivided into feedforward models for direct geometric prediction, and generative models for visual synthesis. We introduce UGG, a unified framework for 4D scene understanding that jointly models RGB video and geometric representations such as depth and camera pose. By assigning different noise levels across modalities and time, UGG formulates visual generation and geometric prediction as conditional completion within a single generative model. This flexible formulation enables the model to learn from diverse, heterogeneous datasets with different subsets of geometric and visual annotations. Furthermore, our generative formulation enables inference-time search over multiple plausible scene hypotheses, using geometric evidence extracted from observed RGB frames to improve geometric prediction without ground truth geometry. We demonstrate UGG’s effectiveness over non-unified baselines across camera-controlled video generation, depth estimation, and camera pose prediction, including in challenging sparse observation settings. Code and visualizations are available at ugg-model.github.io.

1 Introduction

For embodied agents to perceive and act intelligently in the physical world, they must understand its 3D structure and predict how it will evolve over time [(11, 62, 4)]. However, visual observations provide only partial 2D projections of the world, each capturing a limited set of viewpoints, visible surfaces, and changes over time. Robust 4D scene understanding therefore requires inferring what is not directly observed, namely the 3D geometry, camera viewpoint, scene appearance from unseen views, and scene evolution.

Current methods have made strong progress on different parts of this problem, but they are often separated into geometric prediction and visual generation. Feedforward models can directly estimate scene geometry, including depth, camera pose, and 3D structure, from images or videos. These methods are efficient and often accurate under the training distribution, but they typically produce a single deterministic estimate and can struggle when the observations are sparse or out of distribution. Generative models, in contrast, learn strong visual priors for completing missing observations, synthesizing novel views, and predicting plausible dynamic futures. However, they often lack explicit geometric grounding, which can lead to outputs that are visually plausible but inconsistent in 3D. Recent work has begun to narrow this gap by repurposing generative video models for geometric prediction [(21, 34, 77)], or by injecting geometric representations into generative models to improve 3D consistency [(38, 58, 20)]. Nevertheless, generation and prediction are still commonly treated as separate capabilities, rather than as two forms of inference in the same underlying scene model.

In this work, we introduce UGG, a unified generative geometry model that treats visual generation and geometric prediction as different conditional queries of the same underlying 4D scene representation. The appearance (RGB video), 3D structure (depth), and viewpoint (camera geometry) all provide complementary observations of a dynamic scene. Depending on what is observed, a joint model can infer missing scene components from the observed ones.

We instantiate this formulation by representing RGB, depth, and camera geometry as spatially aligned modalities, with camera pose encoded as dense ray maps. A multimodal transformer jointly processes these representation through shared self-attention and modality-specific layers. Modality flexibility is achieved through an extension of Diffusion Forcing [(10)]: different tasks are specified through noise patterns over both modality and time, where observed components serve as conditioning context and missing components are denoised. This conditional completion mechanism enables the same model to condition on a text prompt, a single RGB frame, an RGB sequence, camera poses, depth maps, or any combination of these, and complete the remaining modalities. Moreover, the model can learn from heterogeneous datasets by applying the loss only on available modalities, instead of requiring every example to contain complete annotations of pose and depth.

Our generative formulation also enables inference-time search over multiple plausible scene completions. Instead of committing to a single geometric prediction, we sample multiple candidates and select the one with the strongest cross-modal consistency, measured through photometric reprojection. This inference-time search capability is also consistent with the cognitive theory of perception as inference: human scene understanding requires inferring latent scene causes from incomplete observations, and may rely on internal simulation to evaluate possible scene explanations [(24, 66, 3, 35)].

Overall, our contributions are threefold: i) We formulate 4D scene understanding as joint generative modeling over appearance and geometry, treating visual generation and geometric prediction as missing-modality denoising within a single conditional model. ii) We introduce a unified generative-predictive model that represents RGB, depth, and camera pose as spatially aligned modalities, enabling arbitrary conditioning and learning from heterogeneous datasets with incomplete supervision. iii) Finally, we leverage the generative formulation for inference-time search over multiple 4D scene hypotheses, using geometric consistency to improve geometric prediction.

2 Related Work

Generative Modeling for 4D Scene Understanding.

Geometric prediction is largely dominated by feedforward discriminative models that regress depth, camera pose, and scene flow, or 3D structure from visual observations [53, 25, 68, 51, 40, 60, 55, 23]. While these methods achieve strong performance, they typically produce deterministic, single-pass estimates that struggle with inherent visual ambiguities, including sparse-view observations. To address these limitations, recent work has explored generative priors for pose estimation [9, 67], depth prediction [22, 17, 39], and dynamic 4D reconstruction [21, 77]. Generative models have also been used for novel view synthesis [65, 64]. However, these methods typically treat geometric prediction as a unidirectional mapping from RGB to specific geometric outputs and rely on strictly paired datasets.

Geometry-aware Video and 4D generation.

Recent generative world models have advanced from purely visual synthesis [6, 49, 2, 11] toward geometry-aware generation. One line of work injects 3D scene structure or persistent spatial memory into video generation to improve spatial consistency [38, 69, 20, 59, 73, 28, 61]. Another line studies camera-conditioned generation, using camera trajectories to control synthesized videos [16, 72, 57]. More closely related, One4D [34] and WorldReel [14] jointly generate RGB frames and 4D geometric representations from text or RGB prompts. However, these methods typically follow fixed conditioning and output pathways. In contrast, we treat RGB, depth, and camera rays as symmetric modalities, enabling an any-to-any conditional completion framework for both generation and prediction.

Unified Conditional Modeling.

Our work is related to flexible conditional generation, where diverse tasks are cast as missing-modality completion. Mixture-of-Transformers (MoT) architectures [27], such as Motus [4] and DreamZero [62], show that a single model can process heterogeneous modalities. For flexible conditioning, we build on Diffusion Forcing [10] and DFoT [43], which assign different noise levels to different tokens or frames. Recent works extend this paradigm for long-horizon video generation or embodied planning [12, 52]; in contrast, we apply it to multimodal 4D scene understanding, treating RGB, depth, and camera geometry as symmetric components. This probabilistic formulation also enables inference-time search. Motivated by test-time scaling [71, 31], we use additional inference compute to compare multiple candidate scene completions. We then select the candidate with stronger photometric reprojection consistency to improve geometric prediction.

3 Method

We propose a unified generative-predictive framework for 4D scene understanding. Given partial observations of a scene, our goal is to infer a complete scene representation containing appearance, depth, and camera geometry. We formulate both visual generation and geometric prediction as conditional completion in a joint generative model over spatially aligned RGB, depth, and camera-ray modalities. We specify each task by a noise pattern over multimodal tokens, with observed tokens as zero-noise context and missing tokens as noisy targets. The framework supports heterogeneous training data with incomplete modality supervision, arbitrary partial conditioning, and test-time search over multiple 4D scene hypotheses.

3.1 Unified 4D Scene Representation

We represent a 4D scene as a multimodal sequence of N frames. Each frame i contains an RGB image Iᵢ, the depth map Dᵢ, camera parameters Cᵢ=(Kᵢ,Tᵢ), where Kᵢ denotes the camera intrinsics and Tᵢ denotes the camera extrinsics. Only a subset of this information may be observed. An example may contain one or more RGB frames, optionally with depth or camera parameters, or only a text prompt. Our model is designed to infer missing scene components from arbitrary partial observations.

To spatially align camera geometry with RGB and depth, we represent camera parameters Cᵢ as a dense map of 6D Plücker rays, following prior ray-based scene and camera representations [(42, 67)]. This representation turns camera geometry into an image-like modality. Each pixel (u,v) is associated with a ray moment mᵢ(u,v) in a common world coordinate system, constructed from the viewing direction dᵢ(u,v) and the camera center oᵢ.

Rᵢ(u,v)=(dᵢ(u,v),mᵢ(u,v)), mᵢ(u,v)=oᵢ×dᵢ(u,v).

(1)

The resulting scene representation S contains the appearance and local 3D geometry for each frame i:

S={(Iᵢ,Dᵢ,Rᵢ)}ᵢ₌₁^N.

3.2 Generative-Predictive Transformer

Given the spatially aligned representation S, we design a multimodal diffusion transformer that jointly processes appearance, depth, and camera-ray geometry (Fig. 2).

Aligned Modality Tokenization.

RGB frames and depth maps are encoded into latent tokens using a VAE encoder, producing z^I and z^D. Before encoding, we normalize depth and camera rays using a shared scale factor, making reprojection and cross-frame geometric consistency well-defined. Ray maps are downsampled to the latent spatial resolution and projected directly into ray map tokens, producing z^R_d for ray-direction tokens and z^Rₘ for ray-moment tokens. This yields the complete multimodal token sequence,

z=[z^I;z^D;z^R_d;z^Rₘ].

Each token is processed with modality-specific patch embedding layers and a spatiotemporal RoPE positional encoding over latent spatial coordinates and the frame index [(45)]. If the VAE encoder performs temporal downsampling, then the number of latents and frames could differ; we omit this from our notation for simplicity and continue to refer to the number of frames or latents as N.

At the output stage, RGB and depth tokens are decoded back to pixel space using the VAE decoder. Ray map tokens are directly mapped back to dense ray maps, which can be converted back to camera parameters Cᵢ including rotation, translation, and intrinsics.

Diffusion Mixture-of-Transformers.

The backbone uses a mixture-of-transformers [27] design. Each modality has its own input projections, allowing for modality-specific representation structure. After modality-specific projection, all modalities are concatenated and processed by shared self-attention, enabling cross-modal information exchange. Modalities are separated to modality-specific feed-forward layers and output heads. Optional text prompts are injected through cross-attention.

Each token has its own diffusion timestep. These timesteps are embedded and injected into transformer blocks through adaptive layer normalization modulation [(37)], allowing the model to process clean context tokens and noisy target tokens at different noise levels.

3.3 Conditional Completion with Noise as Masking

We formulate generation and geometric prediction as conditional denoising over a shared multimodal representation. Let M={I,D,R_d,Rₘ} denote the set of modalities, and let z_i,0ᵐ denote the clean latent token at temporal position i for modality m. Which modalities are revealed or corrupted specify different tasks without changing the architecture. For example, RGB-conditioned geometric prediction reveals RGB tokens while treating depth and camera-ray tokens as prediction targets.

Task Specification by Noise Pattern.

Diffusion forcing enables flexible conditional generation by assigning independently sampled noise levels across temporal positions [(10)]. We extend this formulation to multimodal sequences, allowing noise levels tᵢᵐ∈[0,1] to vary across both modalities (m) and temporal positions (i). We construct the noisy input z̃_i,tᵐ through linear interpolation of the clean token z_i,0ᵐ and Gaussian noise:

z̃_i,tᵐ=(1-tᵢᵐ)z_i,0ᵐ+tᵢᵐεᵢᵐ, εᵢᵐ∼ℕ(0,I).

(2)

At tᵢᵐ=0, the token is fully clean, while at tᵢᵐ=1, it is pure noise. By varying the noise levels across both modality and temporal position, we realize different conditional generation and prediction tasks without modifying the model architecture.

Training with Heterogeneous Data.

During training, we sample conditioning patterns that designate subsets of modality tokens as context, and others as prediction targets. Context tokens share a single noise level, while target tokens share a separately sampled noise level. With probability p_clean, context noise levels are set to tᵢᵐ=0 to allow for fully clean context conditioning.

The model is trained using conditional Flow Matching [(30)], with target velocity vᵢᵐ=∂z̃_i,tᵐ/∂tᵢᵐ=εᵢᵐ-z_i,0ᵐ. Given the corrupted multimodal tokens z̃, noise levels t, and optional text conditioning c, the model predicts v̂=f_θ(z̃ₜ,t,c), with the loss:

L_FM=𝔼_z,t,ε[∑_i, m∈Maᵢᵐλᵐ∥v̂ᵢᵐ-vᵢᵐ∥₂²].

(3)

λᵐ is a weight that balances the losses for each modality. Modality availability is denoted as aᵢᵐ∈{0,1}. The availability mask allows a single model to be trained using heterogeneous mixes of RGB-only, RGB-camera, RGB-depth, and RGB-depth-camera data.

Guided Inference Using Available Modalities.

At inference time, the same noise pattern is used, but conditioning is stricter. Observed tokens are clamped to their clean values at every denoising step and assigned tᵢᵐ=0, while unknown tokens are initialized from Gaussian noise and progressively denoised. For example, in a first-last-frame camera-controlled setting, the first and last RGB tokens and all camera ray tokens are clamped as context, while intermediate RGB and depth tokens are generated. We also use History Guidance [43] to strengthen consistency with the observed context.

3.4 Inference-time Search

The generative formulation also enables inference-time search, in contrast with a deterministic predictor that commits to one scene. Given the same observed context, we sample L candidate completions from different random initializations. Each sample yields a complete 4D scene hypothesis:

Ŝ^(ℓ)={(Î^(ℓ)ᵢ,D̂^(ℓ)ᵢ,R̂^(ℓ)ᵢ)}ᵢ₌₁^N, ℓ=1,…,L.

To select among these hypotheses without ground-truth depth or camera pose, we evaluate how well each hypothesis explains geometric evidence extracted from the observed RGB frames. Full equations and hyperparameters are given in App. B.8.

Geometric Evidence Derived from RGB.

We extract pixel correspondences between observed RGB frames using RAFT [(47)]. To remove issues with occlusions and moving objects, we keep correspondences only if forward mapping followed by backward mapping returns a pixel to its original point. For dense observations, we select frame pairs with informative pixel motion, adapting the temporal separation according to the observed optical flow magnitude. For sparse observations, both generation and verification use only the first and last observed RGB frames. These correspondences provide geometric constraints against which candidate depth and camera predictions can be evaluated.

Depth Evaluation.

We evaluate whether a candidate’s predicted depth is consistent with the observed pixel motion. For each frame pair, we first estimate the relative camera pose from image correspondences using essential matrix estimation with RANSAC, shared across depth candidates. Each candidate’s inverse depth is aligned to the observed parallax by fitting an affine transformation. The aligned depth is used to reproject pixels between views, which measures agreement with the observed correspondences. For sparse observations, evaluation uses correspondence residuals after epipolar filtering. For dense observations, we additionally incorporate photometric and DINOv2 feature consistency [(36)].

Pose Evaluation.

For camera pose prediction, we compare each candidate’s relative translation direction against the direction estimated from image correspondences using the candidate’s predicted intrinsics. We compute the angular discrepancy over selected frame pairs, measuring whether the predicted camera motion agrees with the observed images.

Final Candidate Selection.

Depth and pose are selected independently: there is no trade-off between the two scores, and the depth and pose results may come from different candidates. For depth prediction, we standardize and combine the verification residuals, rank candidates within each frame pair, and then aggregate these rankings across pairs. For pose prediction, we use the mean angular discrepancy between predicted and image-estimated relative translation directions. Finally, the model selects the candidate ℓ^* with the lowest task-specific verification score.

4 Experiments

We evaluate UGG on a suite of 4D scene understanding tasks, including camera-controlled generation (Sec. 4.2) and geometric prediction. Geometric prediction tasks under both dense and sparse observation settings include camera pose estimation (Sec. 4.3) and video depth estimation (Sec. 4.4). Our single unified model handles all tasks by changing only the clean/noisy masking pattern, without requiring task-specific architectures. We further show that UGG’s generative formulation enables inference-time search, improving predicted scene consistency with additional samples (Sec. 4.5). Full code and additional visualizations are provided on the project page.

4.1 Model Training

We train on a weighted mixture of real and synthetic video datasets, including DL3DV-10K [29], RealEstate10K [74], TartanAir [54], BEDLAM [5], Aria Synthetic Environments [1], OmniWorld-Game [75], Virtual-KITTI2 [8], and Mid-Air [15]. These datasets provide heterogeneous supervision over RGB video, depth, camera pose, and text; missing modalities are omitted from the loss. UGG is trained with multiple clean/noisy mask patterns over modality tokens to cover generation and geometric prediction tasks. UGG weights are initialized from Wan2.2-TI2V-5B, then finetuned on 50-frame clips at [288×384] resolution. The VAE and text encoder are frozen. Training and preprocessing details, including the full dataset list and mixture weights, are provided in the appendix.

4.2 Camera-Controlled Generation

We evaluate the unified model on camera-controlled video generation, testing whether camera-ray conditioning can guide visual synthesis while preserving appearance and scene layout across viewpoint changes.

Benchmarks and Metrics.

We evaluate on RealEstate10K, SpatialVID, and DL3DV, covering diverse indoor and outdoor scenes. For each sequence, the context contains the target camera trajectory and either the first RGB frame or the first and last RGB frames. The model then generates the remaining frames from this context, which are evaluated against ground-truth videos using PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS [(56, 70)].

Baselines. We compare quantitatively against Aether [76] and SEVA [72], and qualitatively against DFoT [43] and Wan2.1-FLF-14B in a first-last-frame conditioning setting [49]. These baselines represent unified generation and geometry prediction, diffusion-based novel view synthesis, diffusion-forcing-based video completion, and endpoint-conditioned video generation, respectively. In contrast to the task-specific baselines, UGG has the same multimodal architecture for both camera-controlled generation and geometry prediction.

Evaluation results. Camera-controlled generation results are shown in Table 1. Although not trained solely for novel-view synthesis, UGG remains competitive across camera-conditioned generation benchmarks. It achieves the best PSNR, LPIPS, and SSIM on all three datasets in the one-view setting and on RealEstate10K and SpatialVID in the two-view setting; SEVA remains slightly better on two-view DL3DV. This shows that ray-map conditioning supports accurate camera control, even within a broader RGB-depth-camera completion model. We visualize generated examples in Figure 4. Wan2.1-FLF does not take camera trajectories as input, and therefore struggles with complex camera motion. We find that UGG also preserves dynamic content better; SEVA is primarily designed for static scenes, and DFoT distorts or removes moving humans.

4.3 Camera Pose Estimation

We evaluate camera pose estimation from RGB observations in dense and sparse settings, conditioning on either the full video or only the first and last frames. Camera-ray tokens are denoised and converted back into camera parameters, testing whether camera geometry can be predicted as a missing modality within the same conditional-completion framework.

Benchmarks and Metrics.

We report results on RealEstate10K, Sintel [7], TUM [44], ScanNetV2 [13], and ScanNet++. Following Geo4D [21], we align predicted trajectories to ground truth using Sim(3) Umeyama alignment in the dense setting, and report absolute trajectory error (ATE), relative pose error in translation (RPEt), and in rotation (RPEr). In the sparse setting, we evaluate the relative pose between the first and last frames using translation angular error (tAE) and RPEr. Detailed metric definitions and evaluation protocols are provided in Appendix B.7.

Baselines.

We compare quantitatively against Geo4D [21], Gen3R [18], Aether [76], and RayDiffusion [67]. Geo4D estimates 4D geometry using a generative video prior, while RayDiffusion directly models camera rays through a diffusion denoising process. The geometry-focused baselines are more specialized for pose estimation, whereas UGG predicts camera rays as part of a broader RGB-depth-camera scene representation.

Evaluation results. Table 2 reports camera pose estimation results. In the dense setting, UGG achieves lower ATE and RPEt than the external baselines across all five datasets. For example, ATE is reduced from 0.190 to 0.087 on ScanNet++ compared with Geo4D. Figure 5 visualizes representative trajectories. Our predictions better follow the ground-truth motion, while RayDiffusion and Geo4D produce collapsed paths in challenging examples. In the sparse setting, UGG obtains the lowest tAE and RPEr across all five datasets. These results suggest that the model can infer reasonable relative camera poses from only the first and last RGB frames, despite the ambiguity of sparse observations.

4.4 Depth Prediction

We evaluate depth prediction from RGB observations in the dense and sparse settings described in the previous section. In both cases, depth tokens are initialized from noise and denoised, testing whether the unified conditional-completion model learns a useful geometric posterior over scene depth.

Benchmarks and Metrics. We evaluate on ScanNet++, 7-Scenes [41], KITTI, Sintel, and Bonn. These datasets cover driving scenes, synthetic video, and indoor RGB-D scans. Following Geo4D [21], we apply video-level scale and shift alignment before evaluation, and report absolute relative error between the true and predicted depth (Abs Rel) and threshold accuracy, whether the predicted depth differs from the ground truth by less than a factor of 1.25 (δ<1.25).

Baselines. We compare with Geo4D, ChronoDepth [39], Gen3R, Aether, and Marigold [22]. These baselines include specialized depth and 4D geometry models, as well as a unified model, while ours is trained for RGB-depth-camera completion.

Evaluation results. We report depth prediction results in Table 3. Overall, our model is competitive with specialized depth and 4D geometry baselines across both dense and sparse settings. In the dense setting, it obtains the lowest Abs Rel and highest δ<1.25 on ScanNet++ among the external baselines. In the sparse setting, where only an image pair is available, our model improves over the baselines on both metrics on 4 out of 5 datasets. At the same time, Geo4D remains stronger on Sintel and 7-Scenes metrics for the dense setting, indicating that specialized geometry models may still have advantages in some settings. Figure 6 provides qualitative comparisons. The zoom-in crops show that our predictions preserve sharper object boundaries and more coherent local structures in highlighted regions. This suggests that joint RGB-depth training, together with the generative completion objective, helps the model recover fine-scale depth discontinuities while maintaining globally coherent depth maps.

4.5 Test-Time Search on Geometric Prediction

We evaluate whether test-time search (TTS) improves geometric prediction by sampling multiple RGB-depth-camera completions at inference time. For each input, we generate 16 candidates from different noise initializations and select depth and pose independently using their respective verification scores, as described in Section 3.4.

Tables 3 and 2 show that UGG (TTS) improves sparse depth Abs Rel and pose translation angular error on all five benchmarks. It also improves dense depth Abs Rel and pose ATE on four of five benchmarks. These results demonstrate that the verifier selects lower-error depth and camera translation estimates from the model’s sampled hypotheses using image evidence alone. Figure 7 studies how pose and depth accuracy vary with the number of sampled candidates. Larger search budgets often improve the selected result, but the gains are not uniform because the verification score is only a proxy for ground-truth geometric accuracy.

UGG (TTS Oracle) selects one of the same 16 candidates per input by minimizing ground-truth scale-and-shift-aligned Abs Rel for depth, ATE for dense pose, or tAE for sparse pose. All metrics are reported for the selected candidate. Overall, these results show that inference-time search is a promising benefit of the generative formulation, while leaving room for stronger search criteria and verification.

4.6 Ablation Studies

Setup. We study the effects of joint training, training data, architecture, and camera representation using the smaller Wan2.1-1.3B instead of the final Wan2.2-5B model. Unless otherwise specified, we train on TartanAir and RE10K for 7,500 optimizer steps at batch size 8, with the same optimization settings. Additional details on the ablation setup are provided in Appendix B.4.

Joint training. Learning to generate RGB video also helps the model recover geometry. On KITTI, depth Abs Rel more than doubles when RGB generation is removed from training, rising from 0.152 to 0.322. Geometry supervision also benefits the other tasks: depth prediction improves camera estimation, while pose estimation improves camera-controlled generation by 6.92 dB on RE10K (Table 4a–c). Joint training therefore improves what the model learns about both scene appearance and geometry.

Heterogeneous training data. To test whether these benefits extend to data with incomplete annotations, we add RE10K, which provides RGB and camera annotations but no depth supervision. Adding it to TartanAir training improves depth prediction on both Bonn and KITTI, reducing Abs Rel from 0.239 to 0.135 and from 0.196 to 0.152, respectively (Table 4a). The model can therefore use RGB and camera supervision from additional datasets to improve depth prediction without requiring depth labels from those datasets.

Architecture. MoT allows the modalities to share information through attention while retaining separate processing branches. Compared with a single shared transformer, this design improves camera estimation on both benchmarks and generation on all three. Its effect on depth is less uniform: MoT performs better on KITTI, while the shared transformer is slightly better on Bonn (Table 4a–c).

Camera representation. We compare dense ray maps with global camera tokens in models trained only for pose estimation (Table 4b). Dense ray maps improve both trajectory and rotation accuracy on ScanNetV2 and ScanNet++. They also improve camera-controlled generation, yielding higher PSNR than global camera tokens on all three benchmarks (Table 4c). Aligning the camera representation with image locations is thus useful both for recovering cameras from images and for generating images from cameras. Additional results on history guidance are provided in Appendix B.4.

5 Conclusion

We present a unified generative geometry model for 4D scene understanding, formulating visual generation and geometric prediction as conditional completion over RGB, depth, and camera rays. Through noise patterns over modality tokens, a single model supports camera-controlled generation and geometric prediction under dense and sparse observations, while learning from heterogeneous datasets with varying modality availability. Across diverse datasets, UGG achieves strong video generation, depth prediction, and pose estimation performance, and further improves geometric consistency through test-time search. These results suggest that jointly modeling appearance and geometry with generative models is a promising direction toward more general 4D scene understanding.

Limitations.

Our current model is not uniformly stronger than specialized methods: task-specific NVS models still perform better on pixel-aligned metrics, and specialized geometry models remain stronger on several indoor depth metrics. Future work could address these gaps with better dataset balancing, stronger geometric supervision, and improved depth-camera consistency during training. Our test-time search also relies on RGB reprojection error, which is useful but not uniformly reliable; learned or multimodal consistency scores may provide stronger search criteria. Finally, training at larger scale, higher resolution, and with more diverse data could further improve both visual detail and geometric accuracy.

Acknowledgments and Disclosure of Funding

We thank the Kempner Institute at Harvard University for providing computational resources that supported this work. Ayush Tewari acknowledges the NVIDIA Academic Grant Program.

（参考文献见原文。）

Appendix A Visualizations

Comprehensive visualizations across inference settings are available on our project page, including camera-conditioned generations, camera pose estimation, and depth estimation across datasets.

Appendix B Implementation Details

B.1 Datasets and Preprocessing
